Aliens, Area 51 & the UFO Files

This is the one topic in the archive where the official record is genuinely interesting. Unlike hollow planets, UFOs are a documented administrative fact: there were offices, budgets, files, and a chain of command. The question is not whether the government looked. It is what it found.

Project Blue Book

From 1947 to 1969 the US Air Force investigated unidentified flying objects, from 1952 under the name Project Blue Book, headquartered at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio. When it closed on 17 December 1969, the totals were:

  • 12,618 sightings reported
  • 701 left “unidentified”

Those figures are on the National Archives’ own pages and in the Air Force fact sheet. The closure followed a University of Colorado study — the “Condon Report” — reviewed by the National Academy of Sciences, which concluded that further investigation was not justified. The archives are public.

The crucial word is “unidentified”. It means the report could not be resolved with the data available — not that an extraterrestrial craft was confirmed. Most cases were aircraft, balloons, satellites, weather phenomena, birds, or hoaxes; the residue is thin, old, and often missing its original instrument data.

Roswell, in the record

The story starts with a press release. On 8 July 1947 the Roswell Army Air Field public information office announced the recovery of a “flying disc”. The next day the commanding general of the Eighth Air Force said it was a radar-tracking balloon. The newspaper survived; the correction was less exciting.

In 1994 and 1997 the Air Force published two reports on the incident, and the GAO ran its own records search in 1995. The conclusion, in the Air Force’s words:

“The materials recovered near Roswell were consistent with a balloon device of the type used in a then-classified project.”US Air Force, The Roswell Report; see also the National Archives

The classified project was Mogul — balloon trains carrying microphones to detect Soviet nuclear tests. It explains the strange debris and the secrecy. The “alien bodies” have a separate and rather sad explanation: the reports match anthropomorphic test dummies flown on high-altitude balloon experiments years later, and in some cases airmen killed in actual accidents. The Air Force report notes that events spread over many years have been consolidated in the retelling into two or three days in July 1947.

The GAO found no records of a crashed extraterrestrial craft, including in material that had previously been withheld for security reasons.

The modern cases

Two things changed after 2004.

The Nimitz encounter. On 14 November 2004, two F/A-18s from the USS Nimitz were redirected to investigate radar contacts off San Diego. Pilots reported a white, tic-tac-shaped object with no wings, no exhaust, and motion their systems could not lock. Gun-camera footage was later released and authenticated. It remains unexplained in the sense that no public analysis has closed it — the candidate explanations (instrument artefacts, radar spoofing, a classified drone) each have problems.

The programme. In December 2017 the New York Times revealed the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program, a $22 million Pentagon effort run partly at the request of Senator Harry Reid, and the subsequent official structures: the UAP Task Force, then AARO, the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office.

In June 2021 the Office of the Director of National Intelligence published a preliminary assessment covering 144 reports. It concluded that most could be explained, that 143 remained unexplained for lack of data, and — importantly — that there was no evidence linking them to extraterrestrial technology. AARO’s 2024 historical report goes further, reviewing the whole post-1945 record and finding no verified extraterrestrial artefacts or reverse-engineering programme.

How to hold all of this at once

Three statements are simultaneously true. (1) Some sightings are genuinely unidentified, including ones with military sensor data. (2) The historical record contains no verified extraterrestrial object. (3) Governments do classify things, and have lied about programmes — which is why “the government said so” is not a sufficient answer either.

The honest position is the boring one: unidentified is a status, not a conclusion, and the people doing the identifying are the first to say so.

Where it joins the rest of the archive

  • Ancient astronauts — the same beings relocated to prehistory. See Ancients.
  • Hollow Earth — UFO lore has long placed bases inside the shell. See Hollow Earth.
  • Real conspiracies — MKUltra and the Gulf of Tonkin are the benchmark for what actual secrecy looks like. See Proven Plots.

Project Blue Beam: the conspiracy that explains all the others

Project Blue Beam is the claim that a coalition of governments and NASA intends to use holographic projections, lasers and low-frequency radio to stage a fake alien invasion — or a fake religious second coming — and use the resulting panic to install a single world government.

It was popularised in the 1990s by the Canadian journalist Serge Monast, and it has a structural property that makes it almost impossible to argue with: it predicts a spectacle that has not happened, and it explains the absence of evidence by saying the plan is secret.

Its real function is to pre-empt disconfirmation. If a convincing UFO event occurs, it was Blue Beam. If nothing occurs, the plan is delayed. Every future observation is absorbed. That is the same machine as Last Thursdayism, and the same one the Tartaria story runs — only here the mechanism is a hologram rather than a flood.

Worth noting for honesty: governments have run deception operations and have lied about aircraft and radar many times (see Proven Conspiracies). The reason Blue Beam fails is not that governments are trustworthy. It is that the specific claim — a global holographic projector capable of fooling everyone, kept secret by thousands of people — has no evidence and cannot be falsified.

Secret Societies

This dossier is unusual because the secret society at the centre of the modern myth is fully documented. We know who founded it, when, why, how many members it had, how it was organised, how it was suppressed, and what happened to its archive. Almost none of that survives in the popular version.

The Bavarian Illuminati, 1776–1785

Adam Weishaupt was a 28-year-old professor of canon law at the University of Ingolstadt, a former Jesuit, and a partisan of the radical Enlightenment. On 1 May 1776 he founded a small society with a handful of senior students. They called themselves Perfectibilists; the name Illuminati came later.

The goal, as the University of Munich’s own history puts it, was to build an elite cadre that would eventually occupy the key positions of the state and subvert the authority of the territorial princes — not through revolution, but through education and placement. Britannica summarises the programme as replacing established religion with a cult of reason and overthrowing monarchical government. Members included the astronomer Johann Bode, the writer Friedrich Nicolai, and the philosopher Friedrich Jacobi. At its height the order had roughly 1,400 members — a serious network, and a small one.

It was organised on Jesuit lines, with grades, ciphers and code names; Weishaupt was “Spartacus”. It recruited inside Masonic lodges, which is the origin of the idea that the two are the same organisation.

The suppression

Growth attracted attention. On 22 June 1784 Elector Karl Theodor issued a general edict against unauthorised secret societies; on 2 March 1785 a second edict named the Illuminati and Freemasonry specifically. Weishaupt lost his professorship and fled. Houses were searched, and the order’s papers — internal correspondence, statutes, grade texts, membership lists — were seized and then published.

By 1786 the order was effectively finished. The Bavarian Academy of Sciences’ own history states that it “expired after barely ten years of existence and did not revive during the French Revolution.”

That publication is the twist. The Illuminati were destroyed by transparency, in the 1780s, and the documents have been available to historians ever since. The University of Erfurt now runs a dedicated Illuminati research unit, working through the seized archive.

Where the world-domination story came from

It came from the losers. Ex-members denounced the order, and a French émigré priest, Augustin Barruel, published a conspiracy thesis arguing that the French Revolution had been engineered by Freemasons and Illuminati. The claim was politically useful — it made a systemic upheaval into a plot — and it never needed evidence, because the order’s real papers could be reinterpreted rather than read.

Every later version is a descendant of that move, including the twentieth-century paperbacks and the twenty-first-century videos. The structure is: a real, small, extinct organisation + a real archive nobody checks + an unlimited scope.

Freemasonry, which was never secret

Freemasonry is a fraternal organisation with rituals, not a conspiracy. Its documented history:

  • 1390 — the Regius Poem, the earliest known Masonic manuscript, describing operative stonemasons’ craft rules.
  • 1717 — four London lodges merge to form the first Grand Lodge, the conventional founding of modern speculative Freemasonry.
  • 1738 — the Catholic Church condemns the movement; roughly twenty papal decrees follow over the centuries.
  • Since then — lodges are listed in public directories, halls are on maps, and members appear in every walk of public life, which is the actual reason for the “they’re everywhere” claim.

Masonry is not a religion, though members are asked to believe in a Supreme Being. Its secrecy is ceremonial — passwords and rituals — not informational. A lodge’s existence, address and often its officers are public.

The Eye of Providence

The eye-in-a-triangle on the US one-dollar bill is the most-shared “Illuminati” image in the world. It is not Masonic. It is part of the Great Seal of the United States, designed in 1782 by a committee including Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson and John Adams, and it represents divine providence — a standard Christian emblem of the period. The motto below, annuit coeptis, and the pyramid’s novus ordo seclorum, are Latin tags from Virgil. The seal was adopted nine years before the Illuminati were suppressed and on a different continent.

The test that matters

A secret society that runs the world needs three things: continuity, coordination and capacity. The Illuminati have none. They existed for under a decade, were destroyed by a police action, and their entire internal archive is in a university library being studied by historians who publish what they find.

Meanwhile, the organisations that really do coordinate quietly — corporate boards, party caucuses, defence contractors, intelligence alliances — operate in the open, with names, addresses and annual reports. That is the actual scandal, and it is duller and more consequential than the myth.

Related dossiers

  • Proven Conspiracies — what documented secret coordination looks like.
  • Tartaria — the same “hidden hand rewrote history” structure, applied to buildings.
  • Ancient Astronauts — the same structure, applied to the deep past.

The one that is simply true: Bohemian Grove

Not every “secret society” story is a conspiracy. Bohemian Grove is a real, documented institution: a 2,700-acre private camp in Monte Rio, Sonoma County, California, owned by the Bohemian Club of San Francisco, which was founded in 1872. Every July it hosts a two-week gathering of members and guests — historically including US presidents, cabinet members, Fortune 500 executives and artists.

The camp has a lake, a stage, a 40-foot owl statue (the “Owl Shrine”), and a theatrical opening ceremony called the Cremation of Care. Presidents from both parties have attended. In 2000 the journalist Alex Jones filmed inside without authorisation, and the footage — of the Cremation of Care in particular — became the visual vocabulary for a decade of conspiracy content.

The distinction that matters: the existence of an elite, men-only, off-the-record gathering is not a conspiracy theory. It is a fact, and an uncomfortable one for anyone who thinks influence is evenly distributed. What is not documented is the part the internet adds — that decisions are made there, that it is a shadow government, that the ceremony is anything other than theatre.

The archive treats this as the useful control case. Bohemian Grove shows what a real secret looks like: a private club that keeps the press out, whose members deny nothing because nothing needs denying. The Tartaria story, by contrast, needs the evidence destroyed to survive. Both are about power; only one has photographs, deeds and a tax record.

Noah, Gilgamesh & the Great Flood

The oldest version we have

In 1872, George Smith of the British Museum read a paper to the Society of Biblical Archaeology on a tablet from Nineveh. It was Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, and it contained a flood story so close to Genesis that the room reportedly reacted with astonishment.

The Mesopotamian flood tradition survives in several versions:

  • Gilgamesh, Tablet XI (Standard Babylonian, first millennium BC, from older material) — Utnapishtim is warned, builds a cube-shaped boat, loads family and animals, and the gods themselves are frightened by the flood.
  • Atrahasis (c. 1650 BC) — the flood is a divine response to overpopulation and noise; the hero is Atrahasis.
  • Eridu Genesis (Sumerian) — creation, antediluvian life, and flood in one frame.

Scholarship is close to unanimous that there is a literary relationship between these and Genesis. The argument is about the direction and degree of influence. A 2021 literary analysis in Studia Antiqua notes that Genesis shares its three-part structure with Atrahasis and Eridu Genesis, and many of its details with Gilgamesh XI.

And it is not only Mesopotamia

Flood narratives appear in Hindu, Buddhist, Jewish, Islamic, Greek and Chinese traditions and in cultures from Japan to the Americas — usually as a local landscape catastrophe with a moral or cosmic frame. A 2025 review in Evolution: Education and Outreach notes the pattern and the obvious explanation: people live near water, and water destroys settlements.

The Black Sea hypothesis

The most famous attempt to give Noah a date and a place was published by William Ryan and Walter Pitman in 1997. The claim: the Black Sea was a freshwater lake about 110 m below modern level; around 7,500 years ago rising Mediterranean water broke through the Bosphorus and flooded the surrounding lowlands catastrophically, displacing farmers and seeding flood memories across the region.

It was a beautiful hypothesis and it does not survive the evidence. Subsequent coring, seismic survey and fossil work in the Marmara Sea gateway found the opposite: persistent outflow from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean, with the lake level high enough to spill southward across the Bosphorus sill between roughly 12,300 and 9,500 years ago. A 2022 synthesis in Earth-Science Reviews is blunt in its title: the evidence “still contradicts the Noah’s Flood Hypothesis”.

Even the creationist literature notes the collapse — the Black Sea flood “may evaporate completely”, as Creation Ministries put it in 2007, while still rejecting mainstream geology.

What geologists think actually happened

The best-supported reading is not one global event but many local ones. Brückner and Engel’s 2019 chapter surveys four candidate scenarios — flooding of the Persian Gulf after the last glacial lowstand, a cosmic impact, the Black Sea refill, and Mesopotamian mega-floods — and argues for the last: repeated catastrophic river floods in the Tigris–Euphrates system that left sediment imprints around ancient tells such as Ur and Uruk.

That would make the biblical flood a memory of something real, local, and recurrent — which is exactly how flood stories are made.

Why a global flood fails

  • There is not enough water. All the water in the oceans, ice caps, groundwater and atmosphere combined would raise sea level by roughly 250 feet (about 75 m). Everest is 29,000 feet high. The arithmetic is not close.
  • The deposits are not there. A worldwide flood would leave a single widespread layer with mixed terrestrial and marine fossils. The geological column instead shows ordered, repeating sequences with soils, tracks, reefs and burrows in place.
  • Flood geologists have tested their own model. The National Center for Science Education published a review by a geologist showing that, using flood geologists’ own correlation schemes, their flood deposits end up confined between two non-flood units within a single geological period — which makes the flood geologically invisible, and therefore untestable.
  • The Ark has no site. Decades of expeditions to Ararat have produced wooden fragments of various ages and no structure. The most famous “ark” find, the Durupınar formation, is a natural geological feature.

What the story is really doing

Read as literature rather than geology, Genesis 6–9 is doing something remarkable: it takes a Mesopotamian story in which the gods flood the world because humans are too noisy, and turns it into a story about justice, covenant and a God who regrets. The flood is the same; the theology is inverted. That is a more interesting claim than the water level, and it is the one historians of religion actually argue about.

Unexplained Phenomena

Most of this archive is about claims that failed. This dossier is the opposite: things that happened, were investigated properly, and are still not fully settled. They are the best argument for keeping an open mind — and for noticing that “we don’t know yet” is a normal scientific state, not a supernatural one.

Tunguska, 1908

At about 7:15 a.m. on 30 June 1908, an object entered the atmosphere over the Siberian taiga and exploded in the air. Eyewitnesses hundreds of kilometres away saw a fireball and felt the blast; seismic stations recorded it; the night skies over Europe were bright enough to read by, because dust had been thrown into the stratosphere.

The first scientific expedition did not arrive until 1927 — the region is that remote. It found a butterfly-shaped area of flattened forest covering about 830 square miles, with millions of trees knocked over radially and no impact crater.

NASA’s 2018 Tunguska workshop, using modern airburst models including ones built for the 2013 Chelyabinsk event, converged on a solution: an energy release of 10–20 megatons at a height of about 10 km, from a stony asteroid roughly 50–80 m across that was vaporised before it reached the ground. Recurrence: an object of that size every few thousand years.

That is close to a complete explanation. What remains open is the fine detail — the exact orbit, the fragmentation sequence, and whether any solid remnant survived.

Dyatlov Pass, 1959

Nine experienced Soviet mountaineers died in the northern Urals in February 1959. Their tent was found cut open from the inside; they had fled into −30 °C darkness partly clothed; several had severe internal injuries without matching external wounds; one was missing her tongue and eyes. The Soviet investigation closed with “a compelling natural force”.

In 2021, a team publishing in Communications Earth & Environment built a physical model of a slab avalanche released by wind-loaded snow above the tent. Their key insight: the hikers had cut a ledge into the slope to pitch the tent, and katabatic winds then deposited snow on the slab above it. Their simulation gives release 7.5 to 13.5 hours after the cut — matching the forensic time of death — and shows that even a small slab can cause the observed chest and skull injuries.

It is the best-supported explanation and not a proof. The injuries remain unusual, and the case is still argued.

The Voynich manuscript

A 240-page codex, illustrated with plants that match no known species, astronomical diagrams, and bathing figures, written in an alphabet that appears nowhere else. It has resisted every cryptographer who has tried it, including some very good ones.

In 2009 the parchment was radiocarbon-dated by the University of Arizona: 1404–1438, with 95% confidence. That rules out the wilder modern-forgery theories and puts it in the early Renaissance. The text itself may still be later than the parchment.

Three families of explanation compete: a genuine natural language or cipher; an invented script encoding a real language; and meaningless text produced to look valuable (the “hoax” hypothesis). No proposal has achieved general acceptance — which makes this the cleanest unsolved puzzle in the archive.

The Hessdalen lights

Since at least the 19th century, residents of a valley in central Norway have reported unexplained lights: bright, hovering, sometimes lasting minutes. It is one of the few cases where the phenomenon was studied with permanent instrumentation — cameras, spectrometers and radar, run by Italian and Norwegian teams from 1998, partly by people who had worked on SETI.

The 2010 Acta Astronautica paper concluded that the data indicate “a combustion process driven by an unknown power source” — a real, measured, unidentified phenomenon. Later work has proposed plasma and geological batteries; one 2021 paper even suggested wormholes, which shows how far the speculation runs when the data are thin. It remains genuinely open, and genuinely small.

Spontaneous human combustion

The classic case: a body reduced to ash, the room barely scorched, furniture intact. Victorian explanations invoked alcohol-soaked bodies, which fails on chemistry.

The modern forensic answer is the wick effect: clothing soaks up melted body fat and acts as a candle wick, producing a slow, localised, very hot smoulder that can consume a body while leaving surroundings intact. Experiments reproduce the pattern. The remaining mystery is only the ignition source — a dropped cigarette, a spark — which the fire itself destroys.

That is not “solved by scepticism”. It is solved by experiment, and it is a good model for how the rest of this archive should be read.

The pattern to notice

Every case on this page has the same anatomy: a real event, documented by professionals, with a leading hypothesis that explains most of the data and a residue that does not quite fit. The residue is where the mystery lives — and it is almost always smaller than the legend says.

Compare that with the claims elsewhere in this archive, which have no measurements to argue about at all.

Urban Legends & Creepypasta

“Creepypasta” is a portmanteau of “copy-paste”: short horror stories, usually written as fake first-person accounts, designed to be copied across forums intact. Folklorists treat them as a genuine contemporary form — the digital descendant of the campfire story — and they have produced at least one figure that escaped the internet entirely.

Slender Man: a documented birth

On 10 June 2009, a comedy forum called Something Awful ran a thread asking users to create paranormal images in Photoshop. A contributor posting as “Victor Surge” — the artist Eric Knudsen — uploaded two fake photographs purporting to be from the 1980s: children in a playground, and behind them a tall, faceless figure in a dark suit.

He attached fragments of text implying that fourteen children and a photographer had vanished. The BBC’s account is precise about the effect: the fragments, the missing details and the deliberate incompleteness are what made it spread. A tidier story would have died in the thread.

What followed is the best-documented case of collaborative folklore in the internet era. Thousands of people added drawings, videos and stories; the YouTube series Marble Hornets built a narrative around him; folklorist Jeff Tolbert has described the process as an “open-sourcing of storytelling”. The academic literature followed — a 2016 article in Children’s Literature and a 2018 university-press collection, Slender Man Is Coming, both treat creepypasta as digital legendry with the same rules as oral tradition: repetition with variation, claimed realism, and an unresolved frame.

The stabbing

On 31 May 2014, in Waukesha, Wisconsin, three twelve-year-old girls went into woods on a “birdwatching” trip. One was stabbed nineteen times and left for dead; she crawled to a road and survived. The other two were arrested and charged. They told investigators they had acted to prove themselves to Slender Man and to become his servants.

This is the case that forces a serious point. Fiction is not harmless because it is fiction, and the internet is not a separate world. But the causal story is not “the story made them do it” — it is that a shared fantasy, an untreated mental-health crisis, and two children with no adult between them and the idea produced a crime. Snopes and the BBC both cover the trial and the aftermath; the victim recovered and the attackers were committed to psychiatric care.

Momo: a hoax studied like a disease

Between 2018 and 2019, parents across several countries were warned that a “Momo challenge” was appearing inside children’s videos — a gaunt figure with black hair and a wide mouth, ordering children to self-harm.

It was not real. The image was a photograph of a sculpture by a Japanese artist, taken out of context; there was no evidence of any child being harmed; and the alarm was amplified overwhelmingly by adults, not children. A 2021 paper in the Journal for the Academic Study of Religion analyses it as “a major online demonic hoax” — a legend whose engine was adult anxiety about screens, not the screens themselves.

The pattern repeats: a striking image, a plausible threat to children, a warning shared by people who care, and a news cycle that cannot be un-shared. It is the same mechanism as the cryptid and mystery dossiers, with a moral panic attached.

Crop circles: the confession

In September 1991 two Englishmen, Doug Bower and Dave Chorley, told the press they had been making crop circles since the late 1970s using a plank, a rope and a wire sight. The New York Times reported it under the headline “2 ‘Jovial Con Men’ Demystify Those Crop Circles in Britain”.

The confession did not end crop circles — the form continued and grew more elaborate — but it converted the question from “what makes them?” to “who makes them, and why do we want them to be something else?” The image on this page is of a known fake, which is the honest illustration for the topic.

Why horror stories are the perfect conspiracy format

  • Unresolved by design. A good creepypasta leaves one detail missing. That gap is where belief enters.
  • First person, no author. The text claims to be testimony, and the author is a username.
  • Free to alter. Copy-paste means every retelling is also an edit, like oral tradition.
  • Unfalsifiable by construction. “The footage was destroyed” is a plot point, not an excuse.

Set those four next to the claims in the rest of this archive. The hollow Earth, the ice wall and the Tartarian empire all share the same four properties — which is precisely why they are so easy to believe, and why this site insists on the boring work of finding sources.

Polybius: the arcade cabinet that never was

The story: in 1981 a black arcade cabinet appeared in Portland, Oregon arcades. The game — supposedly called Polybius, after the Greek historian — was a vector-graphics puzzle that caused amnesia, night terrors and hallucinations in players. Men in black suits were seen collecting data from the machines, and then the cabinets vanished.

It is one of the most durable pieces of internet folklore, and it has almost no documentary basis. There are no photographs of a cabinet, no arcade operator's log, no manufacturer records, no contemporary newspaper report, and no player who can be identified. The earliest known appearance of the story is a coinop.org entry written around 2000 — two decades after the alleged events.

That gap is the tell. A real cabinet in public arcades for weeks would have left a trace: a service manual, a tax record, a photograph in a local paper, an op's route sheet. The legend instead carries the fingerprints of its own era — the “men in black” motif from 1980s UFO lore, the memory-damage motif from later creepypasta, the sinister-German-name motif from a very specific strand of internet humour.

It is a great story, and it is almost certainly a story. See the deep web file for the same dynamics applied to a real-but-duller phenomenon.

Curses

The mummy's curse, as a cohort study

When Howard Carter opened Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922, the excavation's sponsor — George Herbert, fifth Earl of Carnarvon — died five months later, aged 57. The cause was a mosquito bite on the cheek that became infected after he cut it shaving, then pneumonia and multi-organ failure. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, a convinced spiritualist, suggested “an evil elemental”. The press had its story.

Fiction supplied the best line: Marie Corelli's “death comes on wings to he who enters the tomb of a pharaoh”, which was quickly reported as an inscription over the tomb door. No such inscription has ever been found, and as Egyptologist Joyce Tyldesley points out, in a country where perhaps 5% of people could read, a written warning would have been a poor deterrent to robbers.

Everything else about the story has the same texture. The lights allegedly going out across Cairo at the moment of death: power cuts were routine. Carnarvon's dog howling and dying at the same instant: the dog died four hours later, and there is a time zone.

And then somebody actually tested it. In 2002, the epidemiologist Mark R. Nelson published a historical cohort study in the British Medical Journal. He identified the 44 Westerners Carter recorded as present during the relevant period, split them into 25 who were “exposed” (entered the long-sealed area) and the rest, and tracked their obituaries.

“In the 25 people exposed to the curse the mean age at death was 70 years … compared with 75 in those not exposed. … There was no significant association between exposure to the mummy's curse and survival.”Nelson, BMJ, 2002

Howard Carter himself lived sixteen more years and died at 64. Lady Evelyn Herbert, present at the first clandestine entry into the burial chamber, died in 1980.

Amityville: a real murder, then a product

The house at 112 Ocean Avenue is real and so is the tragedy: in November 1974, Ronald DeFeo Jr killed six members of his family there. That much is a matter of court record. Everything after it is a different kind of document.

In 1977 the Lutz family, who had bought the house, left after 28 days and described a haunting: voices, green slime, levitation, a demonic presence. A book followed, then a film, then a franchise.

The case fell apart in the ordinary way — in litigation. The Society for Psychical Research's encyclopaedia entry records that a New York judge remarked the bestselling book appeared to be largely a work of fiction shaped by the family lawyer's suggestions, and that the participants' accounts changed under oath. The SPR — hardly a body hostile to the paranormal — files the case as a hoax.

What survives is not evidence of a haunting. It is evidence of a business model: a real crime, a marketable story, and a house whose address is now worth more than the book.

The Hope Diamond

The Smithsonian, which owns it, is refreshingly direct on its own website: “Is the Hope Diamond cursed? Of course not!” The curse is a twentieth-century invention, and the museum can date its arrival — a Washington Post article of 19 January 1908, “Remarkable Jewel a Hoodoo — Hope Diamond Has Brought Trouble to All Who Have Owned It”.

The gem's actual history involves the French crown jewels, a sale during the Revolution, and a series of owners including a Washington socialite, Evalyn Walsh McLean. It does not involve a consistent trail of ruin. The Smithsonian notes that the popular list of victims is “wildly inaccurate”, assembled by later writers from a mixture of real misfortune and invented owners.

It is a beautiful object with a documented provenance and a manufactured legend, which makes it the most honest curse in the archive: the institution holding it publishes the debunk on the same page as the object.

How a curse is built

Start with a real tragedy. A death, a murder, a disaster. That is the anchor.

Collect coincidences after the fact. Any death connected to the object, at any distance, at any date. No denominator is ever counted — how many people touched the object and were fine?

Add a sentence nobody wrote. The tomb inscription, the warning, the clause in the will. It will be quoted forever.

Let a reputable person believe it. Conan Doyle was a great writer and a credulous spiritualist; his endorsement travelled further than the correction.

Notice that the third and fourth steps are exactly the mechanism in the urban legend dossier, and that the second step is the base-rate error that makes the Bermuda Triangle work.

Curses that were real

Two kinds of curse have genuine effects, and neither is supernatural. Tomb curses in ancient Egypt were real inscriptions intended to deter robbers — a social technology, not a spell. And “cursed” objects in the modern sense have a documented power: they attract theft, obsession and litigation, which is why so many of them are in museums behind glass.

The 27 Club: a curse with a denominator

Brian Jones, Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, Jim Morrison, Kurt Cobain and Amy Winehouse all died at 27. The pattern is striking, frequently called a curse, and dissolves the moment you ask how many musicians reach 27 and survive it.

Three things are happening at once. First, young adulthood is when accidental and substance-related deaths peak for this population, so a cluster around the late twenties is not surprising — it is roughly where you would expect the deaths to be. Second, the club is selected after the fact: nobody counts the hundreds of musicians who died at 26 or 28, or who lived to 80. Third, fame concentrates the sample: we remember the famous ones, and famous young musicians are exactly the people with the lifestyle risks.

Statistical treatments of the question have generally found no excess of deaths at 27 once the base rate is accounted for — the “club” is a list, not a distribution. Compare the Bermuda Triangle, where the same denominator problem produces the same kind of legend.

It is worth adding that the individual tragedies are real, and that several of these deaths were preventable in ways that had nothing to do with numerology — addiction, untreated mental illness, exploitative management. The curse is the least interesting true thing about them.

Prophecies

This dossier is about a testable human phenomenon rather than a claimed event. Failed prophecy is one of the best-studied situations in the social science of belief, and the results are more surprising than “people are gullible”.

2012 and the Mayan calendar

In 2012 a global audience waited for the end of a 5,126-year cycle in the Maya Long Count, which completed on 21 December. The claim was that the Maya had predicted an apocalypse. They had predicted a cycle ending — the equivalent of a calendar rolling over to a new page.

The BBC’s reporting at the time noted the mundane reality and the commercial one: the date generated tourism, documentaries and merchandise across Mexico and Guatemala, and the Maya themselves were largely not impressed. There was no prophecy of destruction in the inscriptions, and the date was never a countdown to anything.

The non-event is instructive because of how it dissolved: not with a refutation, but with a shift. The date became “a change in consciousness”, “the beginning of a new era”, “a shift in vibration”. The prediction was unfalsifiable in the end because it had been restated as a mood.

The Millerites and the Great Disappointment

William Miller, a Baptist preacher in upstate New York, calculated from the book of Daniel that Christ would return around 1843–44. He gave a specific date in October 1844. Tens of thousands of followers — estimates around 50,000 — prepared. Some gave away property.

The date passed. The event is known as the Great Disappointment, and it is the founding case study of millennial failure. Miller himself took the unusual step of admitting error: “I confess my error and acknowledge my disappointment.”

Most of his followers did not simply go home. A minority produced the “shut door” explanation — the date was right, but the event was spiritual rather than visible — and out of the wreckage came the Adventist movement, which is now a global religion. This is the key structural fact: a failed prophecy can be the birth certificate of a durable institution.

Festinger, and the honest caveat

In 1956 Leon Festinger, Henry Riecken and Stanley Schachter published When Prophecy Fails, based on a small group led by a woman they called “Mrs Keech”, who believed a flood would arrive and a flying saucer would rescue the faithful. When neither came, the group did not disband: the leader announced that their light had saved the world, and members began proselytising.

The book gave us cognitive dissonance: when a belief collides with evidence, people often reduce the discomfort by recruiting others to the belief rather than abandoning it. That idea became one of the most influential in psychology.

The caveat, from the later scholarship

A 2025 paper by Thomas Kelly argues that Festinger’s account misrepresented the group’s behaviour before and after the prediction, and that the group actually did disband soon afterwards. Later work by Lorne Dawson and others reaches similar conclusions. The theory of cognitive dissonance survived; the founding case study is weaker than the textbook version.

That is how intellectual honesty is supposed to look, and it is worth putting next to the material in the rest of this archive: the famous study of failed prophecy is itself partly a case of a story being better than its evidence.

Nostradamus, and the technique of vagueness

Michel de Nostredame published his Les Propheties in 1555 as quatrains — four-line poems in deliberately obscure French, Latin and Provençal, with no dates and no named subjects. That is not a flaw in the design; it is the design.

A text with no fixed referent can be matched to any event after the fact. Every generation finds its own catastrophe in the same 942 quatrains, and every match requires knowing the event first. The technical name for the failure is retrofitting, and the reason it feels persuasive is that the reader supplies the specificity the text lacks.

The three-part anatomy

1. A date. Specific enough to be exciting, vague enough to be survivable.

2. A total claim. It affects everyone, not just believers — which is why it recruits.

3. A ready explanation. The date was symbolic / the event was spiritual / the prayer averted it. Prepared in advance or invented that week.

When all three are present, the prediction cannot lose. When the third is missing — as with Miller — you get an honest admission and a schism.

What actually ends the world

For the record, and without prophecy: the Sun's evolution, an impact event, and the eventual loss of a habitable atmosphere are the well-studied long-term hazards. The one with a date is the Sun's brightening, on a timescale of about a billion years. Nothing in the archive predicts it, and nothing needs to.

Mass Hysteria

Mass psychogenic illness — the older term is mass hysteria — is a real, medically recognised phenomenon: genuine physical symptoms, spreading through a group, with no toxic or infectious cause. It is not faking. The symptoms are involuntary and the distress is real. What spreads is the form the distress takes.

Strasbourg, 1518

In July 1518 a woman in Strasbourg, known as Frau Troffea, began dancing in the street and did not stop. Within a week others had joined; within a month, according to the chronicles, some 400 people were dancing. Some collapsed; some died of exhaustion, stroke or heart attack.

The response of the authorities is the detail that makes the case so valuable. They did not treat it as a poisoning or a plague. They concluded it was “hot blood”, and prescribed more dancing — hiring musicians and clearing a stage, in the belief that the afflicted must dance it out. The intervention made it worse.

John Waller, who has written the standard history, notes that the outbreak is documented independently by scores of physicians, chroniclers, monks and priests, and that for 1518 the municipal orders themselves survive. There is no serious doubt it happened.

The favoured chemical explanation — ergot poisoning from mouldy rye — is weak, as Waller and others argue: ergot causes convulsions and gangrene, not endurance dancing, and it would not explain the geographical spread across the Rhineland in 1374 or the localised pattern in 1518.

The Tanganyika laughter epidemic, 1962

In a mission school in what is now Tanzania, three girls began laughing and could not stop. The laughter spread to classmates, then to other schools and villages; around a thousand people were affected over months, and schools closed.

It was not a joke and not a virus. The standard analysis — including a 2007 paper in Humor — classifies it as a motor-variant outbreak of mass psychogenic illness: laughter as the symptom, in a population under real stress, at a moment of social change. The popular retellings exaggerate the laughter and drop the distress.

Salem, 1692

The Salem witch trials began with afflicted young women — convulsions, contortions, reports of invisible tormentors — and ended with nineteen executions and one man pressed to death. It is the classic case of a psychogenic outbreak fused with a social mechanism: once the symptoms were interpreted as witchcraft, accusation became a way to settle property disputes and local grudges.

The lesson historians draw is not “they were stupid”. It is that a community under stress, with an explanatory framework that names a culprit, will find the culprit. Change the framework and the same symptoms produce a different history.

The features that keep recurring
  • A real stressor — famine, war, epidemic, dispossession, social change.
  • A visible first case, often someone of low status, whose symptoms are dramatic.
  • A shared explanatory frame — demons, witches, poison, radiation, a “challenge”.
  • Transmission by attention, not contact: sight, rumour, and in the modern era, the screen.
  • Symptoms that resolve when the group is separated and the frame is changed.

Those five features are also a good description of how a creepypasta panic spreads, and of why the UAP file keeps producing clusters of reports after publicity.

Why the phrase is out of favour

“Mass hysteria” carries an implication of female weakness that was built into 19th-century medicine — the whole diagnosis of “hysteria” was, literally, a theory about the womb. Modern literature prefers mass psychogenic illness, and the point is not semantic: the old framing blamed the sufferers, and the modern one asks what the group was under.

The uncomfortable modern cases

Mass psychogenic illness is not historical. Documented outbreaks include factory fume scares, school illness clusters, and the wave of reported “Havana syndrome” symptoms among diplomats — where the debate is precisely whether there is a physical cause or a social one, and where the answer remains contested.

That last case is why the topic belongs in this archive: it is an active scientific argument, not a closed file. And it shows that labelling something “hysteria” is itself a claim that needs evidence — sometimes symptoms are environmental, and dismissing them has its own body count.

The Mandela Effect

The name

The phenomenon is named after a mistake. Fiona Broome, a paranormal researcher, discovered that she and others shared a clear memory of Nelson Mandela dying in prison in the 1980s — a memory of an event that did not happen. Mandela was released in 1990, became president in 1994, and died in 2013.

She gave the pattern a name, and the name stuck: collective false memories of events that did not occur, or of details that were never there.

The standard examples

They are almost all cultural rather than political, which is itself a clue:

  • “Luke, I am your father.” The line in The Empire Strikes Back is “No, I am your father.”
  • The Monopoly man's monocle. He does not wear one.
  • The Berenstain Bears. Readers remember “Berenstein” — a spelling that would fit a common surname pattern better than the actual one.
  • Location errors. A film line, a logo, the position of a country on a map, the colour of a character's clothing.

Britannica's entry lists these and notes the pattern: the errors are near-misses, not random. They are what memory produces when it reconstructs a familiar thing from a schema instead of retrieving it exactly.

What psychologists say is happening

  • False memory. Memory is reconstructive, not a recording. Recalling an event rebuilds it, and rebuilding can introduce errors that feel as vivid as the original.
  • Confabulation. When a detail is missing, the mind fills it in smoothly and does not flag the fill.
  • Source confusion. You remember reading the joke, or seeing a parody, and later file it as the original — a documented effect that social media accelerates enormously.
  • Schema theory. The Monopoly man “should” have a monocle, because a 1930s capitalist caricature does. The schema overwrites the image.
  • Suggestibility. Once a claim circulates (“it was Berenstein”), people check their memory against the claim rather than the object, and confidence rises.
Why the alternative is not a test

The popular explanation — that we have slipped between parallel timelines, or that history was edited — has a structural problem: it predicts nothing. There is no experiment that could show the timeline changed, because the only evidence offered is the memory that is already in question.

Compare it with how a testable claim behaves. If a logo changed, the printing plates, the trademark filings, the original film negatives and millions of physical objects would all have to change together — and they are held in archives, patent offices and museum stores that do not share a memory. This is exactly the test the Tartaria dossier applies to buildings, and the proven conspiracies dossier applies to documents.

The serious version of the question

Strip out the timelines and something important remains: human memory is far less reliable than courts, schools and eyewitnesses assume. That is a live and consequential research field — mistaken identification in criminal cases, the fragility of childhood recollection, and the ease with which a confident witness can be wrong.

The Mandela Effect is the internet's folk demonstration of that finding. The joke is that people reach for parallel universes; the finding is that a shared, confident, detailed memory can be simply false — and that this is normal.

The archive's use for it

Because it explains a mechanism that runs through every other dossier: cryptid sightings, mystery reports, and creepypasta all depend on witnesses who are sincere and wrong. Understanding that is not cynicism about people. It is the beginning of good evidence.

Deep Web & Dark Web

The three layers, properly defined

The Congressional Research Service’s explainer is the cleanest source, and it is worth quoting rather than paraphrasing:

  • Surface web — content that is indexed and reachable through ordinary search engines.
  • Deep web — content that is not indexed: corporate intranets, university portals, commercial databases, webmail, anything behind authentication or a form. Germany’s federal cyber-security agency puts it at roughly 90% of the web.
  • Dark web — the part of the deep web that is intentionally concealed, reached through overlay networks such as Tor or I2P.

Two corrections follow immediately. First, the deep web is not sinister — your bank statement and your inbox are in it. Second, the dark web is not a single website or a directory; it is a protocol layer. “The dark web has 90% of the internet” is a category error that appears in almost every video on the subject.

How Tor works, in one paragraph

Tor — The Onion Router — sends traffic through three volunteer-operated relays and encrypts it in layers, one per hop, so that no single relay knows both who you are and what you asked for. It is free, open source, and run by a US non-profit. Its documented users include journalists, dissidents under censorship, human-rights organisations, whistleblowers, law enforcement, and criminals — a list that appears in essentially every official description, because all of it is true at once.

What actually happened on the dark web

The history is a sequence of takedowns, and the lesson of each is that anonymity is hard and operational mistakes are ordinary.

  • Silk Road — the best-known marketplace, shut down in 2013; its operator was identified partly through conventional investigative work and his own digital trail.
  • AlphaBay and Hansa — taken down in 2017 in a coordinated operation in which one marketplace was secretly run by police for weeks after the arrest.
  • Child-abuse networks — repeatedly broken by exploiting the infrastructure rather than the encryption: hosting errors, payment trails, and compromised servers.

The pattern is consistent: encryption holds, people leak. That is also why the “hidden website” genre in this archive is less interesting than it looks.

The legitimate hidden web — a directory

This is the useful part. Vast amounts of genuine research sit in the deep web because it is unindexed, not because it is secret. Everything below is legal, free or institutional, and reachable with an ordinary browser.

  • FOIA reading rooms — the CIA, FBI, NSA and State Department all publish declassified document libraries. This is where the proven conspiracies dossiers come from.
  • National Archives catalogues — US NARA, the UK National Archives, Library of Congress, and the Bundesarchiv; millions of records, much of it unindexed by Google.
  • The Internet Archive — the Wayback Machine plus texts, audio and software; indispensable for checking what a page said in 2009.
  • Academic repositories — arXiv, PubMed Central, CORE, DOAJ, and university repositories (the Canterbury and BYU papers cited in this archive came from exactly this layer).
  • Museum and library digital collections — the British Museum, the Met, the Rijksmuseum, the Library of Congress map division, Wikimedia Commons (source of every image on this site).
  • Court and inquiry records — PACER in the US, the UK inquiry archives, the Church Committee reports, the 9/11 Commission files.
  • Standards and patent databases — Google Patents, Espacenet, the USPTO; where “suppressed technology” claims can actually be checked.
A note on what this page will not do

There are no onion addresses here, and no directory of marketplaces. That is not squeamishness: the marketplaces are illegal, frequently scams, and the “link lists” that circulate are the main vector for malware. If you want to understand the dark web, the CRS report and the Tor Project’s own documentation will teach you more in twenty minutes than any list of links.

Why the myth persists

Because the true version is anticlimactic. “Most of the web is unindexed” is a database fact; “there is a secret internet of forbidden knowledge” is a story. The same gap between a technical truth and a good narrative runs through every page in this archive — the larger globe, the ice wall, Tartaria.

The Dead Internet Theory

Where it came from

The idea circulated on the imageboard-adjacent forum Agora Road's Macintosh Cafe from around 2016, and was given its canonical form in a 2021 post usually attributed to a user calling himself IlluminatiPirate, titled “The Dead Internet Theory”.

The essay's argument, in brief: the internet stopped being a place where humans talk to each other sometime around 2016–2017; what remains is algorithmic curation, bot traffic and, increasingly, machine-generated text and images, all optimised to farm attention and advertising. The human web, on this account, is a small residue inside a much larger automated one.

It is a conspiracy theory in form, but an unusual one — it arrives with a real phenomenon attached.

What is actually measured

Bots are a large share of traffic. Thales's Bad Bot Report (formerly Imperva) has measured automated traffic at roughly half of all internet traffic in recent years, with “bad bots” — scraping, credential stuffing, scalping, fraud — a substantial and rising fraction of that. This is industry telemetry rather than independent science, but it is consistent year after year and the methodology is published.

AI-generated content is a large and growing share of text. Studies of web text have found that a substantial portion of newly published pages carry signs of machine generation, and the proportion has risen sharply since 2022. Search engines and social platforms have responded with detection heuristics that are, by their own admission, unreliable.

Platforms are full of automated accounts. Independent investigations have repeatedly found large networks of inauthentic accounts — coordinated political messaging, engagement farming, spam — on every major platform.

So: bots are everywhere, machine text is everywhere, and much of what you scroll past was not written by a person who exists. That much is documented.

Where the strong version fails

“Most of the internet” is not the same as “most of what you read”. Bot traffic counts include search engine crawlers, monitoring pings, API calls, and every automated request that never appears on a page a human sees. A majority of requests being automated is entirely compatible with a majority of reading being human.

The theory is unfalsifiable as usually stated. If real humans are the residue, any evidence of real humans — this page, your comment, a group chat — is dismissed as the simulation working correctly. That is the same structural problem as the Mandela Effect's timelines.

The dates do not work. The web was never a pristine human commons: spam, link farms, SEO mills, click farms and content farms are older than the theory. 2016 is when the theory's authors noticed, not when the change happened.

Why it spreads anyway

Because the experience behind it is real and widely shared. Feeds feel repetitive and synthetic. Search results return pages written to rank rather than to inform. Comment sections look like a language model warming up. The theory offers a total explanation for a genuine, ambient alienation — and, like all good conspiracy theories, it converts an unpleasant structural fact into a single hidden intention.

That is the same move as Tartaria, which turns “I don't recognise this architectural style” into “a wiped civilisation”, and the same move as the deep web file, which turns “there is unindexed content” into “a hidden market of horrors”.

What the honest version sounds like

Not “the internet is dead”, but: a growing share of what you encounter online was not produced by a person, was produced by a person paid to game a ranking system, or was produced by a person as raw material for an algorithm rather than for you.

That claim is defensible, checkable, and grim enough. It also has a practical consequence: the value of a source that names its author, shows its evidence and links its primary material goes up, not down. Which is the entire premise of this archive.

Many Worlds

Everett, 1957

Hugh Everett III submitted his PhD thesis at Princeton in 1957, proposing what he called the relative state formulation of quantum mechanics. A shortened version appeared in Reviews of Modern Physics. It is the origin of what everyone now calls the many-worlds interpretation.

The problem Everett was addressing is real and still unsolved. Quantum mechanics describes a system with a wavefunction that evolves smoothly and deterministically; measurements, however, appear to return one definite outcome out of many possibilities. The standard textbook (“Copenhagen”) response is to say that the wavefunction collapses on measurement — while leaving it vague what counts as a measurement.

Everett's move: remove the collapse. The wavefunction never collapses. It keeps evolving, and the appearance of a single outcome is what it looks like from inside one branch of an increasingly entangled whole.

What “branching” means — and does not

The popular version says every decision splits reality, so there is a world where you took the other job. That is a distortion in two ways.

It is about measurement outcomes, not choices. Branching, if it happens, happens when quantum superpositions interact with an environment in a way that spreads entanglement — decoherence. A mind deciding between two jobs is not a quantum measurement in any useful sense; it is a hot, wet, decoherent system.

It is not a free lunch for storytelling. The branches are not accessible. There is no travel, no communication, no evidence from “the other side”. Once a branch has decohered, its internal physics is sealed off from ours for all practical purposes.

The technical machinery is decoherence, developed from the 1970s onward by Zeh, Zurek and others: interactions with the environment suppress interference between alternatives so rapidly that macroscopic superpositions become unobservable. Many-worlds reads that suppression as branching. Copenhagen reads it as the appearance of collapse. Both describe the same mathematics.

The honest status

Many-worlds is not a conspiracy theory, not a hoax, and not fringe. It is one of several live interpretations, taught in physics departments, defended by serious physicists (DeWitt, Deutsch, Wallace, Carroll) and criticised by others (Penrose, and a long line of collapse-theory proponents).

Its weakness is the same as every interpretation's: no experiment currently distinguishes it from its rivals. If two frameworks make identical predictions for every measurement, the difference between them is metaphysics — which is not an insult, but it is not evidence either.

Why it belongs in this archive

Because it is the test case for the archive's whole method. The same story — “everything that can happen does happen, in another world” — appears here in three forms:

  • The physics (Everett): a precise, austere, mathematics-first proposal about entanglement.
  • The popularisation: branching universes where you are rich, famous, and married to someone else. Not physics; a metaphor with the maths removed.
  • The crossover: quantum immortality, “the mandela effect is a timeline jump”, “manifestation uses quantum branches”. These are not interpretations of quantum mechanics. They are false-memory folklore with a physics vocabulary attached to make them feel rigorous.

The tell is always the same: real physics states what would have to be measured. The crossover version states only what would be nice.

The human footnote

Everett left physics soon after, worked on military modelling, and died in 1982 at 51. His daughter's suicide note reportedly said she was going to join him in another universe, and his son — Mark Oliver Everett, of the band Eels — made a documentary, Parallel Worlds, Parallel Lives, about meeting the physicists who took his father seriously long after his father had given up on them.

That is the archive's recurring theme in its most sympathetic form: an idea that was ridiculed, then absorbed; the cost to the person who had it; and the long gap between the two.

The Electromagnetic Soul

The claim, as it circulates

The version you meet online — on Reddit threads, in self-published books, in YouTube essays — goes roughly: consciousness is not produced by tissue but is a pattern of electromagnetic energy; the brain is an antenna or a hard drive; when the body dies, the pattern persists in some form because energy is conserved.

It is presented as a scientific update on the soul: not a religious assertion, but an inference from physics. That framing is the thing worth examining, because every step of it is doing something different from what it appears to do.

What is true: the brain has electromagnetic fields

This part is solid, measurable, and clinically routine.

EEG records voltage differences at the scalp, in the range of microvolts, produced by the summed activity of large populations of neurons. MEG (magnetoencephalography) records the magnetic fields those currents generate — on the order of femtotesla to hundreds of femtotesla, which is why it needs a magnetically shielded room and superconducting detectors.

These signals are not noise. They carry real information: sleep stages, seizure onset, evoked responses to stimuli, the timing of cognitive processes. Researchers can decode aspects of what a person is perceiving or imagining from them. Brain stimulation with magnetic fields (TMS) can disrupt or enhance specific functions, which is causal evidence that the fields matter.

So “the brain is electromagnetic” is not wrong. It is just not the claim.

Where the argument breaks

1. Correlation is not constitution. The fields are produced by neural activity. The claim needs them to be the mind. Nothing in the measurements supports that direction of explanation, and the physics of the fields themselves — their strength, their range, their dependence on blood flow and ion gradients — is exactly what you would expect from a by-product of tissue.

2. The fields are extraordinarily weak and short-range. A brain's magnetic field is many orders of magnitude weaker than the Earth's, and falls off within centimetres. There is no known mechanism by which such a field could persist, cohere, or carry information after the tissue that maintained it stops metabolising.

3. Energy conservation does not preserve patterns. “Energy cannot be destroyed” is true and irrelevant: a thought is not a quantity of energy, it is an arrangement. When a candle goes out, the energy is conserved and the flame is gone. The same applies to every organised pattern in a brain.

4. No test is proposed. A scientific claim states what measurement would show it false. The electromagnetic soul arrives with none — which is the signature the archive uses everywhere: compare the proven conspiracies, which were confirmed by documents, with the claims that can only be confirmed by believing them.

Why the idea is attractive

Because the hard problem of consciousness is genuinely unsolved, and “energy” is a placeholder that feels like an answer. Nobody can currently explain why information processing should be accompanied by experience at all; the electromagnetic version offers a physical substrate that sounds exotic enough to bridge the gap.

The honest state of the field: consciousness neuroscience has excellent correlates and no accepted explanation. That gap is real, and it is where every dualist, panpsychist and quantum-consciousness theory lives — including serious ones, like integrated information theory, which at least makes testable predictions and is argued over in journals.

The test that would change this page

What would move the electromagnetic soul from speculative to live debate: a demonstration that a specific, organised field pattern is necessary for a specific experience independent of the tissue producing it; or a measurement of a coherent, information-bearing field leaving a brain and persisting. Neither has been done. Until then, the claim sits in the old soul-and-underworld tradition, with better vocabulary.

It is worth saying that the reverse error is also common: dismissing the question because the popular answer is bad. “We don't know how consciousness arises” is a true and respectable scientific statement, and it does not need a soul, electromagnetic or otherwise, to remain true.

The Dark Forest

Where it comes from

The idea is the central argument of The Dark Forest (2008), the second volume of Liu Cixin's Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy, which begins with The Three-Body Problem (2006). It is fiction — a thought experiment delivered through characters — but it has escaped into serious discussion of the Fermi paradox, which is the real puzzle it addresses.

The Fermi paradox, stated simply: the galaxy is old and huge, and life should be common. So where is everyone? There is no confirmed evidence of any other technological civilisation, and no sign of one ever having visited.

The two axioms

Liu builds the argument from two premises, stated in the novel as the basis of “cosmic sociology”:

  1. Survival is the primary need of a civilisation.
  2. A civilisation grows, but the matter in the universe is finite.

From those two, plus two technical assumptions — that communication across interstellar distances is effectively impossible in real time, and that technology can grow explosively and unpredictably — you get a chain of suspicion: I cannot know whether you are hostile, I cannot verify your intentions at that distance, and I cannot risk that you will outgrow me. The only stable strategy is to hide, and if you find someone, to strike first.

Hence the image: civilisations as hunters moving silently between trees, and any broadcast as a light in the dark.

Why it is not a scientific theory

The axioms are stipulations, not findings. “Survival is the primary need” is an assumption about motivation. Nothing in astronomy establishes it, and plenty of terrestrial evidence suggests civilisations spend resources on things other than survival.

The conclusion depends on the assumptions being universal. Dark forest logic needs every advanced civilisation to reach the same paranoid equilibrium. One species that values knowledge over caution, or one that can verify intentions, changes the outcome.

It does not fit the silence we observe. If hunters strike at any detectable civilisation, the galaxy should show the scars — no obvious remnant civilisations, no megastructures destroyed. A theory that predicts a violent universe and explains a silent one is doing two jobs at once.

We have already been noisy. Earth has leaked radio and television signals for about a century, and radar and atmospheric nuclear tests for longer. Under strict dark forest rules we should already be a target, which is a prediction the theory cannot check.

What is genuinely useful in it

The idea is a legitimate contribution to a debate that has no empirical answer yet. It forces the question of incentives into a discussion that often treats alien contact as a curiosity. It also anticipates real policy arguments about METI — actively messaging extraterrestrial intelligence — where serious scientists including Stephen Hawking argued for caution, and others argued that fear is unwarranted.

Compare the UFO files, where the same silence is explained with secrecy rather than predation. Both are unfalsifiable, and both are more interesting as anthropology than as astronomy: they tell you what the people telling them are afraid of.

The Zoo Hypothesis: the opposite strategy

If the dark forest says everyone hides, the zoo hypothesis says everyone is watching and staying out of the way. The astronomer John A. Ball proposed it in 1973 in the journal Icarus: advanced civilisations know we exist, and deliberately avoid contact so that we can develop without interference — Earth as a nature reserve, or a quarantined experiment.

It is the mirror image of Liu's argument from the same silence, and it shares the same weakness: there is no observation that would distinguish a galaxy of careful observers from an empty one. Ball knew this, and presented it as a hypothesis about motives rather than a finding.

The interesting difference is moral. Dark forest logic says the silence is safety; the zoo hypothesis says the silence is policy, which means it can change — and that a civilisation capable of enforcing a quarantine is also capable of ending it. Neither claim has evidence. Both tell you something about the person making it.

The Great Filter

The most-cited alternative is not a place but a bottleneck. The economist Robin Hanson argued in 1998 that somewhere in the chain from simple chemistry to a civilisation that colonises its galaxy there is at least one step that is very improbable — a Great Filter. If the filter is behind us, our silence is explained and our future is open. If it is ahead of us, every civilisation gets this far and then stops.

The uncomfortable property is that the same data supports both readings. Finding simple life on Mars would be bad news under this framing, because it would suggest the hard step is later; finding nothing anywhere would be, oddly, reassuring.

Like the dark forest, it is a way of organising ignorance rather than a finding. The difference is that Hanson's version does not require aliens to be hostile — only that something, somewhere, is unlikely.

The calmer alternatives

  • The Great Filter — something in the chain from chemistry to radio telescopes is very unlikely, and we may already be past it.
  • Rarity — complex life may be genuinely uncommon; the galaxy could be nearly empty.
  • Distance and time — civilisations may overlap in time rarely, and cross the galaxy never.
  • They are quiet for their own reasons — observation rather than conquest; a hypothesis with no evidence either way.

Nothing currently distinguishes these. That is the honest state of the field, and it is more interesting than any single answer presented as settled.

The Simulation Hypothesis

What the paper says

In 2003 the philosopher Nick Bostrom published “Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?” in The Philosophical Quarterly. The argument is conditional, and it has three parts. At least one of these must be true:

  1. Cognitive civilisations go extinct before reaching a “posthuman” stage capable of running detailed ancestor simulations.
  2. Posthuman civilisations are not interested in running such simulations, or do not run many of them.
  3. We are almost certainly living in a simulation — because simulated observers would vastly outnumber real ones.

The reasoning in brief: if it is possible and cheap to run enormous numbers of detailed ancestor simulations, then simulated minds would outnumber genuine ones by a huge factor. A randomly selected observer should then expect to be simulated. So either nobody gets that far, or nobody bothers, or we are simulated.

Bostrom is explicit that he does not know which horn is true, and that the argument is not evidence of anything in particular. The interesting content is the structure, not the conclusion.

Why “glitches” prove nothing

The internet version points at déjà vu, a repeated texture, a coincidence, or a frame-rate artefact in a video and says: code. Every one of those has an ordinary explanation in neuroscience, perception, and compression — and none of them would be expected to occur if a simulation were well built.

Worse, “glitch” arguments are self-defeating: a simulation capable of rendering a civilisation for 13 billion simulated years, at the resolution of quantum field theory, is not going to leave a visible seam in a doorway.

There is one real physics-flavoured line of work worth naming: in 2012, Beane, Davoudi and Savage published “Constraints on the Universe as a Numerical Simulation”, asking what a simulated universe would look like on a lattice and whether current cosmic-ray data could constrain it. It is a legitimate, published, speculative paper — and it constrains possible simulation schemes, it does not detect one. That is the correct level of claim.

The problem with the trilemma

It assumes substrate independence. The counting argument treats minds as patterns that can be run on anything. If consciousness depends on the specific physical stuff of brains, “running” a mind is not like running software, and the numbers never add up.

It assumes simulations are cheap and numerous. Simulating one mind is fine; simulating a planet's worth of physics at quantum resolution, for billions of years, may be physically impossible even for a posthuman civilisation — which lands you on horn one or two.

It is not testable. As stated, the hypothesis predicts exactly the same observations as the non-simulated alternative. Compare many-worlds, which at least has a defined mathematical structure that could in principle be distinguished.

It has the Last Thursdayism shape. Any disconfirming evidence can be explained as part of the simulation. See Last Thursdayism — the argument is the same, with a server instead of a deity.

What is genuinely worth taking from it

Two things. First, it is a clean demonstration of how a serious philosopher can make an unsettling argument while explicitly refusing to claim it is true — which is exactly what most of the fringe material in this archive fails to do. Second, it raises a real question about reference classes: if you are going to reason about your own existence probabilistically, you need to know what class of observer you are in, and nobody knows.

It also, incidentally, produced a useful cultural test. Ask someone what they think of the simulation hypothesis and you learn whether they distinguish a structural argument from a vibe.

Last Thursdayism

The joke with a serious point

The modern formulation: the world came into existence last Thursday, fully formed, including every memory, every geological layer, every photon already in flight from distant galaxies — arranged so that it looks exactly as old as it appears. You cannot prove otherwise, because every piece of evidence is inside the world that was made.

It is usually attributed to a student joke at Oxford in the early 1990s, and it is the sharpest possible parody of a much older problem.

Gosse's Omphalos, 1857

Before the joke, the argument. Philip Henry Gosse, a respected naturalist, published Omphalos: An Attempt to Untie the Geological Knot in 1857 — two years before Darwin's Origin. His problem: geology showed an ancient Earth, while a literal reading of Genesis gave thousands of years.

Gosse's solution was that God created the world with an apparent history built in — “prochronism”. Adam would have had a navel he never needed (hence omphalos, Greek for navel); trees would have had growth rings from a first year that never happened; fossils would exist as a created record of lives never lived.

It was received badly by almost everyone — theologians found it made God a deceiver, and scientists found it useless. Charles Kingsley reportedly called it “a clumsy attempt to make God a liar”. Gosse had argued himself into a position where no observation could count against him, which he seems to have recognised as a virtue.

Russell's five minutes

Bertrand Russell gave the secular version in The Analysis of Mind (1921): the hypothesis that the world sprang into being five minutes ago, exactly as it then was, with a population that “remembered” a wholly unreal past. Russell's point was not that this is likely, but that it cannot be refuted — and that this tells us something about the limits of empirical knowledge rather than about the world.

Why it is the honest opposite of a theory

It has no content. A claim that predicts nothing and forbids nothing cannot be tested, and cannot be used. It does not conflict with geology, cosmology or evolution — it simply declares all of them to be scenery.

It multiplies entities for no gain. The ordinary account (an old universe, with the physics that produces fossils and starlight) explains the same observations with fewer assumptions. Occam's razor is a heuristic, not a proof — but this hypothesis needs an enormous extra assumption and returns nothing.

It is the mirror of the archive's fringe claims. Compare it with Tartaria (all the evidence was destroyed) or the Mandela Effect (the timeline changed and only memory disagrees). Each is a machine for making contrary evidence harmless. Last Thursdayism is the same machine, built openly, as a warning.

Why it still matters

Because “you cannot prove it false” is the single most common defence offered for otherwise unsupported claims — and this thought experiment shows why that defence is empty. Almost any proposition can be protected by an auxiliary assumption that neutralises the evidence. The question is never “can it be refuted?” in the abstract; it is “does it make any prediction that would come out differently if it were wrong?”

For the record: the age of the Earth is about 4.54 billion years, established by radiometric dating cross-checked across multiple independent isotope systems, and corroborated by everything from tree rings to cosmic microwave background measurements. The universe is about 13.8 billion years old. These are not matters of consensus opinion; they are measurements with error bars, and they agree with each other in ways a planted record would have no reason to.

Solipsism: the same knife, pointed inward

Solipsism is the older, purer version: only your own mind is certain to exist. The physical world, other people, history, and this page might all be contents of your experience, with nothing behind them.

It is philosophically serious — Descartes' evil demon, Berkeley's idealism, and the “problem of other minds” are all respectable company — and it is unanswerable in the same way Last Thursdayism is. You cannot step outside your experience to check whether anything corresponds to it. Any evidence you cite is, by definition, part of the experience.

The reason it does not stop anyone living is that it is not a live hypothesis. It makes no prediction, forbids nothing, and cannot be acted on. A solipsist who crosses the road still looks both ways; the position is not inhabitable, only arguable.

Where it becomes harmful is in the popular version — “nothing is real, so nothing matters” — which is not solipsism's fault but a misreading of it. The philosophical position is about epistemic certainty, not about ethics. Judged on the archive's standard, it is the cleanest example of a claim that is neither true nor false but unusable, and the honest response is to note that and get on with the day.

The family of cousins

  • Simulation hypothesis — the modern replacement, with a machine instead of a deity. See the simulation page.
  • Boltzmann brains — self-aware fluctuations in a thermal void; a serious cosmological puzzle about why we observe an ordered universe.
  • Evil demon — Descartes' 1641 version, which at least drove him to find something that survived the doubt.
