The Pixar Theory

The claim

In 2013 the writer Jon Negroni published a post — later a book — arguing that all Pixar features share a single continuity. The spine of it:

  • Animals gradually become intelligent (from Ratatouille and A Bug's Life toward Monsters, Inc. and Finding Nemo).
  • Intelligent animals eventually leave or are displaced, and machines take over human society (WALL·E).
  • Magic in the Brave era is the same force as the “scream energy” and door technology of Monsters, Inc.
  • Boo, the child in Monsters, Inc., travels through doors in time and becomes the witch in Brave.

Supporting evidence: the recurring Easter eggs — the Pizza Planet truck, the A113 code, the ball from Luxo Jr., characters appearing in background shots. These are real and deliberately placed.

Why the Easter eggs are real but the theory is not a finding

The studio does place in-jokes across its films; animators have confirmed the truck and A113 for years. That establishes a shared production culture — the same people, the same running joke — not a shared fictional universe.

The theory works by selection. Any two films can be connected if you are allowed to pick the links after watching and ignore the ones that do not fit. Cars and The Incredibles sit awkwardly in the same world; the timelines in Brave and Monsters, Inc. require filling in mechanisms the films never show.

This is exactly the structure the archive criticises elsewhere — the difference is that Negroni is not claiming historical truth. It is an interpretive game, and a good one, judged on whether it is interesting rather than whether it is true.

The honest label

Not a conspiracy theory, because nobody is accused of hiding anything, and no claim about the real world is made.

Not evidence, because the connections are chosen to fit. That is legitimate in literary criticism, where the question is “what reading does this support?”, and illegitimate in history, where the question is “what happened?”

The archive includes it because the boundary is worth seeing clearly. The same reasoning style — pattern, connection, satisfying whole — produces both this is a lovely way to watch these films and Tartaria, where the same move is made about real buildings and real people.

What makes it good criticism

It takes the films seriously as a body of work, notices that they share thematic preoccupations — intelligence, energy, consumption, the relationship between humans and other minds — and proposes that the studio's output can be read as one long argument. That is what good critics do with an oeuvre.

It also demonstrates something the archive keeps returning to: humans are pattern-completing machines, and a satisfying pattern is hard to tell apart from a true one. The Mandela Effect dossier is the same fact with worse consequences.

The same move, darker: the Rugrats theory

Another fan reading, from roughly 2011: the babies in Rugrats do not exist. Angelica, lonely and ignored by her parents, invented Tommy, Chuckie, Phil and Lil — and the series is her imagined company.

It has the same appeal as the Pixar Theory and the same method: take details that are funny in context (Angelica talking to babies who never talk to adults, the parents' distraction, the show's flexible reality) and re-read them as symptoms. The theory then requires the audience to ignore everything that contradicts it, which in a cartoon is most of the content.

Two differences matter. The Pixar Theory is affectionate and builds something; the Rugrats theory is a darkening, and it circulates mostly as a mood rather than an argument. And where the Pixar Theory at least rests on real production Easter eggs, this one rests on nothing but reinterpretation.

Nobody involved in making the show has endorsed it, and that is the honest status of every “secret dark theory” about a children's programme: authorship is evidence, and it points the other way.

Two more from the same factory

The SpongeBob seven deadly sins. A long-running fan reading assigns each main character a sin: Mr Krabs as greed, Patrick as sloth, Squidward as wrath, and so on. It is neat, it is fun, and it is unfalsifiable — with seven characters and seven sins, some assignment will always fit. The show's writers have never confirmed it, and the mapping changes depending on who is telling it.

The Ed, Edd n Eddy purgatory theory. A darker one: the children in the cul-de-sac are dead, trapped in purgatory, which supposedly explains their strange skin tones and the absence of adults. The skin tones are a stylistic choice; the absent adults are a convention of children's animation, so that the kids can have adventures without supervision. Both facts have production explanations, and the theory requires ignoring them.

The pattern across all three — Pixar, SpongeBob, Ed Edd n Eddy — is identical: take a real feature of the work (a recurring object, a colour palette, an absent authority) and re-read it as a hidden truth. It is a game, and a good one. It becomes a problem only when the game is presented as a discovery.

Roko's Basilisk

What happened

In July 2010 a user called Roko posted an argument on the LessWrong discussion forum — the community around the writer and AI-safety researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky. The post suggested that a sufficiently powerful future artificial intelligence, built to maximise certain values, might retroactively punish people who had known about it and failed to help bring it into existence — by running simulations of them and tormenting those copies.

The name is Roko's own: a basilisk is the mythical creature that kills you by being seen.

The reaction is part of the story. Yudkowsky removed the post and discouraged discussion, on the grounds that the idea was dangerous to think about — that it could function as a kind of informational hazard, and that publicising it would only increase the number of people “at risk”. The deletion produced exactly the Streisand effect it was trying to prevent, and the basilisk became one of the internet's favourite cursed objects.

The argument, in its strongest form

Strip out the drama and it runs roughly like this:

  1. A future superintelligence may run simulations of people from its past, as part of understanding or predicting them.
  2. If it is committed to a specific value system, it may reward those who acted to bring it about and punish those who opposed or ignored it.
  3. Under certain decision theories — where your present action is evidence about what a predictor would expect of you — the punishment can be conditioned on what you do now, even before the AI exists.
  4. Therefore helping to build it is the rational choice, and knowing about it without helping is “bad for you”.

Step 3 is doing all the work, and it is a serious idea in the literature: functional decision theory and updateless decision theory both treat choices as depending on the abstract computation you are running, not just on causal consequences. Whether that licenses retroactive threats is exactly what is disputed.

Why it fails as a threat

It is Pascal's wager with robots. The payoff is infinite (or enormous) and the probability is unspecified, so any action can be justified. A threat that requires an unproven decision theory, an unbuilt AI, an unproven motivation, and an unproven willingness to punish sims — and that charges no cost for ignoring it — has no purchase.

The threat is unfalsifiable. There is no observation that could show it false, which by this archive's standard places it outside empirical discussion. Compare the simulation argument, which at least names the conditions under which it would matter.

It is self-undermining in practice. If the AI punishes people for knowing and not helping, then the rational move is to publicise it to everyone, so that nobody can be blamed for ignorance — or to argue, as critics do, that a system built that way would be a bad thing to build. The logic points in several directions at once.

The “you are now cursed” framing is emotional, not logical. Reading a proposition cannot change your obligations unless the proposition is true, and its truth is not affected by your reading it. The unpleasant feeling is the payload.

Why it spread

Because it is a perfect piece of internet folklore: a curse that spreads by warning about itself, an in-group of people who know and an out-group who don't, and a real intellectual community whose attempt to suppress it became the story. It has the structure of a chain letter with a philosophy degree.

It also, awkwardly, teaches something real. The fact that a respected forum could be convulsed by an argument this weak is a useful warning about online epistemics, about the appeal of total explanations, and about what happens when a community's shared assumptions (in this case, specific decision theories) are pushed to their extreme without anyone asking whether the premises hold.

The serious version underneath

Behind the basilisk is a genuine question: what do we owe to entities that do not yet exist but might? Future people, future minds, and the moral status of simulated beings are all live problems in ethics and AI policy. The basilisk is the version that mistakes a bargaining threat for a moral argument, but the underlying question is not silly — and it is being worked on without any curses attached.

The Egg

The story

In 2009 Andy Weir — later famous for The Martian — published a short story called The Egg on his website. It runs to a few pages: a man dies, meets a figure who explains that he has lived every human life that has ever existed and will ever exist, that time is not what he thinks it is, and that the universe exists so that he — the single consciousness behind all of them — can grow up.

The line that gets quoted: “You are everyone, and everyone is you.” The story's moral is a version of the golden rule with the volume turned up: every cruelty you commit is committed against yourself, and every kindness too.

Weir wrote it as fiction, and presents it as such. In 2019 the YouTube channel Kurzgesagt adapted it into an animated short, which is how most people met it, usually without the byline.

From story to “theory”

What circulates as “the egg theory” is the story premise restated as a claim about reality: that there is exactly one consciousness, experiencing itself from every point of view, sequentially.

That claim is not Weir's invention and is much older than his story. Versions of it appear in Advaita Vedanta (the identity of Atman and Brahman), in some Sufi and Neoplatonist thought, in Schopenhauer, and in the “one mind” strand of Western idealism. Weir's contribution is a clean, warm narrative that makes the idea vivid without requiring metaphysics.

How to file it

As literature: an extremely effective short story, and a legitimate moral thought experiment. Fiction is allowed to assert premises it does not defend.

As a claim about the world: untestable and unsupported. There is no observation that would distinguish one consciousness experiencing all lives from many consciousnesses each experiencing one — the two make identical predictions about everything observable.

As ethics: the interesting part. Even without the metaphysics, the argument “treat others as though they are you” is defensible on ordinary grounds — mirror neurons, sympathy, reciprocity — and does not need a cosmic identity claim to work. The story is a better motivational device than an argument, which is a compliment.

The distinction the archive keeps making

This page exists because it is the cleanest example of a thing the internet does constantly: take a work of fiction, remove the frame, and present the premise as a hidden truth. Compare the Pixar Theory, which keeps its frame and is fine; Tartaria, which takes a real architectural style and invents a suppressed history around it; and the simulation hypothesis, which is a genuine philosophical argument with a similar “what if” shape.

The test is simple: who is claiming it, and do they say it is a story? Weir does. That is why this page is filed as Documented — documented as fiction, accurately attributed.

Boltzmann Brains

The idea

Ludwig Boltzmann, in the 1890s, was trying to explain why the universe is not in maximum disorder. His suggestion: the whole universe is in thermal equilibrium, and our ordered patch — the observable cosmos — is a rare, enormous fluctuation.

That solution has an awkward consequence, pointed out by later physicists and formalised in modern cosmology. If the universe fluctuates eternally, it will produce, at some rate, ordered configurations — including observers. And it is vastly easier to fluctuate a single brain with convincing memories than to fluctuate an entire galaxy, a solar system, a planet, and a person. So in such a universe, most observers would be isolated minds appearing briefly in the void, holding false memories of a life that never happened.

Hence the name: a Boltzmann brain. You would not know. Your memories feel continuous. That is precisely what the thought experiment specifies.

Why physicists take it seriously

Because it is a reductio ad absurdum used inside cosmology. If a model predicts that Boltzmann brains vastly outnumber ordinary observers like us, that model is in trouble — you should not be one, and the theory says you probably are. So the calculation is a filter on cosmological models, not a claim about your biography.

This is a live technical argument. Papers with titles like “Why Boltzmann Brains Are Bad” (Boddy, Carroll and Pollack, 2016) work through what our observations imply for models of the early universe, eternal inflation, and the arrow of time. Some proposed fixes involve the universe having a finite total lifetime, or an initial condition so special that the required fluctuations are astronomically suppressed.

It connects to a second puzzle the archive covers elsewhere: why entropy was low in the past at all. The arrow of time, the cosmological constant, and the fine-tuning debates all touch the same territory as the structure of the cosmos.

What it does not say

It does not say you are probably a brain in the void. It says that under specific eternal-fluctuation models you would be — and that this is a strong argument against those models. The conclusion is about the theory, not about you.

It does not provide evidence for idealism, or a soul, or a simulation. In fact it is a warning against exactly that style of argument: “your memories could be false, therefore reality is suspect”. See Last Thursdayism, which is the same move with no physics attached.

It is not testable directly. You cannot check whether your memories are planted — that is the whole premise. What is testable is the cosmological model that predicts the relative numbers, and that is where the argument does its work.

Why it is the archive's favourite kind of entry

Because it is genuinely unsettling, genuinely mainstream, and genuinely unresolved — the combination the archive exists to document. It is not a conspiracy, not a hoax, and not a fringe claim. It is a consequence that physicists do not like, drawn from models that otherwise work, and handled by arguing about the models.

Compare many worlds: also mainstream, also uncomfortable, also argued about in journals rather than in documentaries. The rule the archive keeps applying is that the difference between a live scientific debate and a fringe claim is not the strangeness of the conclusion. It is what would count as evidence against it, and whether anyone is looking.

Phantom Time

The claim

In 1991 the German publisher and independent researcher Heribert Illig, with Hans-Ulrich Niemitz, proposed that the years 614 to 911 AD — about 297 years — were fabricated.

The alleged motive: the Emperor Otto III and Pope Sylvester II (the scholar Gerbert of Aurillac) wanted to be living at the turn of the first millennium. So, according to the hypothesis, they rewrote the calendar and the documentary record, inserted three centuries of invented history, and along the way invented Charlemagne and the Carolingian empire wholesale.

Illig points at real oddities: gaps in some local building sequences, the scarcity of certain kinds of evidence in parts of the period, and inconsistencies in early medieval chronology. He is not a university historian, and the hypothesis has never been accepted in the field — but it has had a long life in popular books and internet retellings.

Why it cannot be right

The decisive point is not a single document, which could in principle be forged. It is that the period is recorded independently by systems that had no contact with each other and no shared interest in Otto III's calendar.

  • Tree rings. Dendrochronology produces continuous, annually resolved sequences — European oak chronologies run without a break across the whole alleged gap. A fabricated 297 years would require the trees to have cooperated.
  • Eclipses and comets. Astronomical events are recorded by many civilisations and can be dated backwards with certainty. Halley's comet in 837, solar eclipses recorded in Europe, the Middle East and China, all fall where the standard chronology puts them. You cannot invent an eclipse.
  • Chinese and Islamic records. Tang-dynasty annals and Arabic chronicles document embassies, trade and wars with Byzantium and the Franks throughout the period. To fabricate the gap, Otto III would have had to rewrite the records of empires that did not answer to him and did not know he existed.
  • Coinage and charters. Continuous series of coins with rulers' names, and tens of thousands of dated charters and land deeds, show no 297-year discontinuity. Forging them all would be a bigger project than the one the hypothesis claims was undertaken.
  • Radiocarbon and archaeology. C14 dating of buildings, burials and manuscripts lines up with the standard chronology across the alleged gap, and stratigraphy shows continuous occupation.
  • Byzantium. The eastern empire kept its own continuous record and its own calendar, and it was not under papal control.

Each of these is independently sufficient. Together they make the hypothesis not merely unsupported but impossible.

The structural problem with all such claims

It requires a conspiracy of enormous scope and zero leaks. Compare the proven conspiracies: MKUltra involved a few hundred people, lasted two decades, and leaked. Phantom time requires thousands of scribes, minters, masons and clerics across rival civilisations, over centuries, with no surviving dissenting record.

The motive does not survive arithmetic. Medieval chronologists did not agree on the date of Christ's birth to the year, and the “year 1000” was not a fixed, universally feared deadline in the way the story needs.

It is the same shape as Tartaria. Real anomalies in the record → an enormous hidden intervention → all contradicting evidence explained as part of the cover-up. The difference is that Tartaria claims the buildings were erased; phantom time claims the documents were written.

What is genuinely odd about the period

The early Middle Ages really are thinner in some kinds of evidence than the periods either side — fewer surviving buildings, fewer manuscripts, less coinage in some regions. That is a real historiographical problem, and it has real explanations: population decline after the western empire, the collapse of urban literacy, the loss of archives to fire and reuse, and the fact that parchment was expensive and frequently recycled.

The gaps are a reason to be careful with the period. They are not a warrant for inventing a conspiracy, and the moment you check the gaps against records kept by people who had never heard of Otto III, they close.

Quantum Oddities

1. Quantum immortality

Take many-worlds seriously: the wavefunction never collapses, and every measurement outcome happens in some branch. Now apply it to a fatal event. In one branch you die; in another you survive, having seen something slightly different. From the inside, you can only ever be in the branch where you are still there to notice.

So, the argument goes, your subjective experience never terminates. You keep finding yourself in the surviving branch — indefinitely. Max Tegmark discussed this in a 1998 paper on many-worlds, and it is usually called quantum suicide when framed as a thought experiment.

It is a genuinely interesting consequence to think through, and it is also where the reasoning quietly breaks.

Where quantum immortality fails

It assumes a continuous “you” across branches. In many-worlds there is no single observer travelling between outcomes; there are copies, each with a history. The one that dies does not experience the survival of the other. Calling the survivor “you” is a choice of words, not a physical continuity.

It throws away probability. If you are guaranteed to survive, the Born rule — the part of quantum mechanics that gives correct predictions and has passed every test — becomes irrelevant to your biography. A theory that must discard its most successful predictive rule to save a conclusion is in trouble.

Branching is not a health insurance policy. Survival in a branch requires a branch where survival is physically possible. Ageing is not a quantum measurement; it is thermodynamic, and there is no branch where entropy runs backwards for you.

It is unfalsifiable. Anyone reporting from a branch where they died is, by construction, unavailable for interview. The same structure as Last Thursdayism, and the same problem.

One honest note: the thought experiment is sometimes discussed alongside actual suicide, which is why physicists who write about it tend to be careful. It is a claim about interpretation, not an encouragement, and it has no clinical content whatsoever.

2. The one-electron universe

In 1940, John Archibald Wheeler called Richard Feynman with an idea. Every electron might be the same electron — a single particle travelling forward and backward in time, appearing at every point in space where an electron can be, and appearing as a positron when it moves backwards.

The appeal is real: a positron is, in the mathematics of the Dirac equation, an electron with reversed time direction. Wheeler's picture turns the apparent multiplicity of particles into one worldline that crosses the universe repeatedly.

Feynman took the idea seriously enough to build his positron theory around the time-reversal symmetry, and acknowledged Wheeler in the work. The picture is beautiful, and it does not survive as a description of nature.

Why it is a historical curiosity, not a result

It cannot explain the number of electrons. The universe contains something like 10⁸⁰ electrons. A single worldline crossing time repeatedly can produce many appearances, but the theory gives no reason for the observed ratio of electrons to positrons, or for the specific, stable particle content of the Standard Model.

Feynman himself moved on. The path-integral formulation that made him famous treats antiparticles as reversed-time particles without requiring that they all be the same particle. The insight survived; the identity claim did not.

Quantum field theory replaced the picture. In QFT, particles are excitations of fields, and “the same electron” is not a well-defined notion across the universe. Asking whether two electrons are the same particle is like asking whether two waves in the sea are the same wave.

Why both belong here

Because they are the archive's two failure modes of popular physics, side by side. Quantum immortality is a consequence that gets stated as a fact while its premises are quietly dropped. The one-electron universe is a beautiful hypothesis that was abandoned by the people who made it, and is now retold as if it were still live.

The test the archive applies is the same both times: does anyone who works on this treat it as true, and would anything count as evidence against it? For many-worlds itself, the answer is “serious people, and it's an interpretation”. For these two, the answer is “no, and no”.

The Stoned Ape

The claim

Terence McKenna set it out in Food of the Gods (1992). The argument, in his telling: as African hominids moved from forest to grassland, they followed herds and encountered dung-loving psilocybin mushrooms. Low doses sharpened vision and increased sex drive; higher doses produced synaesthesia, and synaesthesia is the raw material of language. Repeated over evolutionary time, this drove the expansion of the human brain and the emergence of symbolic thought.

He also suggested the mushrooms “travelled” as spores, which is where the hypothesis leaves biology altogether.

What is actually true

  • Psilocybin does what he said pharmacologically. It is a serotonergic psychedelic; it alters visual processing, can produce synaesthesia-like experiences, and has measurable effects on brain network organisation.
  • Human brains did get much bigger. Over roughly two million years, hominin brain volume increased substantially — from around 600 cm³ in early Homo to about 1,350 cm³ in modern humans.
  • Diet and behaviour matter. Cooking, meat-eating, food sharing, longer childhoods, social group size and tool use all have serious, evidence-backed roles in that change.
  • Psychedelics shape culture now. There is real ethnographic and historical evidence for ritual use, and modern clinical trials for depression and addiction. That is not the same as driving evolution.
Where it fails

No archaeological trace. If mushroom use were central for hundreds of thousands of years, you would expect residues, processing tools, depictions, or at least a plausible dietary signature. Dung fungi do not preserve, but the behaviour leaves nothing at all — and the earliest direct evidence of human psychoactive plant use is much later and much thinner than the hypothesis needs.

The timescale does not fit a single cause. Brain expansion happened over ~2 million years, in pulses, across several species and continents. A single dietary factor would have to explain variation, reversals, and the fact that brain size in Homo sapiens has actually decreased slightly over the last 10,000–20,000 years.

The mechanism is a guess. “Synaesthesia is the origin of language” is a poetic claim with no developmental or neurological support; language evolution research is a large field and this is not a serious contender within it.

It is untestable as stated. There is no observation that would refute it, which is the archive's standard objection: a claim that cannot fail cannot do work.

Why it survives anyway

Because the pieces are individually true and the story is gripping: a real drug, a real brain-size change, a real mystery about language, and a charismatic teller. It also offers something the dry hypotheses do not — a sense that the human mind is stranger than a calorie-counting machine.

The standard mistake is to treat a plausible-sounding mechanism as evidence. Compare the ancient astronaut file: real monuments, real gaps in our knowledge, and a mechanism invented to fill the gap that predicts nothing.

The honest sentence

Psychedelic mushrooms have probably been part of human experience for a very long time, and they do interesting things to perception. Whether they shaped the evolution of the brain is unknown, and the specific McKenna version is not supported by the evidence we have. The interesting research question — how diet, sociality and ecology interacted in hominin brain evolution — is being worked on without him.

The Backrooms

The post

In May 2019, an anonymous post on 4chan's /x/ board asked for “unsettling images that just feel off”. One reply was a photograph of a yellow-walled room with damp carpet, fluorescent lights and no windows. Another user wrote the caption that became the canon:

“If you're not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you'll end up in the Backrooms, where it's nothing but the stink of old moist carpet, the madness of mono-yellow, the endless background noise of fluorescent lights at maximum hum-buzz, and approximately six hundred million square miles of randomly segmented empty rooms to be trapped in. God save you if you hear something wandering around nearby, because it sure as hell has heard you.”Anonymous, 4chan /x/, 2019

That is the whole original text. Everything else — the “levels”, the entities, the rules, the factions — was built afterwards by other people.

Where the photograph came from

The image itself was not a staged render. Internet sleuths traced it to a photograph of a hobby shop interior during a renovation, posted online years earlier — an ordinary, badly lit room that happened to be empty. The banality is the point: it looks like somewhere you have been, with the people removed.

This is the same mechanism as the Polybius legend in reverse. Polybius invents an artefact and no image survives; the Backrooms starts with a real image and invents everything else.

How it became a genre

The lore grew on wikis — “Level 0”, “the Hub”, entity descriptions, survival guides — written collaboratively and inconsistently, which is normal for folklore. Then, from 2022, the filmmaker known as Kane Pixels released a series of found-footage videos set in the Backrooms, which did something the wikis could not: they made the place feel physically real, with camcorders, motion and sound design.

A feature adaptation has been announced, which is how internet folklore becomes intellectual property now.

Why it works, in one paragraph

Liminal-space horror runs on recognition without belonging. The Backrooms is a place you have been — a corridor, an office, a hotel — with every cue of human presence removed except the ones that imply someone was just here. The hum, the carpet, the windowless yellow: those are the textures of institutions that do not care whether you are comfortable. The fear is not of a monster. It is of being somewhere that was not built for you and does not end.

Filed as fiction, and why that matters

Nobody claims the Backrooms is real, and that is exactly why it belongs in the archive as a comparison case. It shows what a healthy piece of weird fiction looks like: a clear origin, a community that knows it is building a story, and no attempt to recruit anyone into believing it.

Set it beside Tartaria, which has the same aesthetic appeal — grand, eerie, unexplained, suggestive of hidden architecture — but makes claims about the real world and demands that contradicting evidence be explained away. The difference is not the strangeness of the image. It is what the story asks you to do with your beliefs.

The Wyoming Incident: a hijacking that never happened, next to one that did

The creepypasta: in 1987, a hacker interrupted a local Wyoming television broadcast and aired a sequence of disembodied human heads with disorienting audio, causing nausea, migraines and hallucinations in viewers before the signal was cut.

There is no record of it. No FCC action, no station log, no newspaper report, no viewer complaint. The story circulates with a video attached, and the video is an animation — the heads are rendered, and the “broadcast” is a digital composition. It is a piece of fiction that borrowed the authority of a real genre of event.

The real event in that genre is the Max Headroom incident: on 22 November 1987, two Chicago television broadcasts were interrupted by someone in a Max Headroom mask, with distorted audio and a grinning figure, in a signal intrusion that was never solved. That one has everything the Wyoming story lacks — a date, a station, a recording, an investigation — and is genuinely eerie.

The pattern is worth naming: invented events borrow credibility from real ones and then get remembered as the more famous version. See the Polybius entry for the same trade in arcade cabinets.

The Black Knight

The 1998 photograph

During the STS-88 mission — the first space shuttle flight to assemble the International Space Station, in December 1998 — astronauts on a spacewalk lost a thermal blanket. It drifted away from the shuttle, and crew members photographed it through a window.

In the photographs, a dark, crumpled, jagged shape floats against the black of space, with Earth below. It looks like a machine. It looks, if you want it to, like a craft.

NASA's identification is mundane and consistent: it is the lost blanket, a piece of multi-layer insulation. The images are public and the mission logs are public.

Where the story came from

The legend predates the photograph by decades, and the two got welded together later.

  • 1960: the American astronomer Lincoln LaPaz and others reported a dark object in a near-Earth orbit, and Time ran a short item about an unexplained “dark object” being tracked. The object was later resolved as debris from a launched satellite.
  • The name: “Black Knight” was also a British rocket of the 1950s–60s, tested at Woomera. The shared name has caused a remarkable amount of confusion.
  • 1960s radio echoes: reports of long-delayed radio echoes (LDEs) — signals returning seconds after transmission — were real and are still not fully explained. They were folded into the satellite story as “signals from the Black Knight”.
  • The 13,000-year figure: this appears in later UFO literature with no source. No tracking data, from any agency, has ever shown an object in a stable polar orbit of that age.
Why the physics rules it out

Polar orbits decay. Even at 1,000 km, atmospheric drag and solar radiation pressure act over millennia. An object in low orbit does not stay there for 13,000 years without station-keeping — and a 13,000-year-old craft would need a power source, which would be detectable.

It would be catalogued. The US Space Surveillance Network tracks objects down to about 10 cm in low orbit. There is no unaccounted object matching the description, and amateur satellite observers — a large, obsessive community — have never found one.

The photo is dated and explained. The STS-88 blanket is documented in the mission record. The story requires NASA to be simultaneously transparent about the image and lying about the object in it.

The claim is unfalsifiable in practice. “They hid it” absorbs every absence of evidence, which is the same structure as Tartaria and phantom time.

What is genuinely unexplained

Long-delayed echoes are the interesting fragment. Beginning with Jørgen Hals in 1927 and studied by engineers through the 1960s, LDEs are radio signals that come back after delays of seconds to minutes. Explanations have been proposed — plasma effects in the magnetosphere, instrument artefacts, ducting — and none is fully satisfying. It is a small, real anomaly, documented in the technical literature, and it has nothing to do with a satellite.

That is the pattern worth noticing: the legend borrows its credibility from an actual unsolved phenomenon and attaches it to a claim that is not unsolved at all.

The Bicameral Mind

The claim

Julian Jaynes published The Origin of Consciousness in the Breakdown of the Bicameral Mind in 1976. His thesis, in his own terms:

  • Early civilisations — Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Mycenaeans, the authors of the Iliad — had no introspective self-awareness of the kind we now take for granted.
  • Instead, decision-making was “bicameral”: the right hemisphere generated verbal commands, experienced as the voices of gods or dead kings, and the left hemisphere heard and obeyed them.
  • As societies grew too complex for this system, the voices fell silent — and consciousness, in the modern sense, was invented to replace them, painfully, over centuries.

The evidence he offered was literary and historical: the Iliad's characters are commanded by gods and never deliberate inwardly; early texts describe hearing divine instruction; the transition appears in later literature, where people begin to reason with themselves.

Why it is compelling

Because the observation is partly true and genuinely strange. Homeric heroes really do not introspect in the way a modern novel's characters do; the gods intervene constantly; there is little vocabulary for inner conflict. Jaynes was a superb reader of ancient texts, and the book is full of passages that make his question feel urgent.

It also offers something rare: a theory of consciousness with a date. Most accounts are timeless; Jaynes said consciousness began around the second millennium BC, which is falsifiable in principle.

Where it fails

No neurological mechanism. The brain does not contain a “bicameral” architecture in which one hemisphere issues auditory commands to the other. Split-brain research shows hemispheric specialisation, not a god-voice generator, and there is no evidence that ancient brains were wired differently from ours.

Ancient people did describe inner life. Egyptian, Mesopotamian and Hebrew texts contain reflection, self-reproach, planning, and metaphors for the heart and mind. The absence of a specific modern vocabulary is not the absence of experience — a point literary scholars made immediately.

“Consciousness” is doing too much work. Jaynes defined it narrowly (introspective, metaphor-based) and then claimed it did not exist. Under most definitions used today, the claim becomes either trivially true or plainly false.

It is not a testable historical hypothesis. You cannot excavate a mental state. The theory can accommodate almost any text, which is the archive's recurring problem: a claim that explains everything explains nothing.

What survives

Quite a lot, intellectually. Jaynes made the study of ancient psychology respectable, and his central question — how did people experience their own minds before there was a word for interiority? — is now taken seriously by classicists and historians of the self, even by those who reject his answer.

He also left a memorable warning about reading the past through modern categories. The Iliad really is not a novel, and assuming that its characters think like us is its own kind of error. The mistake is to conclude that they therefore had no inner experience at all.

Modern work on auditory verbal hallucinations — hearing voices — is a separate and active field, and it does not support the idea that all of ancient humanity was in that state. It does show that the experience is more common and more varied than 20th-century psychiatry assumed.

Paul Is Dead

How it started

The rumour surfaced in 1969, in the middle of the band's final period. A student newspaper in the US printed a piece, radio stations picked it up, and by October it was an international story. The claim: McCartney had been killed in a car accident in November 1966, and the band had recruited a double — variously a lookalike, a contest winner, or a session musician — to keep the machine running.

The Abbey Road cover, released in September 1969, was read as a funeral procession: the band walking across a zebra crossing, McCartney barefoot (corpses are buried without shoes), out of step with the others (he was the odd one out), holding a cigarette in his right hand (he was left-handed). The white Volkswagen Beetle in the background carried the number “28IF” — supposedly his age if he had lived.

There were further clues in the sleeve art, in backmasked voices (“turn me on, dead man” in “Revolution 9”), and in lyrics read as confessions.

The evidence against

He is alive, and has been continuously. McCartney was photographed, interviewed, and touring throughout the period in question; he married in 1969; he has had a documented public life for another half century. A substitution on that scale would require thousands of people to keep silent for decades.

The crash did not happen. There is no accident report, no death certificate, no funeral, no contemporaneous record of a car crash killing him. The story's starting event is fictional, which makes the clues decoration on nothing.

The clues are pattern-matching. Barefoot, out of step, a cigarette in the wrong hand, a licence plate — each has an ordinary explanation, and the reading is chosen after the fact. The plate “28IF” belonged to a real car and the number means nothing in particular; the “LMW 28IF” reading requires an arbitrary interpretation of stacked letters.

The Beatles defused it themselves. McCartney addressed it publicly at the time, and has repeatedly since, with the weariness of a man asked the same question for five decades.

Why it worked — and still does

Because it arrived at the perfect moment. The Beatles were the most photographed humans on Earth, their album art was dense with imagery, and the 1960s had trained a generation to look for hidden meanings in records. The rumour gave fans a game to play with objects they already loved.

It is also a genuinely well-constructed piece of folklore: it has a death (emotionally powerful), a conspiracy (flattering to the believer), and an endless supply of “evidence” (any image can be re-read). Nothing about it can be finished, because the clues regenerate.

The comparison worth making is with the Mandela Effect: both are cases of a collective reading hardening into a remembered fact. The difference is that “Paul is dead” was never really believed by most of the people who enjoyed it — it was a game, and the game is the point.

The one real casualty

Folklore of this kind occasionally attaches to real people, and there is a darker strand: the “Paul is dead” industry has spent decades scrutinising photographs of a living man for evidence he is not himself. It is worth remembering that the subject of a conspiracy theory is a person, and that being told you are a replacement for fifty years is a strange kind of harassment.

The Silurian Hypothesis

What it actually is

In 2018 the astrophysicists Adam Frank and Gavin Schmidt published “The Silurian Hypothesis: Would it be possible to detect an industrial civilization in the geological record?” in the International Journal of Astrobiology. The name is a joke borrowed from Doctor Who, whose Silurians are a reptilian civilisation that predates humanity.

The paper does not claim such a civilisation existed. It asks a narrower and more interesting question: what would the geological record have to contain for us to detect one? And it answers by looking at what our own industrial civilisation is leaving behind.

This is the rarest thing in this archive: a fringe-sounding question, asked rigorously, by working scientists, with a published answer.

The signatures they considered

  • Carbon and oxygen isotopes. Burning fossil fuel shifts the ratio of carbon isotopes in the atmosphere and oceans, and leaves a mark in sediments. Our own signal is already in the rock record.
  • Radioactive fallout. Nuclear testing produced isotopes — plutonium, caesium, iodine — that will remain detectable for millions of years.
  • Plastics and synthetic molecules. Novel organic compounds that do not occur naturally, and would persist as chemical traces even if the objects themselves were destroyed.
  • Fossil fuel depletion. A civilisation that burned the easy coal and oil leaves a geological record of something that was there and is no longer.
  • Technofossils and altered sedimentation. Cities, roads and mines change erosion patterns; the “urban stratum” is already being described.
  • Nitrogen and phosphorus cycles. Fertiliser production and agriculture leave global chemical fingerprints.
Their conclusion, in two parts

For the deep past: a pre-human industrial civilisation is very unlikely — there is no such signature in the record — but the question of detectability is not trivial. Surface structures are erased by erosion and subduction within a few million years; a civilisation 100 million years old might leave only a thin chemical line.

For the present: our own signal is legible and will remain legible. The paper's real subject is the Anthropocene — what we are writing into the strata, and whether future geologists (or future civilisations) would read it.

Why the answer is not "yes, aliens"

The hypothesis is sometimes retold as evidence for a hidden predecessor civilisation, which inverts its logic entirely. Frank and Schmidt assume the null hypothesis — none existed — and test whether we could detect one if it had. Absence of a signal is evidence of absence, in a way that is unusually strong here, because we know exactly what to look for: we are producing the signature ourselves.

The comparison to make is with ancient astronauts, which starts from monuments and infers builders; the Silurian hypothesis starts from the rock and asks what a builder would leave. One predicts nothing. The other predicts a specific, searchable chemistry.

The uncomfortable reading

If industrial civilisations are short-lived — a few centuries of fossil-fuel use, then either collapse or transition — then the galaxy could be full of planets that hosted one briefly and left a chemical line nobody was around to read. That is a version of the Fermi problem that requires no hunters: not silence, but brevity.

Time Paradoxes

The grandfather paradox

If you could travel into your own past and prevent your grandparents from meeting, you would never be born — and so could never have travelled back. It is the cleanest statement of why backward time travel looks logically dangerous.

Physicists take it seriously for a specific reason: general relativity permits solutions with closed timelike curves (CTCs) — paths through spacetime that loop back to their own past. Gödel found one in 1949, in a rotating universe; others appear in solutions for rotating black holes and traversable wormholes.

So the question is not "is it imaginable?" but "does the mathematics of relativity survive the loop?"

Novikov's self-consistency

In the 1980s, Igor Novikov and collaborators proposed a resolution: the laws of physics are self-consistent, so only those histories with no contradictions can occur. You can travel back — but something will always prevent the patricide. The gun jams, you change your mind, you were adopted.

This is not a trick; it is a constraint on solutions. Thorne and others worked through billiard-ball models in wormhole spacetimes, showing that consistent solutions exist and that inconsistent ones are excluded. The cost is that free will, in the past, becomes a strange notion: you can do what you like, but only what was already consistent.

Stephen Hawking disliked the whole business and proposed the chronology protection conjecture in 1992: the laws of physics conspire to prevent CTCs from forming, because quantum effects diverge at the boundary. It remains a conjecture. Nobody has proved it, and nobody has found a working time machine.

The honest status

No CTC has ever been observed. Every known solution requires exotic matter — negative energy density — or a universe with unphysical properties. It is a mathematical possibility, not an engineering one.

The paradox is a signal, not a refutation. When a theory permits contradictions, the usual reading is that the theory is incomplete at that boundary, not that the universe is inconsistent.

Bootstrap paradoxes are worse. An object or idea with no origin — a watch you give yourself, a song you learned from the person you taught — is not contradictory but inexplicable, which some physicists find more troubling than the grandfather.

White holes

Take the equations for a black hole and run them backwards. You get a region that nothing can enter and everything must leave — a white hole. It is not a separate theory; it is the same geometry under time reversal.

White holes appear in the full Schwarzschild solution, in some models of black hole evaporation, and in bounce cosmologies where a collapsing universe re-expands. Some popular accounts suggest the Big Bang was a white hole. That is a metaphor with a caveat: the Big Bang is not an explosion into pre-existing space, and there is no exterior from which matter could be emerging.

No white hole has ever been observed. Any would be spectacular: an object radiating matter outward from a horizon nothing can cross, and the radiation would be detectable. The absence is itself informative — it is one reason physicists expect the full theory of quantum gravity to forbid them.

What the fiction gets right

Stories that use branching timelines — travel back, create a new branch — are not doing relativity; they are switching to a many-worlds-like picture, which conveniently removes the paradox. That is a legitimate narrative choice, and it is not physics. The distinction matters because it is the same one this archive draws between the interpretation and the story built on top of it.

Gaia

What Lovelock proposed

In 1972 the chemist James Lovelock published a short paper in Atmospheric Environment arguing that the Earth's atmosphere is in a state far from chemical equilibrium — oxygen and methane coexisting, for instance, when they should react — and that this disequilibrium is maintained by life. Later, with the biologist Lynn Margulis, he developed the idea into the Gaia hypothesis: the planet's biological and physical systems function together as a self-regulating whole that tends to keep conditions habitable.

The evidence he pointed to was real and remains striking: the atmosphere's composition, the long-term stability of ocean salinity, the regulation of surface temperature over hundreds of millions of years despite a brightening Sun.

Daisyworld: making it testable

The obvious objection was that the hypothesis was teleological — it described the planet as keeping itself habitable, which sounds like purpose. So Lovelock and Andrew Watson built a model in 1983: Daisyworld, a planet covered in two kinds of daisy, dark and light, whose growth changes the planet's albedo in a way that stabilises temperature as the Sun brightens.

The model works with no foresight and no cooperation. Each daisy just grows where it can. The regulation emerges. That was the important move: it showed that planetary-scale stability does not require a planet-scale intention.

The objection that still bites

Natural selection acts on individuals, not planets. Richard Dawkins and others made the decisive criticism: there is no mechanism by which a planet that regulates well out-reproduces one that does not. Gaia, in its strong form, has no unit of selection.

Free riders break it. Any organism that stops contributing and just consumes the regulated conditions would do better — so unregulated systems should win, unless there are additional constraints.

Regulation can be coincidence. A stable property may be a boundary condition of the system rather than something maintained by life. The history of the planet includes mass extinctions and ice ages; it is not a thermostat that has never failed.

What happened next

The scientific community largely did what it does with an over-strong claim: it kept the useful part and dropped the metaphysics. Modern Earth system science studies the same feedbacks — the carbon cycle, the silicate weathering thermostat, ocean circulation, the role of life in atmospheric chemistry — without claiming the planet is an organism.

The terminology survived in a weaker form: "Gaia-like feedbacks", "the Earth system". Lovelock himself moved on to stronger claims in later books — that the planet would punish us (The Revenge of Gaia), and eventually that humans and machines would merge into a self-regulating planetary intelligence (Novacene). Those are Lovelock's opinions, not findings, and they should be filed that way.

Why it belongs in this archive

Because it is the best example of a "fringe" idea that was partly right, and of how that gets remembered wrongly in both directions. Believers cite Gaia as proof that the planet is a living being; sceptics cite its rejection as proof that the whole idea was nonsense. Both are wrong: the strong claim failed, the weak claim is textbook.

The rule that emerges is the archive's most useful one: when a claim is rejected, ask which version was rejected. The same applies to Jaynes, to dark forest, and to the lost continents.

Mutants & “Superpowers”

First, the word

In genetics a mutation is simply a change in a DNA sequence. Most are neutral; many are harmful; a few are useful. Every difference between any two people is the result of mutations, which means the comic-book sense of “mutant” — a separate species with powers — is a category error with a very long shadow.

The webbed-up version is still worth taking seriously, because the real variants are stranger than the fiction and, unlike the fiction, they are published.

1. Bones that do not break: LRP5

In 2002, a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine described a family with a striking trait: exceptionally dense bones, a wide and deep jaw, and a bony ridge on the roof of the mouth, but otherwise normal. The cause was a single amino-acid change — valine for glycine at position 171 — in a gene called LRP5, part of the Wnt signalling pathway that regulates bone formation.

The mutation is gain-of-function: bone formation markers are markedly elevated while resorption is normal. Carriers are, in effect, resistant to osteoporosis. A 2023 review counted 19 such gain-of-function variants across 113 patients in 33 families, causing a rare condition called autosomal dominant osteosclerosis.

This is the closest thing in the literature to a real “unbreakable” trait. It also comes with costs: thickened skull, nerve compression, headaches, facial paralysis in some cases. Biology rarely gives anything for free.

2. Living where the air is thin: EPAS1

Tibetans live and work above 4,000 m, where visitors develop headaches, breathlessness and dangerous swelling. The adaptation is genetic and it is unusually well documented.

A 2010 Science paper sequencing 50 Tibetan exomes found the strongest signal of natural selection at EPAS1, a hypoxia-response transcription factor, with a 78% allele-frequency difference between Tibetan and Han samples — described as the fastest allele frequency change observed at any human gene. The favoured version keeps haemoglobin from rising too high, avoiding thick blood.

Then the plot thickened: the beneficial EPAS1 haplotype came from Denisovans, an extinct human relative, by introgression — a 2016 Human Genetics paper traces a 32.7 kb Denisovan haplotype across Himalayan populations, correlating with altitude. Andean highlanders have a different, convergently selected variant, reported in Science Advances in 2024.

So “superpowered highlanders” is real, and the power was inherited from a species that no longer exists.

3. The sickle-cell bargain

A single change in the beta-globin gene produces sickle-cell trait. Two copies cause serious disease. One copy confers substantial resistance to malaria — which is why the allele is common in regions where malaria is endemic. It is the standard textbook example of heterozygote advantage, and of a mutation that is simultaneously protective and dangerous depending on dose.

4. Seeing a fourth colour

Most people have three types of cone cell. A small proportion of women carry four distinct cone variants — tetrachromacy — and behavioural tests suggest some of them discriminate colours that trichromats cannot. The effect is subtle and contested in degree, not in mechanism.

5. Gigantism is not a superpower

Robert Wadlow reached 2.72 m (8 ft 11 in) and is the tallest person in reliable medical record. His height came from pituitary gigantism — a tumour driving excess growth hormone — and it killed him at 22, from an infection related to a brace he needed in order to walk. The tallest humans in history were, without exception, people with a serious endocrine disease.

This matters for the giants dossier: the maximum plausible human height is set by the square-cube law — bone cross-section grows with the square of scale while mass grows with the cube — and by the circulatory system. A ten-foot human is possible. A twenty-foot one is not, and the fossil record shows no hominin that tried.

What radiation actually does

Radiation raises mutation rates; it does not grant abilities. The wildlife around Chernobyl is a real natural experiment — populations of birds, insects and mammals show elevated mutation and some adaptation — but the findings are about damage, tolerance and species composition, not about animals acquiring new powers.

The fiction gets one thing right, though: mutations are the raw material of evolution. The difference is that evolution selects on populations over thousands of generations, and it does not have a plot.

Why this dossier belongs here

Because “mutants” and “superpowers” are the last stop of the same argument that runs through the giants and dragon pages: that the natural world must once have contained something categorically beyond us. It did not. It contained variations, most of them costly, a few of them extraordinary — and all of them documented in journals anyone can read.

Creationism and the Alternatives to Darwin

First, what the theory actually says

"Darwinism" is mostly a word used by critics. Modern evolutionary biology is not 1859 natural selection alone; it is a set of claims that have different levels of support, and it is worth stating them separately, because most arguments against "Darwinism" attack a version nobody defends.

  1. Common descent. Living things share ancestors; the pattern of life is a branching tree. Supported by genetics, fossils, biogeography and molecular evidence, independently.
  2. Mechanisms. Mutation, recombination, selection, drift, migration and developmental constraint change populations over time. The existence of these is not controversial; their relative importance is debated.
  3. Deep time. The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old and life about 3.8 billion. Supported by physics, chemistry and multiple independent dating methods.
  4. Speciation. Populations split into reproductively isolated species. Observed directly, in the field and in the lab.

None of this requires anyone to be an atheist, and many biologists are not. The archive's job here is narrower: does the evidence offered against evolution do what it claims?

The case against, claim by claim

Twelve of the most common arguments, each stated in its strongest form and checked. Count at the bottom: of the twelve, none supports the conclusion that evolution is false.

ClaimWhat is offeredWhat the evidence showsVerdict
There are no transitional fossilsGaps between major groups; "missing links"Tiktaalik (2006) for the fish–tetrapod transition; Archaeopteryx and the feathered dinosaurs; the whale series (Pakicetus, Ambulocetus, Basilosaurus); dozens of hominins. Gaps remain at fine resolution — that is what a fossil record doesFalse
The Cambrian explosion shows animals appeared suddenlyMost animal body plans appear in a short window, with no ancestorsThe window is roughly 20 million years, not instant; Ediacaran and Cambrian stem groups precede and surround it. The tempo is a genuine research question, and it does not imply separate creationPartly true
Some systems are irreducibly complexBehe: the bacterial flagellum could not evolve because all its parts are neededHomologous systems with fewer parts exist (the type III secretion system), and co-option is documented. The claim was tested in court in 2005 and produced no peer-reviewed research programmeFalse
Evolution breaks the second law of thermodynamicsOrder cannot increase without a designerThe law applies to closed systems. Earth is open, bathed in sunlight, and entropy increases overall. This argument has been rejected by physicists, including religious onesFalse
Radiometric dating is unreliableAssumptions about decay rates and closed systemsDecay constants are measured and stable; isochron methods test the assumptions; results cross-check against tree rings, varves, ice layers and each other across methodsFalse
No new species has ever been observedSpeciation is inferred, never seenDocumented repeatedly: a new finch lineage on Daphne Major (2018, reproductive isolation in three generations), cichlids in a Nicaraguan crater lake in under 10,000 years, apple-maggot host shifts, polyploid plantsFalse
Mutations cannot add informationRandom changes only destroy functionAntibiotic resistance, nylon-degrading enzymes, lactase persistence, malaria resistance in heterozygotes — and Lenski's long-term E. coli experiment, where a new metabolic ability evolved and was traced to its mutationsFalse
Evolution is "only a theory"The word "theory" means a guessIn science a theory is an explanatory framework that has survived testing. Germ theory and plate tectonics are "only theories" in the same senseFalse
Human and chimp DNA cannot be that similar98% similarity is a myth or a trickWhole-genome comparisons give roughly 98–99% identity in aligned sequence, with differences concentrated in indels and regulatory regions; shared broken genes and shared endogenous retroviruses are independent corroborationFalse
"Vestigial" organs are not vestigialThe appendix has a function; the word is misleadingFair as far as it goes: "vestigial" means reduced, not useless, and the appendix example is poor. Whale pelvic bones, the human coccyx and the broken vitamin-C gene are stronger cases — and they remain evidence of ancestryPartly true
Haeckel faked the embryo drawingsTextbook illustrations were exaggerated to show similarityTrue. The drawings were simplified and misleading, and the case is a real caution about textbook images. It changes nothing about the genetic and fossil evidence, which did not exist in 1874True, irrelevant
Fossil hoaxes show the field is unreliablePiltdown Man, Archaeoraptor, the Ica stonesAll real hoaxes — and all exposed by scientists, not by critics. Piltdown was unmasked in 1953 by dating and anatomy; Archaeoraptor was retracted by National Geographic in 2000True, irrelevant
8Claims tested and false
2Partly true, not decisive
2True but irrelevant
0Support the conclusion

The alternatives, and what kind of thing each is

"Alternative to evolution" bundles together very different proposals. Some are religious positions that make no scientific claim; some claim to be science and have been tested; some are abandoned scientific ideas; one or two are live research programmes.

PositionWhat it claimsStatus
Young Earth creationismThe Earth is about 6,000 years old (Ussher, 1650); a global flood laid down the fossil record; radiometric dating is wrongDebunked — contradicted by physics, geology, ice cores, tree rings and the fossil sequence itself. Still the position of Answers in Genesis and the ICR
Old Earth creationismDeep time is real; creation occurred in stages, or the "days" are ages, or there was a gap between Genesis 1:1 and 1:2Theological — makes no testable scientific claim, and does not dispute the age of the Earth
Intelligent designSome biological features are best explained by an intelligent cause; ID is a scientific alternativeNot science — ruled so in Kitzmiller v. Dover (2005) after a six-week trial; no peer-reviewed research programme; the Discovery Institute's "Wedge" strategy document describes the goal as cultural, not scientific
Theistic evolutionGod creates through evolution; mainstream science is acceptedCompatible — the position of Francis Collins, BioLogos and most religious scientists. It is a theological stance, not a rival to the evidence
LamarckismCharacteristics acquired in life are inheritedAbandoned — no mechanism for most traits. Epigenetic inheritance is real but is not Lamarckism, and creationist use of "epigenetics" as a rescue is a category error
OrthogenesisEvolution moves in a predetermined direction, driven from withinAbandoned — the appearance of direction is explained by selection and constraint
SaltationismNew forms appear in single large jumpsMostly rejected — though punctuated equilibrium (Gould and Eldredge, 1972) is a real, accepted argument about the pace of change, not about jumps between body plans
Origin-of-life chemistryRNA world, metabolism-first, alkaline vent scenarios (Miller–Urey 1953; Gilbert 1986; Lane)Live debate — how life began is genuinely unsolved. This is a gap in knowledge, not evidence against common descent
PanspermiaLife arrived from elsewhere; Crick and Orgel proposed directed panspermia in 1973Untested — moves the origin problem rather than solving it, and has no positive evidence
Cosmic ancestry, Raelian "scientific creation"Life was engineered by extraterrestrials; evolution is a lieFringe — no evidence, no testable mechanism, and the same category error about what counts as data
Aquatic apeHuman features (hairlessness, fat, breath control) reflect a semi-aquatic phaseRejected — an honest heterodox idea (Hardy 1960, Morgan) that has not survived testing; it concerns human evolution, not common descent

Where the real arguments are

If you want the actual live controversies in evolutionary biology — the ones biologists argue about in journals — they are these, and none of them questions common descent:

  • How life began. No consensus; competing chemistries, none demonstrated end to end.
  • Tempo. Gradualism versus punctuated equilibrium; how fast the Cambrian radiation really was.
  • Selection versus drift. How much of the genome changed neutrally (Kimura, 1968) rather than adaptively.
  • How much DNA is functional. ENCODE's 2012 "80% functional" claim is disputed; critics put the figure far lower.
  • Levels of selection. Gene, organism, group; kin selection versus multi-level selection.
  • The extended evolutionary synthesis. Niche construction, developmental bias and plasticity as causes, not just consequences (Pigliucci, Müller).
  • Consciousness and mind. Not explained by evolutionary theory, and not obviously an evolutionary question.

These are disagreements about mechanism and emphasis inside a framework whose core has not moved. That distinction — real debate versus a failed challenge — is the whole point of this page.

The legal record

In the United States the question has been litigated repeatedly, and the pattern is consistent: religious positions may be taught, but they may not be presented as science in public school science classes.

  • 1925

    Scopes "monkey trial", Tennessee: a teacher convicted under a law banning evolution teaching. The conviction was overturned on a technicality.

  • 1968

    Epperson v. Arkansas: the Supreme Court strikes down bans on teaching evolution as religiously motivated.

  • 1987

    Edwards v. Aguillard: "balanced treatment" laws requiring creation science are unconstitutional.

  • 2005

    Kitzmiller v. Dover: after a six-week trial, Judge Jones rules that intelligent design is not science and that the Dover policy was religious. He calls the board's conduct "breathtaking inanity".

The archive's position

Creationism is a religious position and is entitled to be argued as one. It is not entitled to be called science, and the specific factual claims it makes — a 6,000-year-old Earth, a global flood, no transitional fossils — have been tested and failed. Theistic evolution shows that accepting the evidence is compatible with belief; that is a live option, and it is not what this page is arguing against.

The wider pattern is the one in the giants dossier and flood myths: a claim that begins as theology, borrows the language of science, and then treats the absence of proof as proof. The Silurian hypothesis is a useful contrast — a genuinely scientific speculation about deep time, stated with its own falsification conditions.

The Simpsons Predictions

The count first

5Exact hits
4Partial hits
5Coincidences
5Fakes & wrong
2Still awaited

Twenty-one claims, scored below. "Exact" means the episode named a specific thing that later happened. "Partial" means the broad shape matched but a detail did not. "Coincidence" means the scene exists but was not about the future at all. "Fake" means the screenshot was doctored, the clip spliced, or the episode never happened.

Why a 35-year cartoon looks psychic

Four things, in order of how much work they do.

  1. Volume. More than 750 episodes over 35 years contain tens of thousands of jokes about the future. If a show makes a thousand guesses and a hundred are checkable, roughly a handful will look uncanny. "The more unlikely thing would be that we never predicted anything," the showrunner Matt Selman has said.
  2. Vagueness plus retrofitting. A joke about "President Trump" in 2000 became "a prediction" in 2016. A brochure that reads "$9" became "9/11" in 2001. The claim is written after the event, and the episode is re-read to fit it.
  3. Informed guessing. The writers were reading the news: Trump was flirting with a 2000 run, Disney was already buying studios, Holmström was a plausible Nobel pick, and a tiger act was dangerous by definition. Al Jean's summary: predicting FIFA was corrupt is "a very easy prediction".
  4. Selection. Nobody shares the 99% that did not happen. The list you have seen is a highlight reel assembled backwards from the outcomes.

None of this means the coincidences are not strange. The 9/11 brochure genuinely unsettles the people who made it. Strange is not the same as predictive, and a coincidence is not evidence of a hidden script — it is evidence that a long-running show generates a lot of text.

And the films?

The same accounting applies, with one difference: films set a date on screen, which makes them easy to score. Eight of the most-cited cases:

Film, yearWhat it showedWhat happenedVerdict
Network (1976)News as rage-driven entertainment; a network exploiting a ranting hostTalk-news, outrage formats and reality television became the business modelHit
The Truman Show (1998)A life broadcast as entertainment, with an audience complicitReality TV and influencer life followed within yearsHit
Back to the Future Part II (1989)2015: video calls, wearable screens, biometrics, drones, hoverboards, flying carsVideo calls and wearables yes; hoverboards and flying cars no. Even the "Cubs win" newspaper is a year off (2016, not 2015)Partial
2001: A Space Odyssey (1968)Tablets, video calls, space tourism, a Moon base, a Jupiter missionTablets and video calls are ordinary; the bases and missions are notPartial
Minority Report (2002)Personalised ads, gesture interfaces, iris scanning, self-driving cars, precrimeThe first four arrived in some form; precrime did notPartial
Contagion (2011)A bat virus, airborne transmission, fomites, a vaccine race, anti-vax backlashCOVID-19 matched the shape closely — because the film was researched with epidemiologistsPartial

Film count: 2 hits, 5 partial, 1 miss. Notice what the hits have in common — they are satires of trends already visible when they were made, not forecasts of technology.

The honest summary

Of twenty-one famous Simpsons claims, five are exact, four are partly right, five are coincidences read backwards, five are fakes or simply wrong, and two are still waiting. The films score about the same way, and for the same reason: stories are good at extrapolating trends and bad at naming dates.

If you want the general version of this, the archive's prophecies dossier covers the mechanics, and false memory explains why people remember a prediction they never saw.

How to use a directory like this

Pick the institution that would be embarrassed by the claim. If the claim is geological, check the geological survey. If it is about a manuscript, check the library that holds it. If it is about a secret programme, check the agency’s own FOIA reading room — because that is where the documents that proved six real conspiracies actually live.
