FTX

The structure

FTX was an exchange: customers deposited crypto and dollars to trade. Alameda Research was a trading firm, also founded by Sam Bankman-Fried and run by Caroline Ellison. The two were supposed to be separate.

In November 2022, a leaked balance sheet showed Alameda's assets were largely illiquid tokens issued by FTX itself. A rival exchange's decision to sell its holdings triggered a run, a rescue deal collapsed, and FTX filed for bankruptcy within days.

What the investigation found

The bankruptcy estate's investigators found that customer deposits had been transferred to Alameda to cover trading losses, venture investments and political donations. A code feature in FTX's systems allowed Alameda to carry a negative balance — effectively an unlimited line of credit from customer funds.

Bankman-Fried was convicted in November 2023 on seven counts including wire fraud and money laundering, and sentenced in March 2024 to 25 years. Ellison, Gary Wang and Nishad Singh pleaded guilty and testified.

What makes it a documented conspiracy rather than a failure

Intent was established at trial. The prosecution's case rested on insiders who described knowingly moving customer money, and on documents and code showing the mechanism.

The audit trail exists. Unlike a rumour, this is a case where the ledger, the chat logs and the testimony are all available to courts. The estate has been recovering assets and distributing them to creditors.

It is not evidence that crypto is inherently fraudulent — a distinction the coverage often blurred. It is evidence that an unregulated custodian with weak controls can lose customer assets, which is an old story with new vocabulary.

The lesson for reading claims

The warning signs were public: an exchange also running a proprietary trading firm, a token whose value supported the balance sheet, a founder treated as a genius by the press, and no meaningful audit.

That is a checklist, not hindsight. It is the same structure this archive applies to proven plots: follow the custody of the money, and ask who could verify the claim and did not.

Pegasus

What Pegasus does

Pegasus is commercial spyware sold by the Israeli firm NSO Group to governments. Early versions used links that had to be opened; later versions used 'zero-click' exploits — a crafted iMessage or WhatsApp message that compromises the device without interaction.

Once installed, it can read messages, capture keystrokes, record calls, exfiltrate photos and location, and turn on the microphone. Apple patched the FORCEDENTRY exploit in 2021 after researchers at the Citizen Lab identified it.

The Pegasus Project

In July 2021, seventeen media organisations published a collaborative investigation of 50,000 phone numbers selected for a leaked client list. Forensic analysis confirmed infection or attempted infection on phones belonging to journalists, human-rights defenders and politicians.

The reporting established three things: the spyware existed and worked as described; it was sold to states with poor human-rights records; and the targeting included people whose only crime was reporting or litigating.

What the evidence does and does not show

Documented: the capability, the customers, and specific infected devices confirmed by forensic analysis. NSO was placed on the U.S. Entity List in 2021 and Apple sued it in the same year.

Not documented: that every number on the list was targeted, or infected. A number in a client system is a selector, not proof of an attack — an important distinction the coverage often dropped.

Not established: the full customer list, or which governments ran which operations. NSO has said it sells only to vetted state agencies and has cancelled contracts; independent verification is not possible.

Why it belongs here

Because it is a case where a conspiracy theory — governments secretly reading activists' phones — turned out to be substantially true, with the caveat that the mechanism was commercial rather than a single global plot.

It also shows the archive's rule in reverse: the documented version of a frightening claim is usually narrower and more specific than the rumour, and it is more useful because it can be acted on. Apple's patch, the Entity List designation and the lawsuits are consequences of the specific finding, not of the mood.

The Panama Papers

The leak

In April 2016, the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and more than 100 media partners published findings from the internal archive of Mossack Fonseca, a Panamanian law firm specialising in offshore companies. The data covered four decades and around 214,000 entities.

The documents showed how shell companies, bearer shares and nominee directors were used to hold assets while obscuring ownership — by politicians, business figures, celebrities and, in some cases, sanctions evaders and criminals.

The consequences

Iceland's prime minister resigned after revelations about undeclared offshore holdings. Pakistan's prime minister was disqualified by the Supreme Court. Several countries opened criminal investigations, and the EU moved on beneficial-ownership registers.

Mossack Fonseca closed in 2018.

The nuance the headlines missed

Offshore is not the same as illegal. Many structures were lawful tax planning; holding a company in Panama was not a crime. The story was about secrecy, conflicts of interest and the enabling industry — and about the specific cases where the law was broken.

Ownership, not evasion, was the core finding. The most important number in the reporting was not the money but the opacity: how little of the world's asset ownership could be traced to a human being.

The follow-up matters. The same consortium published the Paradise Papers (2017) and Pandora Papers (2021), showing the structure was systemic rather than one firm's practice.

Why it is a documented case

The documents are primary evidence, the reporting was collaborative and independently checked, and the legal consequences are on the record in multiple jurisdictions. It is the model for how a leak becomes a finding rather than a rumour.

It is also the honest counterweight to the archive's more speculative material: the scale of hidden wealth is genuinely larger than most people assume, and the evidence for it did not come from inference. It came from the files.

The Riemann Hypothesis

The statement

The Riemann zeta function is a sum over the integers, extended to complex numbers by analytic continuation. It has "trivial" zeros at the negative even integers, and infinitely many others. The hypothesis, proposed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, is that every non-trivial zero has a real part of exactly one half — that they all sit on a single vertical line in the complex plane.

That sounds like an obscure fact about a function. It is not. The zeros control the error term in the prime counting function: how far the actual number of primes below x can drift from the smooth estimate. If the zeros lie on the line, the primes are about as well-behaved as they could possibly be. If any zero sits off it, the primes have a hidden irregularity, and the error grows.

Why anyone believes it

Not because it has been proved. Because it has been checked, relentlessly, and because several independent lines of reasoning expect it:

  • Computation. The first 10 trillion zeros have been verified to lie on the line. This is evidence in the ordinary sense, and it is not proof: a counterexample could sit at 1040.
  • Function fields. The analogous statement for curves over finite fields was proved by André Weil in the 1940s. There is a working model in which the phenomenon is true and understood.
  • Random matrix theory. Hugh Montgomery and Freeman Dyson noticed in 1972 that the spacing statistics of the zeros match the eigenvalues of random Hermitian matrices — the same statistics as heavy atomic nuclei. Nobody knows why, but it is a real and testable correspondence.
  • Hilbert–Pólya. If the zeros are the eigenvalues of some self-adjoint operator, the hypothesis follows from spectral theory. Nobody has found the operator.
Why "unsolved" is not "contested"

There are no camps. This is the crucial difference between a conjecture and a controversy. Nobody publishes against the Riemann Hypothesis; the disagreement is entirely about how to prove it, not whether it is true.

It carries a million-dollar prize and a much larger consequence. It is one of the Clay Institute's Millennium Problems. A proof would immediately sharpen results across number theory — including, in conditional form, many statements about primes that are currently assumed.

Its failure would be worse than its absence. A counterexample would not just leave the question open; it would invalidate a large body of published work that assumes the hypothesis, and it would mean the primes are more erratic than anyone expects.

What has actually been proved

Real theorems exist nearby, and they show how progress in this area looks. Hardy proved in 1914 that infinitely many zeros lie on the line. Bohr and Landau showed that almost all zeros are arbitrarily close to it. Levinson and later Conrey established that a positive proportion — over 40% — of zeros are on the line. None of these is the hypothesis, and the gap between "a positive proportion" and "all" has resisted every technique for a century.

There are also relatives worth knowing: the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis extends the claim to other L-functions, and the Riemann Hypothesis itself would imply weak forms of the Goldbach and twin-prime conjectures — which is why those problems are often described as downstream of this one.

Why it is hard

The honest answer is that nobody has a mechanism. Proofs in this field usually come from a structure nobody knew existed — Weil's proof came from algebraic geometry, the prime number theorem from complex analysis. The Riemann Hypothesis is waiting for a structure, and the random-matrix match is the strongest hint that one is there.

It is also worth saying what the hypothesis does not claim. It says nothing about whether primes are "random"; it constrains the error in counting them. Popular accounts often describe it as "the primes follow a hidden pattern", which is poetry rather than mathematics.

How to read the status

If you see a claim that the Riemann Hypothesis has been proved, the correct response is to look for the verification: a proof would be a short paper with a long referee process, announced through a journal, not a preprint with a press release. The 2018 Atiyah claim is the standard cautionary example — presented at a conference, never substantiated.

Where to go next: the open problems index lists the conjectures that sit downstream, and the frontier index covers the physics-adjacent debates, which have the opposite problem — plenty of mechanisms, no data.

Alzheimer's

The orthodoxy

For thirty years the dominant account has been the amyloid cascade: amyloid-beta fragments clump into plaques, plaques trigger tau tangles inside neurons, neurons die, memory goes. It is a clean chain, and it produced a generation of drugs designed to clear amyloid.

Those drugs mostly failed. Then, in the last few years, two of them worked — modestly. That is the fact that reorganises the whole argument.

What the antibodies changed

Lecanemab and donanemab, both approved in the United States, remove amyloid from the brain and slow measurable decline by roughly a quarter to a third on clinical scales over 18 months. The effects are real, statistically robust and small. They also come with a serious risk: amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, including brain swelling and micro-haemorrhages, which require monitoring.

Read carefully, this is evidence for amyloid mattering and against the simplest version of the story. If amyloid were merely a bystander, removing it should do nothing. If it were the whole cause, removing it should do much more than 27%.

Where the list's framings need correcting

"Amyloid is a protective response" is a hypothesis, not a finding. The infection account (herpes simplex, P. gingivalis) has real supporting work, but no trial has shown that treating an infection changes dementia course.

The fraud story is narrower than it is usually told. An investigation published by Science in 2022 reported manipulated images in a 2006 paper on a specific amyloid assembly; that paper was subsequently retracted. It did not falsify the amyloid cascade, and it does not mean the plaques are irrelevant.

"Type 3 diabetes" is a metaphor with a real observation inside it. Brain insulin signalling is impaired in Alzheimer's. Intranasal insulin trials have mostly failed to produce benefit, which is the part usually left out.

Amyloid alone does not equal dementia. A substantial fraction of people with plaques on a PET scan are cognitively normal. Something else — vascular damage, tau spread, inflammation, resilience — decides who converts.

The better-supported shift

The most useful change in the last decade is not a rival theory but a change of timing. Biomarkers — especially plasma p-tau217 — now detect the disease process years before symptoms. That reframes Alzheimer's as a decades-long process with a long silent phase, which is why prevention trials are the interesting frontier and why "cure the plaques at the end" was always likely to disappoint.

It also explains the field's loudest argument. If the process begins twenty years before memory loss, then a drug given at diagnosis is being given very late, and a 27% slowing in late disease is not obviously a failure of the hypothesis — it may be a failure of timing. That reading is respectable and unproven; the prevention trials will decide it.

The competing accounts, honestly weighted

  • Infection and immunity — genuine epidemiological signals, plausible mechanism, no successful intervention yet.
  • Vascular contribution — strong and underweighted: most dementia in old age is mixed pathology.
  • Tau spread — correlates better with symptoms than amyloid does, which is why tau PET is now central.
  • Metabolic/insulin — real signal, weak therapeutic record.
  • Amyloid — necessary-ish, insufficient, and the only target with disease-modifying drugs that work at all.

What would settle it

A prevention trial in biomarker-positive people with no symptoms, showing that clearing amyloid before damage begins prevents decline. That is running now. Until it reports, the honest position is the uncomfortable one: the leading hypothesis is neither vindicated nor dead, and the field spent two decades overconfident in both directions.

Enshittification

The claim

Cory Doctorow's term, coined in 2022 and elaborated in a 2023 essay, describes a predictable lifecycle for platforms that sit between users and suppliers:

  1. Good to users. The platform subsidises itself, loses money, and is delightful — it has to be, to win the network.
  2. Good to business customers. Once users are locked in, it starts charging the suppliers — the sellers, the drivers, the publishers, the app developers — and delivers them the audience it captured.
  3. Abuse both. Once both sides are locked in, it charges suppliers for reach and charges users in attention, data and degraded service, extracting the difference for shareholders.
  4. Death, or irrelevance. Users leave, or regulators intervene, and the cycle ends.

The mechanism is not greed in the abstract; it is switching costs plus captured audiences. You can only mistreat someone who cannot easily leave, which is why the pattern is strongest in markets with network effects and weakest where switching is cheap.

Why it is documented rather than speculative

The fable is new; the behaviour has court records. Amazon's own advertising business grew while its marketplace search results filled with sponsored placements — the seller pays to reach customers who were already there. The U.S. FTC sued Amazon in 2023 over exactly this dynamic. Apple's App Store takes a commission from developers who have no alternative distribution channel, a fact at the centre of multiple antitrust cases. Search results pages have filled with advertising and answer-boxes that keep the click on the platform.

None of those facts is in dispute. What is in dispute is whether they add up to a law of platform economics or a description of a particular regulatory moment.

Where the idea is weaker than its reputation

It is not a theory with predictions. As stated it can accommodate almost any outcome: a platform that stays good is "not yet enshittified"; one that dies is the fourth stage. That flexibility is why economists have been slow to adopt the word.

The word is a moral judgement, and that is the point. Doctorow is an advocate, and the essay is an argument for regulation (interoperability, end-to-end neutrality, privacy law). That does not make it wrong — it makes it a brief, not a measurement.

Some "degradation" is competition working. Rising ad load can reflect a market maturing, not a conspiracy. The two-sided-market literature predicts much of this without needing a villain.

Counter-examples exist. Some platforms have improved and kept users: message apps that stayed free, Wikipedia, Linux. The pattern is common, not universal, and the exceptions are informative.

The testable core

Strip the rhetoric and there are testable claims: (1) quality declines as market concentration rises; (2) this shows up first in features that are hard for users to verify — search ranking, feed ordering, ad load; (3) regulation that lowers switching costs reverses it. European interoperability rules and the DMA are, in effect, the experiment.

The evidence so far partly supports (1) and (2). The third is being run in public, and the results will be more informative than another decade of argument.

Why it belongs in this archive

Because it is the rare case where a phrase coined on a blog became the standard description used by regulators, and where the accusation is largely true and the causal story is contested. That is the same position as the proven plots and the opposite of the dead internet theory, which names a real worry and then overstates the mechanism.

Göbekli Tepe

What is actually there

On a limestone ridge in southeastern Turkey, about 15 km from Şanlıurfa, are at least eight circular stone enclosures built from T-shaped limestone pillars, some weighing 16 tons, carved with foxes, snakes, boars, cranes and scorpions. The site is dated to roughly 9500–8000 BC — before pottery, before metal, before writing, and before farming arrived in the region.

That date is the reason for its fame. The excavator Klaus Schmidt argued that the scale and craft implied organised labour, specialist skills and ritual purpose among people who were still hunter-gatherers. The headline followed: the temple came before the farm.

The claim that outran the evidence

"Hunter-gatherers built a temple, so religion came before agriculture" is a strong reading of a site that has been only about 5% excavated. Three corrections matter:

  • The enclosures may not be temples. "Ritual" is an inference from carvings and arrangement, not a finding. Some researchers argue for domestic or communal use, with feasting and storage as plausible functions.
  • The builders were not necessarily pure foragers. Sedentary or semi-sedentary communities, wild-cereal harvesting and intensive gathering are all compatible with the evidence. The farming/hunting binary is the modern frame, not the site's.
  • It does not overturn the Neolithic. It revises the local sequence — complexity before domesticates in this region — and that is a real revision, not a revolution in world prehistory.
Claims to treat with suspicion

"It is 12,000 years old and was deliberately buried." The oldest enclosures are around 11,500 years old (calibrated), and the site was indeed backfilled — but the reason is unknown. Abandonment, rebuilding and intentional closure are all consistent.

"The pillars encode a calendar and record a comet strike." A 2024 paper proposed a solar-calendar reading of one enclosure; it has been widely criticised by specialists as over-reading the carvings. Treat it as a hypothesis, not a finding.

"It was built by an unknown civilisation." The builders are the local late-Epipaleolithic population, continuous with the region's archaeology. There is no vanished culture required.

"The site proves Atlantis / ancient astronauts." No. Every claim of that kind depends on ignoring the excavated assemblage — the tools, the faunal remains, the grinding stones.

What it genuinely changed

Before Göbekli Tepe, the textbook sequence was: farming, surplus, sedentism, then monuments. The site, together with Karahan Tepe and other Taş Tepeler sites, shows monumental construction by communities without domesticates — which means the causal arrow between farming and complexity is at least sometimes reversed, or at least entangled.

It also changed the practice of archaeology in the region: a large landscape project now studies the whole ridge complex rather than one hill, and the site has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 2018.

Why this entry is "live debate"

The dates and the objects are documented. What is contested is meaning: temple or village, ritual or feasting, specialised priesthood or communal labour. Those questions are exactly what the next decades of excavation will address — which is a healthier situation than either the "it rewrites everything" headline or the "it is just a hill" reaction.

Room-Temperature Superconductivity

What superconductivity is

Below a critical temperature, some materials carry current with exactly zero resistance and expel magnetic fields. The effect has been known since 1911, explained by BCS theory in 1957, and used commercially for decades — MRI magnets, maglev, particle-accelerator magnets.

The problem is temperature. Conventional superconductors need cryogenic cooling; the cuprates, discovered in 1986, work at up to about 130 K under ambient pressure, still far below a room at 293 K. Hydrides under extreme pressure have reached higher temperatures, but only inside a diamond anvil.

The two famous failures

LK-99 (2023). A Korean team posted preprints claiming a lead-apatite compound superconducts at ambient pressure and temperature. Within weeks, labs worldwide had reproduced the material and found no superconductivity; the resistance drop was traced to a copper-sulfide impurity, and the magnetic 'levitation' to ordinary diamagnetism. The claim collapsed in under a month.

The Dias retractions. Ranga Dias's high-pressure hydride results were retracted by Nature in 2023 after concerns about data handling; the University of Rochester later concluded misconduct. That case damaged trust in the whole high-pressure field, which had produced genuinely reproducible results in the same period.

Why the failures matter more than the hype

Reproduction is the test, not the press conference. In both cases the material was easy to make, and that is what killed the claims: hundreds of groups tried, and the effect was not there.

The mechanism was the tell. LK-99's proposed mechanism required a structural distortion that first-principles calculations did not support. When the theory is hand-waved and the data are noisy, the field now knows to wait.

The real frontier is different. Cuprates, iron-based superconductors, nickelates and hydrides under pressure are all live research areas with published, replicated results. None of them is room-temperature at ambient pressure, and the honest answer to 'when?' is that nobody knows.

What to watch

A genuine claim will look different: a material that several independent groups can synthesise, with resistance measured four ways, magnetic susceptibility consistent with perfect diamagnetism, and a specific heat anomaly at the transition. Any of those alone can be mimicked by artefacts.

The archive labels this 'live debate' because superconductivity is real and the search is active — not because the room-temperature claims are credible. They are not.

Sonoluminescence

The phenomenon

Sound waves in a liquid can trap a small gas bubble at a pressure node. As the wave compresses it, the bubble collapses violently, and for a fraction of a picosecond it emits a pulse of light. Single-bubble sonoluminescence was made stable in 1989, which is what turned a curiosity into a research field.

The flash is extremely short, the spectrum is broad and featureless, and the inferred conditions inside the collapse are extreme — thousands of kelvin at minimum, with estimates reaching much higher depending on the model.

The competing explanations

Adiabatic compression. The simplest account: the gas heats as it is crushed, and the flash is thermal emission from a hot, dense plasma.

Vaporised material. In some liquids, a little of the surrounding liquid enters the bubble and is vaporised, changing the spectrum — which is why the colour of the flash can depend on the liquid and the dissolved gas.

Micro-plasmas and shock waves. Refinements add ionisation, a shock front inside the bubble, and bremsstrahlung. Each version fits some of the data and not all of it.

The claim that keeps returning

Every few years, a paper or a press story suggests the bubble reaches conditions for nuclear fusion — 'sonofusion'. The 2002 Taleyarkhan claims in particular were investigated and contested, and independent replication failed.

The physics problem is scale: the energy in a collapsing bubble is tiny, and the fraction that could reach fusion conditions is smaller still. The measurements needed to settle it — temperature, density, duration — are at the limit of what can be inferred from a flash.

So the honest position is that sonoluminescence is a real, reproducible effect whose emission mechanism is still under debate, and whose most dramatic interpretation has not survived replication.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the phenomenon is not in doubt, the mechanism is genuinely unsettled, and the fringe version has attached itself to a real experiment. The archive's label reflects the real uncertainty and rejects the fusion claim.

It also sits next to turbulence as a reminder that classical fluid mechanics still contains unsolved problems — the equations are known, the solutions are not.

Turbulence

The problem

The Navier–Stokes equations describe how fluids move. They are known, they are used constantly, and they are not solved in general. Turbulence — the chaotic, multi-scale eddying of fast flow — is where the difficulty lives: energy cascades from large eddies to small ones, and the range of scales grows with the Reynolds number.

The Clay Institute's Millennium Problem is narrower and sharper than 'explain turbulence'. It asks whether, in three dimensions, smooth solutions always exist for all time, or whether they can blow up. Nobody knows.

What is actually used

Engineering does not wait for the proof. Aircraft design uses Reynolds-averaged models and large-eddy simulation; weather models use parametrisations; pipe flow uses empirical correlations that have been refined for a century.

The gap between practice and theory is the point: the models work in the regimes they were tuned for and fail outside them. That is why a new aircraft or a new reactor still needs wind tunnels and test campaigns.

Where the honest uncertainty sits

Existence and smoothness is the mathematical question — open, and worth a million dollars.

A predictive theory of turbulent statistics is the physical question — also open, and arguably harder, because it may not have the kind of clean answer mathematicians want.

Kolmogorov's scaling (1941) is the closest thing to a law: in the inertial range, energy spectrum follows a −5/3 power law. It is observed widely, and it is not a derivation from first principles for all flows.

Why it belongs with the open problems

Because it is the best example of a problem where 'we know the equation' and 'we understand the phenomenon' are very different statements, and where the gap has practical consequences — in climate models, in fusion confinement, in aircraft design.

The open problems index carries the mathematical statement; this page carries the physical one.

Time Crystals

The idea

Frank Wilczek proposed in 2012 that a system could have a ground state whose structure repeats periodically in time, the temporal analogue of a crystal lattice. The claim was immediately contested: a genuine ground state cannot move, because moving costs energy.

The resolution came from relaxing the definition. A discrete time crystal is driven periodically and responds at a different period — typically half or twice the drive — in a robust, many-body way. That is not perpetual motion; it is a subharmonic response protected by interactions and disorder.

What was built

In 2017, two groups published realisations: one using trapped ions with programmable disorder, one using nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond. Both observed the subharmonic response and its persistence, which is the signature.

Later work extended the idea to other platforms, and the related concept of a 'time crystal' in dissipative systems has been explored. The phenomenon is now a small but real corner of non-equilibrium physics.

What the name oversells

It is not perpetual motion. A discrete time crystal is driven; energy goes in. The protected pattern is the response, not a free lunch.

It is not a new state of matter in the everyday sense. It is a non-equilibrium phase, and its defining property is robustness of the period, not any exotic material behaviour.

Continuous time crystals — repeating without any drive — remain contentious, and the theorems that killed the original proposal still apply to closed systems in equilibrium.

Why it is documented rather than debated

Because the effect has been observed in independent platforms and published in peer-reviewed journals, with a clear signature that is hard to fake: the subharmonic response survives disorder and scales with system size.

That puts it in the same category as other quantum simulator results: a real phenomenon with a modest interpretation, which is more than most of the archive's material can claim. The contrast with the holographic principle is instructive — both are real physics, but only one is a tool you can build.

The Origin of Life

The two families

Genes first. The RNA world hypothesis notes that RNA can both store information and catalyse reactions. If a molecule could replicate itself and improve, Darwinian evolution starts before proteins or DNA. The problem is that RNA is hard to make prebiotically and unstable in water.

Metabolism first. An alternative starts with self-sustaining chemical cycles on mineral surfaces — proton gradients across iron-sulfide membranes, driven by geothermal energy. Replication comes later. The problem is that a cycle without a gene cannot inherit improvements.

The two locations

Alkaline hydrothermal vents. Natural proton gradients, mineral catalysts, and compartments in the rock. The 'inside-out' theory (Russell, Martin, Lane) argues the first cells were mineral structures, and the membrane came later.

Warm little ponds. Wet-dry cycles concentrate nucleotides, and UV and wet-dry chemistry can assemble RNA precursors. Laboratory work has produced nucleotides and short RNA chains under plausible conditions, though not self-replication.

What the experiments actually show

Nucleotides can be made under prebiotic conditions — several routes, none of them the whole story, and yields are low.

RNA can be made to evolve in the lab: directed evolution experiments produce ribozymes that polymerise RNA. That shows RNA can do the job, not that it did.

Protocells can be built from fatty acids, and they can host reactions. Again: a demonstration of possibility.

Nobody has a continuous, plausible chain from simple chemistry to a self-replicating, evolving system in one pot. That is the honest gap, and it is not a small one.

Why it is a live debate rather than a mystery

Because the disagreement is productive: it has generated specific, testable chemistry, and the camps are converging on a picture in which vents supply energy and gradients, ponds supply concentration and wet-dry cycling, and the order of genes and metabolism may differ by environment.

It is also the place where the archive's labels do the most work. 'We do not know' is not the same as 'it is impossible', and the difference is exactly what the evidence supports.

The First Eukaryote

The settled part

Lynn Margulis's endosymbiotic theory was resisted for years and is now standard: mitochondria descend from an alphaproteobacterium, and chloroplasts from a cyanobacterium. The evidence is genomic, structural and phylogenetic — mitochondria have their own DNA, bacterial-type ribosomes and a double membrane.

This is one of the archive's clean cases: a once-fringe idea that became textbook science because the molecular evidence arrived.

The open part

Who was the host? The traditional picture is an archaeon that engulfed a bacterium. An alternative, the 'inside-out' model, argues the bacterium was engulfed by protrusions of an archaeal cell. A third possibility is that the host was already complex, with a cytoskeleton and internal membranes.

When? Estimates range from about 1.6 to 2.7 billion years ago, depending on which fossils and molecular clocks you trust. The oldest uncontroversial eukaryote fossils are around 1.6 billion years old; some claims push earlier.

Was it one event or several? Asgard archaea — discovered in deep-sea sediments — carry many 'eukaryotic' genes, which suggests the host lineage was already part-way there before the merger.

Why this matters beyond a family tree

The merger is the reason complex life exists. A cell with mitochondria can generate far more energy per gene than a bacterium can, which is the basis of Lane and Martin's 'energetics' argument for why complexity arose once.

It is also a case study in how a theory becomes accepted: not by argument, but by a new kind of evidence — in this case, DNA sequencing of organisms nobody had cultured.

What the label means

'Live debate' here is about mechanism and timing, not about whether the merger happened. That is worth keeping separate, in the same way that the Gaia hypothesis has a settled core and an unsettled extension.

The next decade of work is comparative genomics of Asgard archaea and better constraints on the fossil record — neither of which is likely to overturn the endosymbiotic theory itself.

Where Viruses Came From

The three hypotheses

Virus-first. Viruses, or virus-like replicons, existed before cells and contributed to the RNA world. The problem: viruses need hosts to replicate, so a world of only viruses is hard to sustain.

Regressive. Viruses are degenerate cells that lost the machinery of life — the way some parasites do. The problem: the largest viruses (mimiviruses) have genes no cell would need to lose, and their genomes do not look like reduced cells.

Escaped genes. Viruses are fragments of cellular genomes that acquired a capsid and the ability to move between cells. The problem: this explains plasmids and transposons well, and giant viruses badly.

What the data say

Comparative genomics finds viral genes with no cellular homologues — the 'viral hallmark genes' — which supports deep viral ancestry for at least some lineages. It also finds clear cases of recent escape, which supports the third hypothesis for others.

The most likely answer is that all three happened, at different times and for different virus families. That is unsatisfying as a slogan and probably correct as biology.

Why this is not settled by definition

The 'are viruses alive?' argument is semantic. What matters scientifically is whether viruses have a single origin, several origins, or are a polyphyletic collection of mobile genetic elements — and the evidence currently favours the last.

Giant viruses complicate the picture further: their size and gene content blur the line between virus and cell, and their discovery revived the regressive hypothesis in a form that is still being tested.

The stakes

Origins research matters for surveillance: knowing which viral families have ancient, stable relationships with hosts predicts which are likely to jump. It also reframes the tree of life — viruses are not a branch on it so much as a network across it.

The honest label is 'live debate'. Unlike the archive's fringe material, the disagreement is between working virologists with the same sequence databases.

Punctuated Equilibrium

The claim

In 1972, Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould proposed that speciation happens in geologically brief bursts, and that species then remain stable for millions of years. The pattern in the rocks — stasis, then abrupt replacement — is the data the theory was built to explain.

The contrast was with phyletic gradualism: slow, continuous transformation of lineages. Gould's essays made the debate famous, and the popular version became 'Darwin was wrong about gradualism'.

The reconciliation

Most biologists now regard the two as ends of a spectrum rather than rivals. Speciation can be rapid on geological timescales while still being gradual in generations; the fossil record's resolution is coarse enough that a process taking 50,000 years looks instantaneous.

The real content of the debate is about modes: whether change is concentrated at speciation events, and whether stasis is a real phenomenon needing explanation (stabilising selection, developmental constraints) rather than an artefact.

What is often overstated

'Darwin was wrong.' Darwin emphasised gradualism, but he also accepted rapid change and gaps in the record. Punctuated equilibrium is a claim about tempo and mode within evolutionary theory, not a refutation of it.

'Evolution happens in jumps.' The bursts are geological, not single-generation. Nothing in the theory requires saltation, and the evidence for large single-step changes is limited to specific cases.

'Stasis proves nothing changes.' Stasis is a pattern to explain, and the explanations — stabilising selection, habitat tracking, developmental constraint — are testable.

Why it still matters

Because it changed how palaeontologists read the record: species are now treated as individuals with durations and stability, not just points on a transformation series. That is a real methodological shift.

It is also a good example of a scientific debate that became a cultural one, which is the pattern this archive keeps finding: the settled version is narrower, and more interesting, than the famous version.

Peto's Paradox

The paradox

Richard Peto noted in 1977 that cancer risk across species does not scale with body size or lifespan. If every cell has some chance of becoming malignant, a large, long-lived animal should accumulate far more tumours.

The observation has held up: elephants and whales have cancer rates comparable to or lower than humans, despite vastly more cell divisions and decades more exposure.

The proposed answers

More tumour suppressors. Elephants have around 20 copies of TP53, the 'guardian of the genome', against our two. Cells with damaged DNA are killed more readily — a mechanism demonstrated in elephant cells in culture.

Slower metabolism per cell. Large animals have lower mass-specific metabolic rates, which may mean less oxidative damage per cell.

Cell-size and division-rate differences. Whale cells are not proportionally bigger, but their division dynamics may differ.

Evolutionary tuning. Species with large bodies and long lives may have been selected for stronger cancer suppression, because the alternative is extinction.

Why it is not settled

The data are thin. Cancer prevalence in wild cetaceans is hard to measure: they are rarely necropsied systematically, and many die of other causes before cancer would appear. The low rates may be partly ascertainment.

TP53 copy number is not the whole story. Elephants are not cancer-proof; they still get tumours. And some large, long-lived species do not have extra TP53.

The mechanism might be general rather than special. Better DNA repair, tighter cell-cycle checkpoints, and immune surveillance could all contribute without any single trick.

Why it matters

Because if large animals have evolved better cancer suppression, the mechanisms are potential drug targets. Comparative oncology is now a real field, and the elephant TP53 result is its founding observation.

It is also a clean example of the archive's method: a real paradox, several plausible mechanisms, and a lot of popular writing that presents one of them as the answer.

The Gut–Brain Axis

The routes

There are at least four channels: the vagus nerve, which carries signals from gut to brain; the immune system, via cytokines and inflammation; microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids and neurotransmitter precursors; and the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, which responds to stress and changes gut permeability.

That the routes exist is not in dispute. Germ-free mice, which have no microbiome, show differences in anxiety-like behaviour, stress response and brain development — and those differences partly reverse with colonisation.

Where the evidence gets thin

Mouse to human. Most mechanistic work is in rodents. Human studies are largely observational: people with depression differ in microbiome composition from controls, but diet, medication, sleep and stress all differ too.

Probiotic trials. Effects on mood are small, inconsistent, and often not replicated. The strongest claims come from small trials with multiple outcomes measured.

Specific diseases. Parkinson's has the most intriguing link — alpha-synuclein pathology appears in the gut years before motor symptoms, and vagotomy is associated with lower risk in some cohorts. That is suggestive, not causal.

The conceptual problem

The microbiome is not a fixed organ; it changes with diet, antibiotics, geography and age. That makes 'the microbiome causes X' hard to test, because the exposure is unstable and the direction of causation is often bidirectional.

Faecal transplant for recurrent C. difficile is the one place where the causal chain is clear and the therapy works. It is also the exception that shows how high the bar is: an infection, a defined pathogen, a measurable cure.

How to read the claims

Treat microbiome claims like nutrition claims: plausible mechanisms, weak human trials, and a strong commercial incentive to overstate. The archive's open problems page files the related 'leaky gut' hypothesis under live debate for the same reason.

What would move it: large, preregistered trials with defined strains, objective endpoints and long follow-up. Some are running. Until they report, the honest answer is that the axis is real and its clinical importance is not established.

Pilot-Wave Theory

What the theory says

Louis de Broglie proposed in 1927 that a particle has both a real position and a wave that guides it; he abandoned the idea under criticism. David Bohm rebuilt it in 1952, and it became the standard example of a hidden-variable theory that works.

The rule is simple: particles have definite positions at all times, and their motion is determined by the wavefunction through a guidance equation. There is no collapse and no fundamental randomness — the apparent randomness comes from not knowing the exact initial positions, which are distributed according to the Born rule.

Why it is not the mainstream view

The guidance equation is explicitly nonlocal: the motion of one particle depends on the positions of all the others, instantly, however far apart. That is exactly the kind of influence Bell's theorem showed any hidden-variable theory must have, so this is not a flaw — but it does mean the theory needs a preferred notion of simultaneity, a foliation of spacetime.

Making that relativistic has been the project ever since. There are versions (bohmian field theory, the Dirac sea reinterpretations, relativistic beables) that reproduce quantum field theory results in restricted settings; none is a clean, generally accepted relativistic formulation. That is the honest reason most physicists work with the instrumental formalism instead.

The scorecard

Predictions: identical to ordinary quantum mechanics, which means no experiment yet distinguishes them. That is not a weakness; it is the definition of an interpretation.

Virtues: no measurement problem, no collapse, no observer needed, and a clear account of why detectors click where they do.

Cost: an unobservable preferred frame, nonlocal dynamics, and a quantum equilibrium assumption that has to be postulated rather than derived.

A theory that cannot be distinguished by experiment is not thereby meaningless — but it is not science in the naive falsificationist sense either, and the archive labels it a live debate rather than a result.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the strongest version of a claim the fringe gets wrong constantly. 'Quantum physics proves reality is a dream' and 'consciousness creates the world' are not what the formalism says; pilot-wave theory is one honest way of taking realism seriously, and it is taught in foundations courses.

It sits with objective collapse and quantum Darwinism as the three serious attempts to say what is actually happening between measurements.

Objective Collapse

The measurement problem, stated plainly

Schrödinger's equation is smooth and deterministic. It spreads a particle's possibilities into a superposition. Then, at measurement, we are told to collapse the superposition to one outcome — a rule that appears nowhere in the equation and has no definition of 'measurement' attached.

Copenhagen-style teaching says not to ask. Objective-collapse models say: add a term to the equation that makes superpositions of sufficiently large, sufficiently spread-out objects collapse spontaneously, at random, with a fixed rate.

The models

GRW (1986). Ghirardi, Rimini and Weber proposed that each particle has a tiny probability per second of its wavefunction spontaneously localising. For one particle the rate is so low it is never seen; for 10²³ particles acting together, collapse is effectively instantaneous.

Continuous models. Later versions (CSL) make the collapse a continuous stochastic process rather than discrete jumps, which handles identical particles and relativity better.

Diósi–Penrose. A different route: gravity itself causes collapse when a superposition of mass distributions becomes distinguishable by its own gravitational field. This makes the collapse rate mass-dependent, which is what experiments test.

What makes this testable, and what the tests say

Because collapse is a physical process, it adds a little noise and heat. Very small systems are protected by being small; the prediction is a threshold somewhere between molecular and visible scales.

Underground experiments at Gran Sasso, levitated optomechanics, and cryogenic cantilevers have all been used to rule out chunks of parameter space. So far the predictions of standard quantum mechanics keep winning, which pushes the collapse parameters into harder-to-reach territory — but has not closed them.

This is the rare foundations debate that could end with a measurement. That is why the archive treats it as live rather than philosophical.

Why it is in the archive

It is the clean counterexample to 'quantum theory means everything is uncertain until you look.' Here the uncertainty is real and physical, and looking has nothing to do with it.

See also pilot-wave theory, which keeps the wave and removes collapse entirely — the two proposals are opposite solutions to the same problem.

The Arrow of Time

The puzzle

Newton's laws, Maxwell's equations, Schrödinger's equation and general relativity are all invariant under time reversal, with the small exception of the weak interaction's CP violation, which is far too small to explain everyday irreversibility.

Yet entropy increases, memories exist, causes precede effects, and eggs do not unscramble. Boltzmann's statistical mechanics explains the increase: there are vastly more disordered arrangements than ordered ones, so a system wanders into disorder. But that argument is time-symmetric too — it works just as well predicting disorder in the past.

The past hypothesis

The standard answer, associated with Boltzmann and sharpened by David Albert and others, is that the universe started in an extraordinarily low-entropy state. Given that starting point, entropy increases in both directions away from it, and we live downstream.

This works, and it moves the question rather than answering it. Why was the early universe so smooth and so low in entropy? Gravity makes this worse: a uniform gas has low gravitational entropy, so the nearly-uniform early universe is a very special state, and inflation is supposed to explain how it got that way — without a fully accepted account of the entropy accounting.

What is settled and what is not

Settled: the thermodynamic arrow is real and statistical; the second law is not a fundamental law but a consequence of initial conditions plus counting.

Settled: quantum measurement does not create the arrow. Decoherence is also time-symmetric.

Open: why the initial condition was what it was. This connects to the cosmology pages and to quantum gravity, and there is no consensus answer.

Misused: the arrow is often invoked to 'prove' that the past exists, that time is an illusion, or that retrocausation is impossible. None of those follows from the physics.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a genuine unsolved problem that gets sold as a solved one in both directions — mystics claim physics has proved time is unreal, and some popularisers claim the whole thing is just statistics and there is nothing left to explain.

The honest statement is narrower: the asymmetry we observe follows from a special initial condition, and the origin of that condition is an open question in cosmology.

Quantum Darwinism

The mechanism

Decoherence explains why superpositions vanish for big objects: interaction with the environment entangles them with countless degrees of freedom, and the interference terms become unobservable in practice. That solves part of the problem — it explains the absence of interference, not the presence of definite outcomes.

Wojciech Zurek's addition is einselection plus redundancy. Certain states — the 'pointer states' — survive interaction with the environment; others get scrambled. Those surviving states are the ones the environment then copies, not once but many times, into light, air molecules and heat.

Why redundancy matters

If the environment holds many independent copies of the same information about a system, then any observer who samples a small part of the environment gets the same answer. That is a candidate explanation for objectivity: 'the cat is alive' is true because the information is available in millions of places, not because a mind collapsed anything.

Quantum Darwinism makes this quantitative: the mutual information between the system and a fragment of the environment should rise steeply with fragment size, saturating once the fragment holds one copy.

Where the argument is incomplete

Supporting experiments: photonic and spin systems have shown the predicted redundancy structure, which is real evidence the mechanism operates.

The gap: redundancy explains why observers agree, not why exactly one outcome occurs. It is compatible with a single world where all outcomes happen (many-worlds) — Zurek's own reading — and with interpretations that add collapse.

The criticism: the derivation assumes a split between system and environment that is itself vague, and the 'classical' states it selects depend on the interaction, not on anything absolute.

So the label is live debate: the physics of decoherence and redundancy is well established, and the claim that this fully solves the measurement problem is not.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most physically grounded attempt to explain why the world looks classical, and because it is frequently reported as if it had finished the job.

It pairs with pilot-wave theory (which removes the need) and objective collapse (which adds physics to finish it).

Magnetic Monopoles

Why theorists expect them

In 1931 Dirac showed that if even one magnetic monopole exists anywhere in the universe, electric charge must be quantised in units of a fixed value. Since charge quantisation is observed and otherwise unexplained, that is a strong hint.

Grand unified theories go further: they predict monopoles with masses around 10¹⁶ GeV, produced abundantly in the early universe. That prediction caused a problem — so many monopoles should have survived that they would overclose the universe. Inflation was partly motivated as a solution, by diluting them away.

What has been found

No elementary magnetic monopole has ever been detected. Searches include the MoEDAL experiment at the LHC, IceCube's look for monopoles in cosmic rays, and induction experiments using superconducting loops — the classic 1982 Blas Cabrera event was a single candidate that never repeated.

Meanwhile, condensed-matter physicists have made monopole-like quasiparticles. In spin ice, magnetic moments arrange so that emergent monopoles appear at the ends of 'Dirac strings', and in 2009 these were observed collectively. They are real excitations of a material, not fundamental particles — an important distinction the popular coverage often drops.

Three different claims, three different verdicts

Fundamental monopoles exist somewhere in the universe: expected by most unified theories, not observed. Live debate.

Monopoles can be made in a lab as material excitations: done, repeatedly, since 2009. Documented.

A monopole can be harvested to give free energy / break physics: fiction. The quasiparticles are not usable as a power source; creating them costs at least what you get back.

The pattern is worth noticing: a genuine, subtle result in condensed matter becomes 'scientists create magnetic monopole' becomes 'free energy'. The archive links the real papers.

Why it is in the archive

Because the null result is scientifically load-bearing. The absence of monopoles constrains every unification scheme, and the monopole problem is one of the reasons inflation is taken seriously.

See dark matter for the same logic applied to a different missing particle.

IIT versus Global Workspace

The two theories

Integrated information theory (IIT), developed by Giulio Tononi from 2004, starts from experience and asks what physical system could have it. Its answer: a system with high integrated information, denoted Φ (phi) — information that is more than the sum of its parts. IIT predicts consciousness depends on the structure of the causal network, with the posterior cortex as the hot zone.

Global neuronal workspace (GNW), from Bernard Baars's workspace idea formalised by Stanislas Dehaene and colleagues, says conscious content is whatever gets broadcast by a network of long-range pyramidal neurons, especially prefrontal and parietal. Unconscious processing stays local; conscious processing goes global.

The adversarial test

The Cogitate consortium — IIT and GNW theorists plus independent labs — ran a preregistered study with fMRI, MEG and intracranial electrodes, comparing the theories' predictions on the same data. The results, published in 2025, were mixed on purpose: some predictions of each theory were supported and others were not.

GNW's prediction of prefrontal ignition found less support than expected; IIT's prediction of sustained posterior synchrony found some. Both camps claimed partial vindication, which is roughly what an honest adversarial collaboration produces.

The trouble with measuring consciousness theories

Theories must be falsifiable to be science. In 2023 a group of researchers published an open letter calling IIT 'pseudoscience' on the grounds that its core claim — that Φ measures experience — is not testable. The letter was widely criticised as overreach, but the underlying point about operationalising Φ is serious: computing it exactly is intractable for real brains, so tests use proxies.

Proxies weaken tests. When a theory's central quantity can only be approximated, a failed prediction can always be blamed on the approximation.

Both theories could be wrong. The adversarial result does not crown a winner, and neither theory explains why any of this is accompanied by experience — the 'hard problem' is untouched by both.

Why it is in the archive

Because this is the best current example of consciousness science trying to behave like science: preregistration, adversarial collaboration, predictions stated in advance.

The archive also keeps the fringe at arm's length: quantum consciousness (Orch-OR and its relatives) makes claims that this literature does not support.

Readiness Potentials and Free Will

The experiment

Libet asked subjects to flex a wrist whenever they felt like it, and to note the position of a fast-moving clock hand at the moment they felt the urge. Scalp electrodes recorded a readiness potential (RP) — a slow negative wave over motor cortex — that began roughly 300–500 ms before the reported urge, and well before the movement.

The inference drawn was dramatic: the brain initiates the action before the person is aware of deciding, so the conscious will is not the cause.

Why the inference is contested

The timing method is shaky. Subjects report the position of a clock hand from memory, and the 'moment of awareness' is reconstructed, not measured. Small systematic errors matter when the effect is a few hundred milliseconds.

The RP may not be a decision. Aaron Schurger and colleagues argued in 2012 that the RP looks like stochastic accumulation of background noise crossing a threshold — a process that would produce the same signal even with no decision being made. Their model reproduces the data without any pre-conscious 'choice'.

Libet himself did not conclude free will is dead. He proposed a conscious veto: the urge arises unconsciously, but the person can cancel it. That is a different claim from 'the decision is made for you'.

What the evidence does and does not show

Shown: deliberate actions are preceded by measurable preparatory brain activity, and the feeling of having decided is not the first event in the chain.

Not shown: that the outcome is fixed before the person is aware, or that conscious deliberation plays no role. Later experiments with more careful timing and better modelling have narrowed the gap substantially.

Philosophically undecided: whether determinism at the neural level is compatible with responsibility. That is a separate argument — compatibilism versus libertarian free will — and no experiment settles it.

The popular summary, 'science proves you have no free will', is doing a lot of work that the papers do not support.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the single most over-claimed result in neuroscience, and the correction is interesting in its own right: the same data support a picture of the brain as a noisy accumulator tipping into action.

See gut-brain signalling for another case where a real effect gets a much bigger story attached.

Ego Depletion

The claim

Roy Baumeister and colleagues reported in 1998 that people who had just exerted self-control — resisting cookies, suppressing emotion, making choices — performed worse on a second demanding task. The explanation was a limited resource, 'ego depletion', and the metaphor was a muscle or a battery.

A later addition was that the resource was glucose: depleted subjects who rinsed their mouths with sugar water showed restored self-control, which was presented as evidence for a physiological fuel.

The collapse

A 2016 registered replication across 23 laboratories, with over 2,000 participants and a protocol agreed with the original authors, found an effect size statistically indistinguishable from zero.

Meta-analyses corrected for publication bias shrank the effect dramatically. The glucose studies came under separate criticism: the amounts involved are far too small to matter metabolically, and mouth-rinsing effects are better explained by reward signalling than by fuel.

The theory also ran into a conceptual problem: 'self-control' was measured by dozens of different tasks that did not correlate with each other as a single resource model requires.

What survives

Debunked: ego depletion as a general, glucose-fuelled, domain-general resource that can be exhausted and replenished.

Still real: fatigue, motivation, boredom and attention all affect performance. People do perform worse on long sequences of demanding tasks — for reasons that involve motivation and strategy, not a depleting fuel tank.

Still taught: the battery metaphor appears in pop psychology, management training and self-help long after the evidence left. That lag is the reason this page exists.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest case of a plausible-sounding theory with a memorable metaphor that did not survive preregistration — and because the correction is not 'willpower is fake'. It is that the specific mechanism was wrong.

It pairs with other replication failures in the archive, including priming and the Mozart effect.

Screen Time and Teen Mental Health

The case that something changed

Around 2012, rates of reported depression, self-harm and suicide-related hospitalisation among adolescents in several English-speaking countries began rising, especially among girls. Jonathan Haidt and Jean Twenge argue the timing matches smartphone and social-media adoption, and that the effect is large enough to matter at population scale.

The argument is partly about aggregates rather than individuals: even a small per-person effect, multiplied by near-universal exposure, could move population statistics.

The case against the strong claim

Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski's 2019 analysis of three large datasets found the association between digital technology use and adolescent well-being was negative but tiny — comparable to eating potatoes or wearing glasses, and far smaller than sleep, bullying or family relationships.

Measurement is a serious problem: screen time is self-reported, lumped into one number that ignores what the screen is being used for. A video call with a grandparent and an algorithmically boosted comparison feed are the same 'hours' in most datasets.

The trend data are also disputed: some countries show rises without matching smartphone adoption, and reported distress measures changed over the same period.

Where the disagreement actually is

Agreed: heavy use is associated with somewhat worse outcomes on average, and some specific patterns — late-night use, passive scrolling, appearance comparison — look worse than others.

Disputed: whether the association is causal, and how large the causal effect is. Randomised and quasi-experimental studies exist but are small and short.

Overstated on both sides: 'phones are destroying a generation' and 'the effect is trivial, nothing to see'. The second can be true statistically and still miss a real, unevenly distributed harm.

The archive labels this live debate because the disagreement is about inference from weak observational data, not about whether teenagers use phones.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the moral panic framing and the debunking framing are both partly right, and the archive's job is to keep the numbers visible.

See the gut-brain axis for a related case where a real effect gets an inflated story.

The Younger Dryas Impact

The claim

The Younger Dryas impact hypothesis, proposed in 2007, holds that a large comet or asteroid broke up and struck the Laurentide ice sheet around 12,800 years ago. The proposed consequences: a shutdown of the Atlantic circulation, a return to glacial conditions for about 1,200 years, extinction of many large mammals, and the end of the Clovis hunting culture.

The supporting evidence offered includes a black carbon-rich sediment layer ('black mat') at many sites, nanodiamonds, magnetic microspherules, platinum anomalies, and meltglass.

The problems

Replication of the markers. Independent groups have failed to find nanodiamonds and spherules at the same layers, and some reported markers turn out to be common in ordinary sediments.

Dating. A Bayesian analysis of many sites (Kennett et al., 2015) argued for synchroneity around 12,835–12,735 cal BP; critics note that the sites are few, the dating uncertainties large, and the selection of sites not independent of the hypothesis.

No crater. No impact structure of the right age and size has been found. The proposed Greenland Hiawatha crater is much older than the Younger Dryas.

The extinctions are not synchronous. Megafaunal losses played out over thousands of years and at different times on different continents, which is hard to reconcile with a single hemispheric event.

What a fair reading looks like

Established: the Younger Dryas cooling itself, its abruptness, and its likely link to freshwater forcing of the Atlantic circulation.

Contested: whether an impact occurred, and whether it mattered. A 2023 review in Earth-Science Reviews argued the hypothesis is comprehensively refuted; proponents dispute the review's selection of evidence.

Fringe version: a global cataclysm that destroyed an advanced civilisation, encoded in myths. That is not supported by any archaeological evidence, and it is the version that circulates most widely.

The archive labels this live debate because serious scientists still publish on both sides, while flagging the civilisation-destroying version as fiction.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a genuine scientific dispute that has been absorbed into a much larger pseudo-historical story, and the two need separating.

It connects to Göbekli Tepe and flood myths, both of which are frequently dragged into the comet narrative without warrant.

AMOC Tipping

What AMOC is

The Atlantic meridional overturning circulation moves warm surface water north, where it cools, sinks, and returns south at depth. It carries a large fraction of the heat that keeps north-west Europe milder than its latitude suggests.

Direct monitoring began in 2004 with the RAPID array of moorings across 26.5°N. Before that, estimates come from proxies — sediment, corals, ice cores — with much larger uncertainties.

The evidence of weakening

The RAPID record shows variability but no unambiguous trend over its short length. Proxy reconstructions suggest a weakening since the mid-twentieth century, and one widely cited reconstruction (Caesar et al., 2021) concluded the circulation is at its weakest in a millennium.

Model projections under high emissions consistently show weakening. A 2023 study (Ditlevsen & Ditlevsen) applied statistical early-warning analysis to a proxy record and concluded collapse could occur around mid-century — a conclusion contested by other specialists who note the proxy's limits and the short observational baseline.

What the IPCC actually says

Very likely: AMOC will weaken over the twenty-first century under continued warming.

About collapse: the IPCC assesses an abrupt collapse before 2100 as unlikely, with low confidence — not impossible, and not well constrained, because the models that would show it have biases and coarse resolution.

The stakes: a collapse would cool the North Atlantic region, shift tropical rain belts, and raise sea level on the US east coast faster. Even the weakening, without collapse, matters for regional climate.

The honest position: a low-probability, high-impact outcome, where the probability is poorly known and the observations are too short to settle it.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where 'the science is settled' and 'scientists warn of collapse next year' are both wrong, and where the correct answer involves confidence levels that do not fit a headline.

Related: other places where a measurement's uncertainty is the story.

The Ediacaran Organisms

The organisms

The Ediacaran biota appeared after the Cryogenian glaciations and before the Cambrian explosion. The most famous is Dickinsonia, a flattened oval with rib-like segments, up to a metre across, with no mouth, gut, or obvious organs. Others include Charnia, frond-like and anchored to the sea floor, and Kimberella, which left scrape marks consistent with grazing.

They are found worldwide, often in sandstone beds that record microbial mats, and they vanish from the record before the Cambrian.

The competing readings

Early animals. The mainstream view now, supported by cholesterol biomarkers preserved in Dickinsonia fossils (Bobrovskiy et al., 2018), which indicate animal-grade sterol synthesis. Kimberella's grazing traces and Ikaria's putative bilaterian features support it.

Vendobionts. Adolf Seilacher argued they were a separate kingdom of quilted, fluid-filled organisms with no modern descendants — an experiment in large size that failed.

Other options. Retallack proposed some were land-dwelling lichens; others have suggested giant protists or colonial organisms. Each has fossil evidence in favour and problems with it.

What is agreed

Agreed: they were large, soft-bodied, mostly sessile, and ecologically important — the first complex ecosystems with tiered structure.

Agreed: at least some were animals, or stem-group animals, based on biomarker chemistry.

Disputed: whether the whole assemblage is one clade, several, or a mix of animals and non-animals; and how much of the 'weirdness' is preservational.

The archive labels this live debate rather than documented because the flagship claim — 'these are the first animals' — is only partly established.

Why it is in the archive

Because the deep past is where the fringe and the real science overlap most confusingly: the same fossils appear in creationist timelines, in 'ancient alien' seed-life stories, and in serious palaeontology.

See the Ancient collection for the pseudo-historical uses of deep time.

Strings versus Loops

What each proposes

String theory replaces point particles with one-dimensional strings. Its vibrational modes give the known particles, and one of them is a graviton — which is why it is a theory of gravity at all. It needs extra dimensions (ten in the common versions, eleven in M-theory) and supersymmetry to be consistent.

Loop quantum gravity keeps spacetime itself as the thing to quantise. Space becomes a discrete network of spin labels — quantised area and volume — and the theory is background-independent by construction, which string theory is often criticised for not being.

Neither has been formulated completely. String theory has no non-perturbative definition outside special backgrounds; loop quantum gravity has struggled to recover ordinary smooth spacetime and to couple to matter convincingly.

The scoreboard

String theory's assets: a graviton comes for free; it produced AdS/CFT, a conjectured duality that has been enormously useful in nuclear and condensed-matter physics even if it is not a theory of our world; and it is mathematically extraordinarily rich.

String theory's problems: the landscape of possible vacua is astronomically large, so the theory may not predict anything; supersymmetry has not appeared at the LHC; and the predicted extra dimensions, cosmic strings and heavy relics have not been seen.

Loop quantum gravity's assets: background independence, a concrete picture of quantum geometry, and applications to black-hole entropy and early-universe cosmology (loop quantum cosmology).

Loop quantum gravity's problems: recovering a smooth four-dimensional spacetime at low energy is not fully demonstrated, and the theory has no clear route to unification with the other forces.

What an outsider should take away

Neither is established physics. Both are candidate frameworks, and both are taught as research programmes rather than results.

Popular books oversell both. 'Theory of everything' claims are premature in either direction, and the rhetoric on both sides has been ungenerous for decades.

The honest test is experiment. Any quantum-gravity effect is suppressed by the Planck energy, roughly 10¹⁹ GeV — far beyond any collider. Plausible tests are cosmological (primordial gravitational waves, black-hole echoes) and none has returned a signal.

The archive labels this a live debate because it is a real disagreement among physicists about which programme to pursue, not about whether the question is worth asking.

Why it is in the archive

Because 'quantum gravity' is a favourite of the fringe — used to justify everything from consciousness to free energy — while being an ordinary, unfinished research problem.

Related: the holographic principle, the firewall paradox.

Inflation versus a Bounce

What inflation does

In 1980 Alan Guth proposed a brief period of exponential expansion in the first instant. It flattens the universe, smooths it, and stretches quantum fluctuations into the seeds of galaxies. Those seeds have a specific statistical signature: a nearly scale-invariant spectrum of density perturbations.

The cosmic microwave background matches that prediction with remarkable precision. Planck's maps show a spectrum with a slight tilt from perfect scale invariance, and a lack of detectable primordial gravitational waves so far. That is inflation's strongest card: it predicted something subtle and the data agreed.

The criticisms

The measure problem. Inflation may never end globally, producing infinitely many pocket universes. Any outcome happens somewhere, so the theory struggles to make probabilistic predictions without an arbitrary choice of measure.

It is hard to falsify. The inflaton field's potential is a free function; almost any observation can be accommodated by choosing it. Critics — notably Ijjas, Steinhardt and Loeb — argue this makes inflation unfalsifiable in practice.

The singularity remains. Inflation sits after a beginning it does not explain, and the initial conditions it was invented to explain may simply be assumed.

The bouncing alternatives

Bounce cosmologies avoid the singularity by having the universe contract and re-expand — the ekpyrotic model, loop quantum cosmology's bounce, and various string-gas models.

Their appeal is that a contracting phase can also generate the observed spectrum, and the singularity is replaced by a bounce. Their problem is that a bounce requires conditions that are hard to arrange: the universe must remain smooth through the contraction, and the entropy problem has to be solved rather than postponed.

Where the evidence sits: the data do not yet separate the two families. Both predict a nearly scale-invariant spectrum; they differ on tensor modes, non-Gaussianity and running — quantities the next generation of CMB experiments is designed to measure.

The archive calls this a live debate. It is a disagreement between serious cosmologists about how a theory should behave, and it has not been settled by observation.

Why it is in the archive

Because 'the Big Bang' is routinely presented either as a proven beginning of everything or as a myth, when the honest picture is a well-tested hot expansion plus an unsettled story about the first instant.

Related: quantum gravity, the Hubble tension.

How the Moon Formed

The hypothesis

Proposed in the 1970s, the giant-impact idea holds that a body roughly the size of Mars — often called Theia — struck the proto-Earth at a glancing angle around 4.5 billion years ago. Debris thrown into orbit coalesced into the Moon.

It explains several awkward facts at once: the Moon has a small iron core and low density (it formed from mantle material, not a whole planet), the Earth–Moon system has high angular momentum, and the Moon's orbit is close to the ecliptic.

The isotopic problem

The prediction is that the Moon should be made largely of Theia's material, which should differ from Earth's. Instead, lunar rocks returned by Apollo have oxygen, titanium, silicon and tungsten isotope ratios almost identical to Earth's mantle.

That similarity is difficult to produce in a standard impact. Possible answers: the impactor was made of the same material as Earth (a coincidence that needs explaining), the impact was more energetic and the two bodies mixed thoroughly, the Moon formed from a vapour-rich synestia, or the Moon formed after a series of smaller impacts.

The competing refinements

Canonical impact: one big grazing hit. Simple, but struggles with the isotope match.

Synestia: a rapidly spinning, partly vaporised mass, with the Moon condensing inside it. Explains mixing; requires fine-tuned conditions.

Hit-and-run and multiple impacts: several collisions with similar bodies, each mixing material. Growing support, harder to model.

Capture or fission: old alternatives, effectively excluded by dynamics and angular momentum.

What is settled

That the Moon formed from a giant impact is close to consensus; how exactly is not. Samples from Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 and improved numerical modelling are the current front line.

The archive labels this live debate rather than documented because the mechanism is accepted while the standard model's details fail to match the best measurements.
