The Wow! Signal

Seventy-two seconds of narrowband radio at the hydrogen frequency, recorded once and never again. It is still the best candidate for a signal from elsewhere, and it is not evidence of one.

The detection

On 15 August 1977 the Big Ear radio telescope at Ohio State University recorded a narrowband signal at 1420.456 MHz — close to the 21 cm hydrogen line, a frequency chosen by SETI because it is a natural beacon. It lasted 72 seconds, the length of a single pass of the telescope's beam, and it rose and fell in exactly the shape a point source crossing the beam would produce.

Jerry Ehman circled the sequence 6EQUJ5 on the printout and wrote 'Wow!' beside it. The signal was about thirty times the background noise, extremely narrow in frequency, and has never been detected again in any follow-up observation.

The candidate explanations

Interstellar scintillation can amplify a weak signal, but the shape fits a single beam crossing. Terrestrial interference is the standard objection — the frequency band is protected but not perfectly quiet. A 2017 proposal that the signal came from comets passing near the hydrogen line did not survive scrutiny, because the comets' positions and the beam crossing do not line up.

The honest position is that the observation is unexplained and unrepeated. An unexplained single detection is exactly what a real signal might look like — and exactly what an instrumental artefact looks like too, which is the problem.

What the evidence supports

Documented: a narrowband 72-second detection at 1420 MHz, with a beam-crossing profile.

Documented: no repeat, in any of several follow-up campaigns.

Not established: an artificial origin. One detection cannot be distinguished from one interference event.

Not established: a natural source. No comet, satellite or known emitter explains it.

The honest label: live debate, with the weight on 'we do not know', and no basis for saying 'they called'.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is what the discovery of extraterrestrial intelligence would actually look like on day one: ambiguous, brief, and impossible to confirm without a second event. The archive keeps it as the counterweight to every confident UFO page in the collection.

The Face on Mars

A mesa in the Cydonia region looked like a face at Viking resolution. Higher-resolution images, taken twenty-two years later, show a mesa. The interesting part is why the first image looked the way it did.

The image

In 1976 NASA released a Viking 1 image of the Cydonia region showing a mesa with what looked like a face: two eye-like depressions, a nose and a mouth. The image was about 43 metres per pixel, taken in low-angle sunlight that produced strong shadows, and there was only one of it.

The resemblance was seized on by writers who argued it was artificial — a monument, a marker, evidence of a lost Martian civilisation. NASA was accused of concealing the rest of the frames.

The later pictures

In 1998 the Mars Global Surveyor imaged the same feature at about 1.5 metres per pixel, in different lighting. It is a natural mesa, eroded and partially buried, with no symmetry and no facial geometry. Further images in 2001 and after, from several spacecraft and at higher resolution still, confirmed the reading. The 'other' frames were released; they show the same hill.

The mechanism is pareidolia: the human visual system is tuned to find faces, and it finds them in noise, clouds, rock and toast. Low resolution removes the detail that would break the illusion, and a single viewing angle supplies the shadows that complete it.

What is established

Documented: the feature is a natural mesa, imaged at high resolution from multiple angles.

Documented: the original image was low-resolution, single-angle, and shadow-heavy.

Documented: the resemblance disappears at higher resolution.

Not established: any artificial structure, or any concealment by NASA.

The lesson: pareidolia is not a failure of intelligence — it is a feature of perception that misfires on ambiguous input.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest demonstration in the collection of how a single low-information observation becomes a monument. Every step — the low resolution, the one angle, the shadow, the human face-detector — is ordinary, and the conclusion was extraordinary.

The Phobos Monolith

A boulder casting a long shadow on the Martian moon was described by a former astronaut as a 'monolith'. It is a boulder, about 85 metres across, on a moon covered in boulders.

The object

In 1998 the Mars Global Surveyor photographed Phobos and returned an image containing a small, bright, roughly rectangular object casting a long shadow across the surface. The image was circulated with the claim that it was a monolith — an artificial structure — and the claim was amplified when Buzz Aldrin referred to 'a monolith' on Phobos in a 2009 interview.

What the image shows

The object is about 85 metres across, sitting in a cratered landscape. It casts a shadow consistent with a boulder of that size under a low sun. Phobos is covered in boulders — the same mission imaged many — and a rectangular-looking boulder is not a surprising shape for a fractured ejecta block.

Aldrin's remark was about a boulder and about the oddity of a single large block on a small moon; it was reported as though he had said 'structure'. He has since been clear that he was describing a rock.

What is established

Documented: a large boulder on Phobos, imaged in 1998, casting a shadow.

Documented: the moon is covered in boulders of comparable origin.

Not established: any artificial structure, or any geometric regularity beyond a blocky shape.

Not concealed: the image was publicly released by the mission that took it.

The pattern: the same as the Face on Mars — a real object, a suggestive shape, and a claim that outruns the resolution.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the same error as the Face on Mars in a smaller frame, and because it shows how a careful sentence from a credible person ('a monolith') becomes a claim about aliens once it passes through headlines.

Tired Light

Redshift could be caused by photons losing energy on the way, rather than by the expansion of space. It was a serious alternative for sixty years, and three measurements have closed it.

The claim

In 1929 Fritz Zwicky proposed that cosmological redshift might be a loss of energy by photons travelling through space — 'tired light' — rather than a Doppler or expansion effect. The appeal was that it avoided an expanding universe, and later that it avoided a beginning.

For decades it was a minority but respectable position. It is now excluded, not by one observation but by three independent ones.

The three tests

First, time dilation. If redshift comes from expansion, distant events should appear slowed by a factor of (1+z) — supernova light curves should stretch. They do, measured to high precision. A photon losing energy in transit would not slow the events that emitted it.

Second, the cosmic microwave background. Tired light cannot produce a blackbody spectrum at 2.7 K with the measured distortions; expansion can, and does.

Third, surface brightness and angular size. In an expanding universe, surface brightness falls with redshift in a specific way; in a static tired-light universe it falls differently. The measurements match expansion.

What is established

Documented: supernova light curves are time-dilated by (1+z), as expansion predicts.

Documented: the CMB is a near-perfect blackbody, which tired light does not produce.

Documented: surface-brightness and angular-size tests favour expansion.

Not established: any tired-light mechanism that reproduces all three.

Why it is still argued: because it removes the Big Bang, which is a conclusion some people want removed. The measurements do not care.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's best example of a rival theory that was taken seriously and then killed by data — not by ridicule, not by consensus, but by three measurements that could have gone the other way.

The Boötes Void

A region of sky about 330 million light years across contains far fewer galaxies than it should. It is real, it is not empty, and it is not evidence of anything stranger than large-scale structure.

The finding

In 1981 Robert Kirshner and colleagues reported that a survey of the Boötes region found far fewer galaxies than expected for a volume of that size. The underdense region is roughly 330 million light years across — enormous, and one of the largest structures known.

The press called it the Great Nothing. The measurement does not support that name: the void contains galaxies, dozens of them, just far fewer per unit volume than the cosmic average.

What it means

Voids are a prediction of structure formation. Gravity pulls matter into filaments and clusters, leaving underdense regions between them; the largest voids are hundreds of millions of light years across, and the observed distribution matches the models. The Boötes Void is a large example, not an anomaly.

It has been recruited for stranger claims — a region cleared by an advanced civilisation, a 'hole in the universe' — and those claims have no measurements behind them. The void is not empty, and its shape follows the filamentary structure around it.

What is established

Documented: an underdense region in Boötes, roughly 330 million light years across.

Documented: it contains galaxies, at a fraction of the average density.

Documented: voids of this kind are predicted by and consistent with structure formation.

Not established: emptiness, a sharp boundary, or any artificial cause.

Why it is interesting: because it is one of the largest structures we can see, and it is made of absence.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's reminder that 'structure' includes holes. The universe's largest features are not only clusters but the gaps between them, and the gaps are as informative as the clusters.

The Ganzfeld Effect

Put half ping-pong balls over someone's eyes, play white noise, and within minutes most people start to hallucinate. The effect is real; the parapsychology built on top of it is not.

The effect

In a ganzfeld experiment the visual field is made uniform — half ping-pong balls over the eyes, a red light — and the auditory field is filled with white noise. Deprived of structure, the brain begins to generate it: within minutes, most participants report shapes, colours, scenes and sometimes voices. The name is German for 'whole field'.

The effect is well established and is a standard demonstration in perception teaching. It is the mild end of the same continuum as sensory deprivation, and it explains a great deal of what happens in darkened rooms, long drives and floatation tanks.

What was built on it

From the 1970s the ganzfeld was used in parapsychology as a telepathy test: one participant views a target image, the other sits in the ganzfeld and describes what comes to mind, and a judge picks the matching image from a set. Meta-analyses reported small positive effects; the results have been contested on methodological grounds — sensory leakage, randomisation, analysis flexibility — and independent replications have been inconsistent.

What is established

Documented: the ganzfeld produces vivid imagery in most participants within minutes.

Documented: the effect is a consequence of removing structure from sensory input.

Contested: whether ganzfeld telepathy experiments show an effect beyond chance. The meta-analytic signal is small and the methodological criticism is substantial.

Not established: telepathy. The imagery is generated by the participant's brain, which is what the effect predicts.

The archive's label: the effect is documented; the psi claim built on it is not, and they are different claims that share a name.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest case of a real phenomenon being used as the apparatus for an unreal one, and because the distinction is invisible in most popular writing: 'the ganzfeld works' is true, and 'therefore telepathy' does not follow.

The Tetris Effect

Play Tetris for hours and the falling blocks follow you into sleep and into the shower. The effect is real, it has a name, and it turned out to be a window on how memory consolidates.

The effect

The Tetris effect is the experience of seeing a repeated task's patterns after you stop — blocks falling as you fall asleep, lines to clear on a tiled floor. The term was coined by Jeffrey Goldsmith in 1994 and studied by Robert Stickgold and colleagues from 2000, who found that a majority of intensive players reported game imagery, including during sleep onset.

What the studies showed

Stickgold's experiments used novices playing Tetris for hours and asked them to record imagery at sleep onset. Most reported game images, and amnesic patients with no memory of having played also reported them — which was the interesting result. The effect does not require conscious recall of the task, which suggests it is a low-level consolidation process, not a deliberate replay.

The phenomenon generalises: the same intrusive imagery is reported after repetitive work of many kinds, and the broader category is called game transfer phenomena.

What is established

Documented: repetitive tasks produce intrusive imagery of the task, including at sleep onset.

Documented: the effect occurs in amnesic patients who cannot recall playing.

Documented: it generalises beyond games to other repetitive activity.

Not established: any harm. The effect is transient and not associated with pathology.

Why it matters: it is a clean experimental handle on memory consolidation, obtained with a video game.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a documented, ordinary, slightly unsettling fact about minds — and because it is the honest version of a claim the fringe makes constantly: that what you look at changes what you see when you close your eyes. Here the claim is small, measured, and true.

Chronostasis

Glance at a clock and the first second seems to last longer. The clock is fine; your brain is filling a gap it never recorded.

The illusion

Look at a wall clock with a ticking second hand, and the first tick after your eyes move seems to last about a second and a half. The effect is called chronostasis, or the stopped-clock illusion, and it was characterised by Kielan Yarrow and colleagues in 2001.

The cause is a saccade: when the eyes move, the visual system suppresses input for a fraction of a second to avoid a blur of motion. During that gap it has no image, and it backfills the gap with the first stable image it receives — so the second hand appears to have been still for longer than it was.

What it tells us

It is a direct demonstration that perceived time is constructed, not measured. The brain does not have a clock; it has a set of processes that estimate duration from events, and when the events are missing, the estimate is patched.

The illusion is small, reliable, and easy to demonstrate, which is why it appears in every perception course. It is also the reason 'time seemed to slow down' is a poor basis for any claim about the nature of time.

What is established

Documented: the illusion occurs reliably, and the magnitude is measurable.

Documented: it is tied to saccades and to the suppression of visual input during them.

Documented: it is a construction of the visual system, not a change in time.

Not established: any general mechanism for 'time slowing' in danger, which is a different and much weaker claim.

The lesson: subjective duration is an estimate made by a system with holes in its data.

Why it is in the archive

Because the archive's pages on time — the arrow, phantom time, time paradoxes — all depend on the difference between time as measured and time as experienced. This is the smallest, cleanest demonstration of that difference.

Alien Hand Syndrome

A hand that acts on its own — unbuttoning a shirt, grabbing a tool, resisting the other hand — is a real consequence of damage to the connections between the hemispheres.

The phenomenon

Alien hand syndrome is a rare neurological condition in which one hand performs purposeful actions that the person does not intend and cannot suppress. The hand may grasp objects, undo clothing, or conflict with the other hand. Patients typically describe it as acting of its own accord, and some deny ownership of the limb.

It appears most often after surgery severing the corpus callosum — the bundle connecting the hemispheres — and after strokes affecting the medial frontal cortex or the supplementary motor area. Variants differ: some involve involuntary grasping, others a conflict between the two hands.

What it shows

The condition is a demonstration that voluntary action is not a single command but a set of competing systems that are normally coordinated. When the coordination is damaged, one system's output reaches the limb without the other's consent.

It also complicates the idea of a unified self: the patient experiences a limb that is theirs, moved by an agency that is not. That is philosophically striking and neurologically mundane — a lesion, a circuit, a behaviour.

What is established

Documented: the syndrome is real, rare, and associated with specific lesions.

Documented: it occurs after callosotomy and after strokes in particular regions.

Documented: the movements are purposeful, not random — the hand does things.

Not established: any supernatural or 'possession' explanation, which is where the popular literature goes.

Why it matters: it shows that the sense of agency is a computation, and that it can be selectively broken.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a documented case where the language of the paranormal — an alien presence controlling a body — is the honest description of a neurological lesion. The archive files it as documented and lets the vocabulary be strange.

The Green Children of Woolpit

Two children with green skin and an unknown language appeared in a Suffolk village in the twelfth century. The story is in two chronicles, and the explanations on offer are all more ordinary than the story.

The story

According to William of Newburgh and Ralph of Coggeshall, two children — a boy and a girl — were found near Woolpit in Suffolk in the twelfth century. Their skin was green, their clothing was of unfamiliar material, and they spoke a language nobody understood. They were taken in, and the boy died. The girl learned English, lost her green colour, and said they had come from a land of perpetual twilight called St Martin's Land.

The two accounts differ in details, which is what independent medieval chronicles usually do. Ralph says they were found at a wolf pit; William gives a different setting.

The explanations

The most cited natural explanation is dietary: a child with severe anaemia or malnutrition can look green, and 'green sickness' was a recognised condition. The 'unknown language' and the strange land are harder, and the suggestion that they were Flemish immigrants — common in twelfth-century Suffolk — would explain unfamiliar speech and clothing, if not the colour.

The folkloric explanation is that the story is a changeling tale, or a version of a widespread motif about visitors from another world, retold by chroniclers who collected marvels.

Where the evidence stands

Documented: two independent twelfth-century chronicles record the story.

Not documented: any contemporary record, physical evidence or named witness.

Plausible: malnutrition or anaemia for the colour; Flemish immigration for the language.

Not established: a subterranean world, an alien origin, or a specific identification.

The honest position: an unusually well-attested medieval marvel, with several ordinary explanations and no way to choose between them after 850 years.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the oldest story in the collection that still gets told as though it were evidence, and because it shows what a real medieval mystery looks like: two chroniclers, a village, and no artefact — which is also what a folktale looks like.

'Oumuamua as a Solar Sail

The first object known to come from another star was oddly shaped, tumbled, and accelerated slightly more than gravity explains. One astronomer argued it was a light sail. The argument is interesting and the evidence is thin.

The object

1I/2017 U1, named 'Oumuamua, was detected on 19 October 2017 by Pan-STARRS in Hawaii. Its speed and trajectory showed it had come from outside the solar system — the first interstellar object observed. It was already leaving when it was found, and it was observed for only a few weeks.

Two features were strange. Its brightness varied by a factor of about ten as it tumbled, implying an elongated shape — perhaps ten to one — and no coma or tail was detected. And after accounting for gravity, it showed a small non-gravitational acceleration, the kind outgassing produces in a comet.

The claim

In 2018 Shmuel Bialy and Avi Loeb argued in Astrophysical Journal Letters that a thin artificial light sail could explain the acceleration without detectable outgassing, since a sail needs no gas. Loeb developed the argument in a book; the paper itself was more careful, offering it as a possibility rather than a conclusion.

The counter-arguments are that other explanations exist — outgassing of volatiles that are hard to detect (CO or H₂ ices), a nitrogen-ice fragment, or torques from the tumbling — and that no observation favours artificial over natural. Breakthrough Listen found no radio emission.

Where the evidence stands

Documented: an interstellar object, elongated, tumbling, with a small non-gravitational acceleration.

Documented: no outgassing detected, which is the puzzle.

Not established: an artificial origin. It is one hypothesis among several, and it is not favoured by any measurement.

Not established: the natural explanations either — none has been demonstrated conclusively.

The honest label: fringe, because the claim is not supported by evidence, not because it is absurd. 'Oumuamua remains genuinely unexplained in detail.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the rare case of a fringe claim made by a credentialed scientist about a real anomaly, and it shows how thin the line is: the same object supports a cautious paper, a bestselling book, and a great deal of nonsense.

The Kardashev Scale

A three-step classification of civilisations by energy use, invented for a Soviet radio astronomy paper. It measures nothing we can observe, and it is used constantly as though it did.

The scale

Nikolai Kardashev proposed the scale in 1964, in a paper about the detectability of extraterrestrial civilisations. Type I uses the energy available on a planet, Type II the energy of a star, Type III the energy of a galaxy — roughly 4×10¹², 4×10²⁶ and 4×10³⁷ watts.

The useful part was instrumental: it told radio astronomers what a civilisation at each level might look like, and therefore what to search for. The useless part is the ranking. There is no evidence that civilisations develop along it, no reason to think the steps are steps, and no measurement that puts any real civilisation on it.

What it is used for

Humanity is usually placed at about 0.73 by interpolating between the levels — a number with more precision than meaning. The scale has been extended (Type IV, Type V, heat-loss classifications, exergy-based versions), which is a sign that it is a vocabulary rather than a measurement.

What is established

Documented: the scale, its definition, and its purpose in SETI thinking.

Documented: human energy use, and the arithmetic that puts us below Type I.

Not established: that any civilisation has ever been at Type II or III, or that the progression is real.

Not measurable: any object observed so far has been classified as a candidate for a structure, never confirmed as one.

The honest use: a way of asking what a detectable civilisation would look like. Not a ladder.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the concept most often quoted as though it were a finding — 'we are a Type 0.7 civilisation' — and because it is a good example of a thought experiment doing useful work in one direction and misleading in another.

The Great Attractor

Galaxies across a wide region flow toward something in the direction of Centaurus, and for two decades nobody could see what. The answer turned out to be larger than the thing they were looking for.

The anomaly

In the 1980s a group of astronomers — nicknamed the Seven Samurai — mapped the motions of elliptical galaxies and found that the local Hubble flow did not match a simple expansion. Galaxies across hundreds of millions of light years appeared to be streaming toward a region in the direction of Centaurus and Norma.

That region sits behind the Milky Way's disc, in the Zone of Avoidance, where dust hides everything. So there was a gravitational pull with no visible source.

What was found

The Norma Cluster, Abell 3627, was identified as a major mass concentration at about 200 million light years, with a mass of order 10¹⁶ solar masses. It is not, however, big enough on its own to explain the flow — the motion is better explained by the combined pull of the Norma Cluster, the Shapley Supercluster beyond it, and the local filamentary structure.

In 2014 the flow was placed in context by the definition of Laniakea, our home supercluster, in which the Great Attractor is a local basin rather than the master of the motion.

What is established

Documented: a coherent bulk flow of galaxies toward the Centaurus–Norma direction.

Documented: the Norma Cluster as a major mass concentration, hidden by the galactic plane.

Documented: larger structures (Shapley, Laniakea) that explain the flow better than one attractor.

Superseded in part: the original single-attractor picture. The name survives; the model has moved on.

The lesson: a name can outlive the hypothesis that produced it.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the mystery was real, the answer was found, and the popular name kept the shape of the original mistake — which is how most 'unexplained' labels in astronomy survive their own explanations.

Cosmic Censorship

General relativity allows singularities with no event horizon — naked points where physics stops and the universe can be seen to break. Penrose conjectured they cannot form. Nobody has proved it.

The conjecture

In 1969 Roger Penrose proposed that general relativity forbids naked singularities: whenever matter collapses, an event horizon forms and hides the singularity from outside observers. The weak version covers gravitational collapse; the strong version says no observer anywhere encounters a singularity that is not hidden.

The motivation is that a visible singularity would break predictability. Physics at a singularity is undefined, so if light could escape from one, the future of the universe would not be determined by its present state.

The state of the proof

The weak conjecture is supported by every numerical simulation of collapse performed so far, and by the observed spins of black holes, which sit below the Kerr limit that would expose a singularity. The strong version is more contested: there are numerical solutions in which it appears to fail, and the question is entangled with the information paradox.

Penrose shared the 2020 Nobel Prize for the singularity theorems that made the conjecture precise. The prize was for the theorems, not for a proof of the conjecture, which remains open.

Where it stands

Documented: the singularity theorems, and the Kerr limit on black hole spin.

Well supported: the weak conjecture, in every collapse simulation to date.

Contested: the strong conjecture, with numerical counterexamples in some settings.

Not proved: either version, in general.

Why it matters: it decides whether general relativity is a complete theory of the classical world or one that fails in public.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a live debate with no fringe attached — a clean example of physics arguing about a conjecture that matters and cannot yet be settled, which is the category the archive tries hardest to label honestly.

  • Wikipedia, “Kerr metric” — the spin limit that mattersen.wikipedia.org

The Black Hole Information Paradox

Hawking radiation carries no information about what fell in. If that is true, quantum mechanics is wrong; if it is false, relativity is. Fifty years of work has produced progress and no experiment.

The paradox

In 1974–76 Stephen Hawking showed that black holes radiate thermally, and that the radiation depends only on mass, charge and spin. When the hole evaporates completely, what is left is thermal radiation — which carries no information about the object that formed it.

Quantum mechanics requires that information about a system's initial state is preserved under unitary evolution. General relativity, in this calculation, destroys it. One of the two must give.

The progress

The dominant line of work since the 1990s is holographic: the information is encoded on the horizon, and the evaporation is unitary if you compute it carefully. The 2019–2020 'island' calculations, using the replica trick from quantum information theory, recovered the expected Page curve — the entropy of radiation rises then falls, as unitarity requires — in several simplified models.

That is genuine progress and it is not a resolution. The models are toy models, the assumptions are strong, and no observation can distinguish the options.

Where it stands

Documented: Hawking radiation, its thermality, and the resulting paradox.

Progress: holographic and island calculations reproduce the Page curve in simplified settings.

Not resolved: a full quantum theory of gravity, and therefore the question in the real world.

The firewall argument: a 2012 result showing that unitarity plus the equivalence principle plus no drama at the horizon cannot all hold.

The honest position: the most productive unsolved problem in theoretical physics, with no experimental test in sight.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's example of a debate where everyone agrees on the facts and disagrees about what they mean — and where the disagreement is a sign of health, not of confusion.

Jung's Synchronicity

A meaningful coincidence with no causal connection, offered as an acausal principle of nature. The concept names something people experience; as a claim about the world it cannot be tested, which is the problem.

The claim

Jung introduced synchronicity in a 1952 essay written with the physicist Wolfgang Pauli, describing it as an 'acausal connecting principle' — events that are meaningfully related without being causally connected. His favourite illustration involved a patient describing a dream of a scarab beetle, after which a beetle tapped at the window.

The idea was intended as a bridge between psychology and physics: if mind and matter are aspects of one reality, perhaps meaning can order events as causality does.

Why it cannot be tested

The definition is retrospective. A coincidence is called synchronous when it is meaningful, and meaning is assigned after the fact by the person it happened to. There is no way to specify in advance which events would count as non-synchronous, which means there is no way to compute how often it happens by chance.

Coincidences are common, and the arithmetic of large numbers makes them commoner than intuition allows: with many events in a life, improbable pairings happen constantly. That does not make them meaningless to the person who experiences them — it makes them uninformative about the world.

What is established

Documented: the concept, its history, and the Jung–Pauli collaboration.

Documented: people experience meaningful coincidences, often vividly.

Not testable: the claim that they are produced by an acausal principle. No prediction, no falsification.

Not supported: any statistical demonstration. Attempts have found what chance predicts.

The honest label: fringe — not false, but unfalsifiable, and therefore not a claim about the world that evidence can reach.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most respectable unfalsifiable idea in the collection: written by a major figure, co-authored with a Nobel physicist, and still impossible to test. The archive files it as fringe rather than debunked for exactly that reason.

Tulpas

A practice imported from Tibetan Buddhism and rebuilt on internet forums: deliberately create a second mind in your head, and talk to it. The reports are real; the claim that there is a second mind is not testable.

The word and the practice

In Tibetan Buddhism, a sprul-pa — often rendered 'tulpa' — is an emanation generated by an advanced practitioner, described in the context of tantric practice and hagiography. The modern internet tulpa is a different thing: from around 2009, forums developed a practice of 'forcing' an imagined companion, giving it traits, talking to it daily, and reporting that it eventually replies in its own voice.

The reports are consistent and often detailed: a sense of a separate voice, distinct opinions, sometimes visual or auditory presence. People describe it as beneficial, and some describe distress.

What can and cannot be said

What is documented is that people can construct an elaborate imagined agent and experience it as autonomous. That is not surprising in itself — imaginary companions in childhood, characters in writers' heads, and the voices of the recently bereaved are all in the same family, and the psychology of mental simulation is well studied.

What is not documented is that the tulpa is a separate mind. There is no test that distinguishes a richly simulated agent from a second consciousness, and the tulpa literature is almost entirely self-report from communities with a shared vocabulary and strong expectations.

What is established

Documented: people report sustained, autonomous-seeming imagined agents, with consistent phenomenology.

Documented: the practice borrows a Tibetan term for something it does not replicate.

Not established: a second consciousness, or any measure of it.

Not studied: almost nothing peer-reviewed. The evidence is forum surveys, which is a weak instrument.

The honest label: fringe. The experience is real; the metaphysics is not evidenced.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the internet produced a practice with a borrowed sacred vocabulary and no research literature, and the archive's job is to say which part is experience and which part is claim.

The Savant Reservoir

The claim that everyone carries a hidden savant inside, unlocked by injury or effort. Acquired savant syndrome is real; the reservoir is an inference with nothing behind it.

The claim

Savant syndrome describes people with developmental conditions or brain injury who show exceptional ability in a narrow domain — calendar calculation, hypermnesia, drawing, music — alongside significant disability elsewhere. Acquired savant syndrome, where a skill appears after injury or illness, is documented in a small number of cases.

From those cases comes a larger claim: that the capacity is latent in everyone, and that the disability or the injury releases it. It is a popular idea in self-help and in writing about psychedelics and brain stimulation.

What is actually known

Savant skills are usually procedural, domain-specific, and appear early. Their presence correlates with intense practice and with a narrow focus, not with a general unlocking. The acquired cases are rare and often show skills the person had some prior interest in.

The reservoir claim has no mechanism and no measurement: nobody has demonstrated a suppressed ability in a typical brain that some intervention releases. It is also unfalsifiable in its usual form, since failure to unlock is attributed to not trying the right method.

What is established

Documented: savant syndrome, and a small number of acquired cases.

Documented: the skills are narrow, procedural and often appear with intense practice.

Not established: a latent reservoir in everyone, or any method that unlocks it.

Not established: the popular claim that brain stimulation or psychedelics produce savant abilities.

The honest label: fringe. The phenomenon is real and the explanation is a story about it.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim that flatters everyone — you might be a genius, if only something were switched on — and because the real cases are more interesting than the fantasy: narrow, hard-won, and attached to a life that is usually difficult.

The Call of the Void

Standing at a height, a small number of people feel a sudden urge to jump. It is not a death wish, it is common, and it has a name in French that predates the research.

The phenomenon

The 'call of the void' — l'appel du vide in French — is the intrusive thought of jumping or swerving when near a height or a moving vehicle. Surveys find that a substantial minority, sometimes around half of respondents in student samples, report having experienced something like it, usually once or a few times, and usually without any wish to act.

It is not a symptom of suicidal intent. The people who report it describe the thought as alien and unwelcome, and it appears in people with no history of self-harm.

What it appears to be

The leading account is that these are intrusive thoughts, which are near-universal, combined with a misinterpretation signal: the brain produces a safety-related impulse ('do not step closer') and the conscious mind experiences it as its opposite. Some work links the phenomenon to anxiety sensitivity — a heightened awareness of bodily signals — rather than to depression.

What is established

Documented: the experience is common, and distinct from suicidal ideation.

Documented: it is reported as intrusive and unwanted.

Supported: an association with anxiety sensitivity in the small literature available.

Not established: a precise mechanism, or a clinical threshold at which it becomes a symptom.

Why it matters: it is a clean example of a thought that is not a wish, which is a distinction a great deal of writing about the mind gets wrong.

Why it is in the archive

Because the archive spends most of its time on claims about the world, and this one is about the difference between a thought and an intention — the same difference that separates a fringe claim from a lie.

The Global Consciousness Project

A network of random number generators, said to deviate from randomness when large numbers of people are emotionally engaged. The statistics do not survive the way the events were chosen.

The claim

From 1998 the Global Consciousness Project, founded by Roger Nelson at Princeton, ran a network of hardware random number generators around the world, recording their output continuously. The claim is that during events that focus mass attention — the 9/11 attacks, New Year, major disasters — the network's output deviates from randomness in a way consistent with a global effect of consciousness.

The reported effect is small, and the project has published it as significant over the full dataset.

The problems

The first is event selection: the events were chosen by the researchers, largely after the fact or with knowledge of what would be emotionally significant, and the number of candidate events is unbounded. Choosing which days count is choosing the result.

The second is multiple comparisons: the analysis looks at many time windows, many event definitions and many statistical measures, and reports the ones that come out significant. A 2010 re-analysis by Peter Bancel and others found that the effect disappears under pre-registered event definitions. Independent replication with a fixed protocol has not produced the result.

What is established

Documented: the network ran, and the data exist.

Documented: the reported effect depends on post-hoc event selection.

Not replicated: with pre-registered events and a fixed analysis.

Not established: any link between consciousness and random number generators.

The lesson: this is the archive's cleanest case of a statistical artefact that looks like a discovery — and the reason pre-registration exists.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-documented attempt to measure a global effect of mind, it ran for twenty years with real equipment, and it failed in the specific way that statistics fails when the analyst is also the chooser.

Life in Venus's Clouds

The surface of Venus is hot enough to melt lead. Fifty kilometres up, the pressure and temperature are almost Earth-like — which is why the cloud layer keeps being proposed as a habitat, and why the phosphine claim of 2020 mattered.

The proposal

In 1967 Carl Sagan and Harold Morowitz suggested a Venusian aerial biosphere: microbes living in cloud droplets, where the temperature is 30–70 °C and the pressure is about one atmosphere. The idea has been taken seriously because the surface is uninhabitable and the clouds are, physically, the least hostile place in the solar system after Earth.

The chemistry is hostile in a different way. The droplets are 75–96% sulfuric acid, and the water activity in them is extremely low — comparable to the driest places on Earth, and far below what any known organism requires.

The phosphine claim

In September 2020 a team led by Jane Greaves reported phosphine in Venus's atmosphere at about 20 parts per billion, from two telescopes, and noted that no known abiotic process readily explains it. Phosphine is a biosignature on Earth.

The claim did not survive intact. Independent reanalyses found that the spectral feature could be explained by sulfur dioxide absorption and by calibration artefacts in the data; later work found phosphine at most at a small fraction of the original figure. The original team stood by part of the analysis, and the dispute was technical and public.

Where it stands

Documented: the cloud layer is physically the mildest environment off Earth.

Documented: the droplets are concentrated sulfuric acid with very low water activity.

Contested then reduced: the phosphine detection. Independent analyses found SO₂ and artefacts; the abundance is now at most a trace.

Not established: any life, or any biosignature that survives reanalysis.

Testable: yes — several Venus missions are planned, which is more than most pages in this collection can say.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a live scientific question that was briefly reported as a discovery, and because the correction happened in public, in under a year, in the literature. That is what the process looks like when it works.

Europa's Ocean

Beneath fifteen kilometres of ice, Europa has more liquid water than all of Earth's oceans. Whether anything lives in it is unknown, and a spacecraft is on its way to look.

The evidence for the ocean

Europa's surface is ice, cut by long curved fractures, with very few impact craters — a young surface being resurfaced. The Galileo mission's magnetometer detected an induced magnetic field, which requires a conductor near the surface: a salty ocean, responding to Jupiter's rotating field.

The numbers are not in dispute. The ice shell is roughly 15–25 km thick, the ocean beneath it perhaps 60–150 km deep, and tidal heating from Jupiter keeps it liquid. The total volume is about twice Earth's oceans.

What is not known

Whether the ocean is habitable, and whether it is inhabited. Water alone is not enough: life needs an energy source, and the chemistry — salinity, pH, the availability of oxidants from the surface — is unknown. Plumes of water vapour reported by Hubble in 2012 and 2016 have not been confirmed by later observations.

Europa Clipper launched in October 2024 and arrives in 2030; it will characterise the ice shell and the ocean's composition from orbit. It is not a life-detection mission, and its planners say so.

What is established

Documented: a global salty ocean beneath an ice shell, by magnetometry and geology.

Documented: tidal heating and a young, resurfacing surface.

Not established: habitability — the chemistry is unknown.

Not established: life, or any biosignature. No mission has sampled the ocean.

Testable: Clipper's instruments will constrain composition, which is the next real step.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's model of a claim where the evidence is strong, the inference people want is one step further, and the honest answer is 'the water is there; nothing else is yet'.

Mirror Matter

Every particle could have a mirror twin in a hidden sector that interacts only gravitationally. It would be dark matter, and it would be invisible. It is an elegant idea with no detection.

The idea

In 1956, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang noted that the weak interaction might not conserve parity, and asked whether the universe could be symmetric in a hidden way: a mirror sector of particles, identical in their physics but interacting with ours only through gravity.

The appeal is that it needs no new tuning. If the mirror sector exists, its particles would clump like ours, and the clumps would be dark matter — a natural candidate that arrives from a symmetry rather than an invented particle.

Why it is untested

Mirror matter interacts only gravitationally, so it cannot be seen, and its presence can only be inferred through gravity. Experiments look for mixing — photon–mirror-photon oscillation, neutron–mirror-neutron oscillation — and have set tight limits without finding anything. The parameter space shrinks but is not closed.

The deeper problem is that the idea makes few predictions sharp enough to fail. A theory that can accommodate any dark matter distribution is hard to distinguish from a description of it.

Where it stands

Documented: the symmetry argument, and the mixing experiments that constrain it.

Not observed: any mirror particle, or any mixing effect.

Not excluded: the parameter space, which is large and shrinking.

Not favoured: by any data — WIMPs, axions and primordial black holes all have more experimental traction.

The honest label: fringe — a serious idea with a real literature, filed here because it has no evidence rather than because it is unreasonable.

Why it is in the archive

Because the archive distinguishes fringe from crank: mirror matter is proposed by working physicists, published in physical review journals, and tested. It is fringe because it is unevidenced, not because it is silly.

The Big Bounce

If the universe contracts before it expands, the Big Bang is not a beginning. The idea is mathematically developed and observationally untested, and the cosmic microwave background is where it would show.

The idea

A bounce cosmology replaces the initial singularity with a contraction that reverses into the expansion we see. Two main routes exist: loop quantum cosmology, in which quantum geometry provides a repulsive force at high density, and the ekpyrotic model, in which the visible universe is one of two branes that collide.

The motivation is that a singularity is where the theory stops, so a model that avoids it is doing less violence to the physics — and because a bounce can, in principle, leave observable traces.

What would show it

A bounce imprints on the cosmic microwave background in specific ways: a suppression of large-scale power, a particular non-Gaussianity, or a preferred direction. Planck's measurements have constrained these, and have not found the signatures the models predicted in their simplest forms. The models have been adjusted in response, which is the normal and slightly worrying life of a cosmological idea.

Where it stands

Documented: the models, their mathematics, and their predictions.

Constrained: by the CMB — the simplest versions are disfavoured.

Not excluded: the class of models, which is large.

Not observed: any bounce signature, or any evidence that the universe contracted.

The honest label: live debate in the technical literature, with no observational support yet.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's example of a claim that is entirely respectable and entirely unevidenced, and because the difference between that and a fringe claim is where it is published, not how it sounds.

  • Wikipedia, “Cosmic microwave background” — where the test livesen.wikipedia.org

The Baader–Meinhof Effect

Learn a new word and it appears everywhere for a week. Nothing has changed except your attention — which is why it is also called the frequency illusion.

The effect

The Baader–Meinhof phenomenon is the experience of encountering a recently learned thing everywhere. The name comes from a 1994 letter to the St. Paul Pioneer Press, in which a reader described learning about the German faction and then seeing it mentioned repeatedly.

The mechanism has two parts, and neither is mysterious. Selective attention makes you notice the thing once it is salient, and confirmation bias makes the notices memorable while the non-notices are not counted. The linguist Arnold Zwicky named it the 'frequency illusion' in 2005, which is the better name.

Why it matters here

Because it is the mechanism behind a large fraction of the claims in this archive: a pattern noticed after it is named, and then reported as though the naming revealed it. It is also why 'I keep seeing this everywhere' is not evidence of anything except attention.

What is established

Documented: the effect is robust and easily demonstrated.

Documented: it is produced by selective attention plus confirmation bias.

Documented: the frequency of the thing does not change.

Not established: any external cause. There is nothing to explain beyond the two biases.

The useful lesson: salience is not prevalence, and the archive's job is mostly to keep them apart.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the perceptual error underneath several of the stranger pages here, and because naming it is the cheapest debunking tool the archive has.

  • Wikipedia, “Attentional bias” — the first halfen.wikipedia.org

Folie à Deux

A delusion shared by two people in a close relationship, usually one dominant and one suggestible. It is rare, it is real, and the modern diagnostic manuals have quietly stopped calling it a separate illness.

The syndrome

Folie à deux was described by Charles Lasègue and Jules Falret in 1877: a delusional belief shared by two people, typically living closely together, with one (the 'inducer') psychotic and the other adopting the belief. The shared content is often persecutory, and separation usually resolves the second person's delusion — which is the strongest evidence that the sharing is social.

The modern term is shared psychotic disorder, and DSM-5 folded it into the schizophrenia spectrum rather than keeping it as its own category. Variants exist for more than two people (folie à trois, and so on) and for the direction of influence.

Why it matters

Because it is the clearest clinical demonstration that beliefs are social objects. The mechanism is ordinary — proximity, dependence, a shared frame — and it scales in ways that are uncomfortable: the same dynamics appear in closed groups, in families, and online.

What is established

Documented: the syndrome, its typical structure, and its resolution on separation.

Documented: it is rare in clinical settings.

Not established: a distinct mechanism. It is described, not explained.

Not established: a general 'contagion' of delusion in crowds, which is a different and weaker claim.

Why it is in the archive: because the archive's subject is claims, and this is the clinical case where a claim is transmitted by relationship rather than by evidence.

Why it is here

Because it is the human-scale version of every group belief the archive documents, and because the treatment — separation, not argument — is a fact worth knowing.

Collective Effervescence

Durkheim's term for what happens when a crowd assembles and feels something together. It is not mysticism; it is the mechanism by which rituals make beliefs feel true.

The concept

Émile Durkheim introduced the term in The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912), describing the heightened emotional state produced when people assemble for a ritual. In his account, the experience is real and its object is the group itself: the participants feel a power, and the power is the collective.

Durkheim's argument was that this is how beliefs become sacred — not because the object is divine, but because the assembly generates an intensity that gets attributed to the object.

What modern research finds

The concept has measurable correlates: synchronous movement and chanting raise pain thresholds and social bonding, mediated by endorphins; shared attention and arousal increase felt solidarity and conformity. The effects are real and are studied in labs as well as at festivals.

What is established

Documented: assembly and synchrony produce measurable arousal, bonding and altered pain thresholds.

Documented: the effect strengthens group identity and conformity.

Not mystical: nothing in the findings requires a force beyond physiology and social psychology.

Durkheim's larger claim: that this is the origin of religious feeling — an interpretation, not a measurement.

Why it is in the archive: because it explains how a crowd can make a claim feel true, which is a recurring mechanism in the pages here.

Why it is here

Because the archive documents claims that spread, and this is the oldest and best-studied account of the social mechanism that makes them stick: not argument, but assembly.

The Berenstain Bears

A generation remembers the books as 'Berenstein'. They were always 'Berenstain'. The spelling is the archive's neatest case of a false memory shared by thousands of people.

The claim

Around 2012, people began reporting online that the children's series had changed spelling: they remembered 'Berenstein Bears', and the books said 'Berenstain'. The discrepancy was folded into the Mandela Effect, and from there into claims about parallel universes and altered timelines.

The books were written by Stan and Jan Berenstain, whose surname was always spelled with an 'a'. There is no edition, anywhere, with 'stein'.

Why the memory is wrong in that direction

'-stein' is far more common in English-speaking countries than '-stain' as a surname ending, so a reader's memory regularises an unusual spelling to a familiar one. The series was read aloud to children who rarely saw the spine closely, and the pronunciation of the two endings is nearly identical. Every condition for a confident, systematic false memory is present.

What is established

Documented: the surname was always Berenstain; no edition says Berenstein.

Documented: a large number of people remember otherwise, consistently.

Explained: by memory regularisation toward a common spelling, plus low attention to the spine.

Not evidence: of parallel universes, timeline shifts, or a mass edit.

The value of the case: it is a demonstration that a shared, confident, consistent memory can be wrong — which is the strongest argument in the archive against testimony alone.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest case of a false memory that is checkable against a physical object, and because it shows how quickly a memory error becomes a cosmology.

  • Wikipedia, “False memory” — how confident errors formen.wikipedia.org

Who Were the Sea Peoples?

Egyptian inscriptions record a coalition of peoples attacking the Nile Delta at the end of the Bronze Age. Nobody knows where they came from, and the question is older than archaeology.

The record

The Sea Peoples appear in Egyptian texts from the reign of Merneptah (c. 1208 BC) and, most fully, in the inscriptions and reliefs of Ramesses III at Medinet Habu (c. 1177 BC). They are named as a coalition: Peleset, Tjekker, Shekelesh, Denyen, Weshesh, Sherden and others. The texts describe a war by land and sea, and a defeat.

The same period saw the collapse of the Hittite empire, the destruction of Ugarit, and the end of Mycenaean palace society. The Sea Peoples are one thread in the wider Bronze Age collapse — not the whole explanation, and probably not the cause.

The competing answers

The Peleset are widely identified with the Philistines, who appear in the Levant shortly afterwards, which supports an Aegean or Anatolian origin for at least that group. The Sherden and Shekelesh have been linked, on linguistic grounds, to Sardinia and Sicily — a link that is suggestive and contested. Others may be Anatolian, or displaced populations from the collapsed states.

The honest position is that the Egyptian texts give names, not addresses. There is no settlement, no cemetery and no material culture that can be pinned to the coalition as a whole.

Where it stands

Documented: the coalition, its named groups, and the Egyptian campaigns against it.

Documented: the contemporaneous collapse of several eastern Mediterranean states.

Likely: that the Peleset are the Philistines, and that migration was involved.

Contested: the origins of the other groups, and whether 'Sea Peoples' describes one movement or several.

The honest label: live debate, with the evidence for origins thin and the evidence for the events good.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a genuine historical mystery that has been recruited for claims about Atlantis, and because the archive wants at least one page where the honest answer is 'we know the names and not the places'.

  • Wikipedia, “Medinet Habu” — where the inscriptions areen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Philistines” — the group most likely identifieden.wikipedia.org

The Amber Room

A room panelled in amber, looted by the Nazis in 1941, and lost in 1945. The reconstruction is finished; the original is still missing, and the search has produced a great deal of theory and no amber.

The object

The Amber Room was a set of amber panels given by Prussia to Peter the Great in 1716 and installed at the Catherine Palace near St Petersburg. It was one of the largest pieces of amber work in the world, and it was dismantled by German forces in 1941 and taken to Königsberg.

In 1945, as the Red Army approached, the crates disappeared. The castle where they were stored was destroyed; the room was never found.

The theories

The main candidates are destruction — in the castle fire, or in the sinking of a ship carrying evacuees — and concealment, in a mine, a bunker or a lake. Searches have been conducted in Germany, the Czech Republic and the Baltic, including a well-publicised 2020 dig in Poland that found nothing.

Documents suggest the panels may have been moved to a castle in what is now Poland, and some accounts indicate they were destroyed in a fire there. No amber from the room has been identified since 1945.

What is established

Documented: the room, its construction, its gift, its looting and its disappearance.

Documented: the reconstruction, completed in 2003 from photographs and surviving fragments.

Not established: where the original is, or whether it survives.

Not established: any of the burial, bunker or shipwreck claims — all have been searched and none has produced the room.

Why it persists: because a lost object of enormous value is a permanent invitation to claim it has been found.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real loss, with real documents, that has attracted four decades of unverified claims — and because the reconstruction is an honest answer to an unanswerable question: build it again, and say so.

The Dendera Light

A relief at Dendera shows a bulb-shaped object with a snake inside it. The claim that it depicts an electric lamp ignores the rest of the scene, which explains it.

The image

In the Hathor temple at Dendera, a relief shows what looks like a large glass bulb with a wavy filament inside, held up by a figure, with a cable-like stem running to a base. In the 1990s it was circulated as evidence of ancient Egyptian electric lighting — a Crookes tube, no less, with the snake as the glowing filament.

The relief is one panel of a larger scene, and the scene is a creation myth. The 'bulb' is a lotus flower, the 'snake' is a serpent emerging from it — a standard Egyptian motif for the emergence of life from the primordial waters — and the 'cable' is the lotus stem, which the supporting figure holds.

What would be needed

A working lamp needs glass, metal electrodes, a vacuum and a power source. None of these appears in the Egyptian record: no glass vessels of that shape, no wires, no batteries with terminals, no residue of a power system. The relief also sits among inscriptions that describe the scene, and they do not describe lighting.

What is established

Documented: the relief exists, and looks like a bulb to a modern eye.

Documented: it belongs to a creation scene with a lotus and a serpent, and the inscriptions match that reading.

Not documented: glass bulbs, electrodes, wires or any electrical technology in Egypt.

The pattern: the same one as the Baghdad Battery — a shape recognised from a modern context, then read as its modern meaning.

Why the label is debunked: the claim is not merely unsupported; the scene it was taken from has a documented explanation.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's clearest case of an image being removed from its context and read as a photograph of technology. The relief is not ambiguous once you look at the rest of it.

The Giza Power Plant

The claim that the Great Pyramid was a machine for generating electricity, with the King's Chamber as a resonant cavity. It is an engineering hypothesis with no artefact of any machine in it.

The claim

Christopher Dunn argued in 1998 that the Great Pyramid was a power plant: the King's Chamber, lined with granite containing quartz, would resonate at a specific frequency; the 'shafts' would act as waveguides; chemical reactions in the chamber would supply energy; and the structure would convert it to microwave power.

The argument leans on the precision of the masonry and on the granite's quartz content, which is real — granite does contain quartz, and quartz is piezoelectric.

The problems

The hypothesis requires machinery that is absent: no coils, no conductors, no electrodes, no insulators, no residue of any working fluid, no transmission hardware. The chamber is a plain room with a stone coffer in it.

The precision of the masonry is real but has ordinary explanations — careful surveying and a workforce with generations of experience — and it does not imply a function beyond a tomb. The piezoelectric effect in granite is minuscule at any plausible stress and would not produce usable power in a static structure.

Where it stands

Documented: the precision, the granite, the shafts, the chamber.

Not documented: any component of a power system.

Not plausible: the piezoelectric output of stressed granite at the scale required.

The reasoning error: inferring a function from a material property, without any artefact of the function.

The honest label: fringe. It is an engineering thought experiment, not a finding.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most technically literate of the pyramid claims, and it fails for a reason worth stating plainly: a machine leaves parts, and this one has none.

  • Wikipedia, “King's Chamber” — the room at the centre of the claimen.wikipedia.org

The Copper Scroll

One Dead Sea Scroll is not a text but a treasure map: sixty-four locations, quantities of gold and silver, and no treasure ever found. It is the only scroll in the collection that reads like an inventory.

The object

The Copper Scroll (3Q15) was found in 1952 in Cave 3 at Qumran: two rolled sheets of copper, corroded into a solid mass. Because it could not be unrolled, it was cut into strips in Manchester in 1956 and read from the fragments.

Its text is unlike the rest of the Dead Sea Scrolls. It is a list — sixty-four entries — of hiding places, each with a description and a quantity of gold, silver or vessels. The totals, if taken literally, run to tens of tonnes of precious metal.

The argument

If the list is a real inventory, it describes the treasure of the Second Temple, hidden before the Roman destruction in 70 CE — which would make it the most valuable document in the collection. If it is not, it is a literary or folkloric object, or a record of a much smaller cache.

Searches have been conducted at several of the locations. None has produced treasure. The language is Mishnaic Hebrew, later than the other scrolls, and some of the place names are otherwise unknown.

Where it stands

Documented: the scroll, its text, and its sixty-four entries.

Documented: its language and physical form differ from the other Qumran scrolls.

Not established: that the treasure is real, or that it was the Temple's.

Not found: any of it, at any of the locations searched.

The honest label: live debate — a genuine document whose reference is unknown, in a field where the answer would be worth a great deal.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's best case of a document that is definitely authentic and definitely not understood — and because 'the treasure is still out there' is a claim that has survived seventy years of searching without a single find.

Arthur as a Roman Commander

The earliest mention of Arthur is a battle list written three centuries after he supposedly lived. The claim that he was a Roman officer is a modern attempt to fill the gap.

The sources

The earliest text to name Arthur is the Historia Brittonum, attributed to Nennius, written in the ninth century — three hundred years after the events it describes — which lists twelve battles. Gildas, writing in the sixth century, mentions the British victory at Mount Badon but does not name Arthur.

There is no contemporary reference: no inscription, no letter, no chronicle written while he was alive. The medieval romances are later still, and are literature.

The Roman hypothesis

The modern argument is that if there was a historical Arthur, he was a post-Roman British war leader — possibly a cavalry commander — and several candidates have been proposed, including Lucius Artorius Castus, a second-century Roman officer whose name resembles Arthur's and who served in Britain.

The name link is suggestive and the chronology is wrong: Artorius Castus lived some three hundred years before the period Arthur is supposed to have fought in. The identification requires the legend to have migrated across centuries, which is possible and unevidenced.

Where it stands

Documented: a post-Roman British elite, warfare, and a victory at Badon.

Documented: the name Arthur in ninth-century sources.

Not documented: Arthur himself, in any contemporary source.

Contested: every candidate identification, including the Roman ones.

The honest position: a legend with a possible historical core, and no evidence sufficient to name the man.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's example of a claim where the absence of evidence is itself the finding, and where the search has been going on for so long that the absence has become the subject.

Yamashita's Gold

The claim that the Japanese army buried billions in looted treasure in the Philippines at the end of the war. Seventy years of digging has produced plaques, tunnels and lawsuits, and no gold.

The claim

The story holds that Japanese forces under General Tomoyuki Yamashita looted Southeast Asia and buried the proceeds — gold, gems, art — in tunnels and caves across the Philippines in 1945, and that the locations were encoded in maps and marked with symbols. It became a fixture of treasure-hunting literature and of Filipino politics in the Marcos era.

The evidence

The tunnels are real; many are wartime. The treasure is another matter. Searches have been conducted for decades, including a well-publicised case in which a Filipino treasure hunter, Rogelio Roxas, sued Ferdinand Marcos in Hawaii; the court found in his favour on some claims and awarded damages, but no gold was ever produced or verified.

Declassified US documents show that American investigators looked for Japanese war loot in the Philippines and found little. The claim's structure — maps that cannot be checked, sites that are always just about to be opened, a legal case that establishes a wrong without establishing the object — is the structure of a legend, not a recovery.

What is established

Documented: Japanese forces looted Southeast Asia, and wartime tunnels exist.

Documented: decades of searches, and a lawsuit that produced damages but no gold.

Not established: the existence of the hoard, its size, or any of the maps.

Not found: a single verified item.

The honest label: fringe — a real war, real tunnels, and a treasure that has never existed outside testimony.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows how a real historical crime becomes a permanent rumour: the loot was real, so the hoard must be somewhere, and the somewhere is always the next site.

The Lunar Wave

Videos show a ripple crossing the Moon's face. The claim is a hologram or a projection. The explanation is the atmosphere, the camera, and the way a bright edge behaves in a turbulent sky.

The claim

From 2016, videos circulated showing a dark band or ripple passing across the Moon's disc when filmed at high magnification. The claim was that the Moon is a hologram or a projection, and that the wave is a refresh artefact.

The explanation

The artefact is atmospheric. At high magnification, the Moon is seen through a column of turbulent air, and the image distorts — the same effect that makes stars twinkle and distant roads shimmer. When a bright, high-contrast edge moves across the field, the distortion appears as a travelling band.

The pattern is consistent with that: the wave moves at a rate set by the atmosphere and the camera's exposure, it appears at high magnification and low elevation (more air), and it disappears on nights of good seeing. No observatory has recorded anything similar with adaptive optics or from orbit.

What is established

Documented: the videos exist, and show a real distortion in the recorded image.

Documented: atmospheric turbulence produces exactly this class of artefact.

Documented: the effect depends on magnification, elevation and seeing.

Not established: any anomaly in the Moon itself, or any projection.

The test that settles it: the same phenomenon appears on planets, on the Sun (with a filter) and on any bright object at high magnification.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's cleanest imaging artefact: the claim is not about a hidden object but about the instrument, and the instrument explains itself.

  • Wikipedia, “Mirage” — the family of atmospheric distortionsen.wikipedia.org

Earth Was Terraformed

The claim that Earth was engineered for life — by an earlier civilisation, or by design. It borrows the language of a real scientific debate about fine-tuning and rare Earth, and then adds an agent nobody has evidence for.

The claim

The terraforming claim says that Earth's habitability is too convenient to be accidental: a stable star, a large moon, a magnetic field, plate tectonics, a water inventory, a Jupiter that absorbs impacts. On this reading, something engineered the planet — an earlier civilisation, or a designer — and the evidence is the fine-tuning.

What is real in it

The underlying observations are real and are studied. The Rare Earth hypothesis argues that complex life requires an unusual combination of conditions; the fine-tuning debate notes that several physical constants appear to sit in narrow ranges that permit complexity. Both are live scientific arguments.

Neither implies an agent. Fine-tuning arguments have well-known responses — the anthropic selection effect, a multiverse, or simply that the constants are not as fine-tuned as claimed — and none of them requires a designer. The terraforming claim takes a genuine puzzle and inserts a cause with no independent evidence.

What is established

Documented: Earth's habitability depends on an unusual set of conditions.

Documented: the Rare Earth and fine-tuning arguments exist in the scientific literature.

Not established: any agent, earlier civilisation or designer.

Not testable: in its usual form, because any evidence either way is absorbed.

The honest label: fringe. The observations are real; the explanation is an insertion.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's example of a claim built from real science by adding one unevidenced noun, and because the real debate — why is this planet like this — is more interesting than the answer it is used to support.

The Gateway Process

A 1983 CIA report describes consciousness as a hologram and out-of-body travel as a change in brainwave frequency. It is a literature review written by one officer, and it is cited as though it were a finding.

The document

In 1983 a lieutenant colonel, Wayne McDonnell, wrote a report for the US Army titled 'Analysis and Assessment of Gateway Process', describing the Monroe Institute's Hemi-Sync audio programme. It was declassified in 2003 and has circulated ever since as evidence that the CIA 'confirmed' that consciousness is a hologram and that out-of-body experiences are real.

The report is a review. It summarises the Monroe Institute's claims, offers a speculative physical model involving holography and brainwave frequencies, and recommends further study. It is not a study, contains no data, and was written to inform a programme, not to conclude one.

What the programme produced

The army's interest was part of the remote viewing programme later called Stargate, which ran for two decades and was terminated in 1995 after an evaluation found no actionable results. The evaluators' conclusion — that the programme had produced nothing of operational value — is the finding, and it is rarely quoted alongside the Gateway report.

What is established

Documented: the report exists, was written in 1983, and is declassified.

Documented: it is a literature review and a speculative model, not an experiment.

Documented: the associated remote viewing programme was closed in 1995 for lack of results.

Not established: any of the physical claims — the holographic model, the frequency shifts, the out-of-body travel.

The pattern: a real document, cited for a claim it does not make.

Why it is in the archive

Because declassification is not evidence, and because this document is the most-quoted 'government confirmation' in the collection. Reading the last page of the file is usually enough.

Timewave Zero

A curve derived from the I Ching, claimed to map the novelty of the universe and to end in 2012. The date passed; the curve was fitted, not derived.

The claim

Terence McKenna developed 'timewave zero' from 1975: a graph of novelty — the rate of change and complexity in the universe — derived, he said, from the sequence of hexagrams in the I Ching. The curve was fractal, self-similar at every scale, and was claimed to describe the past and predict the future.

Its endpoint, the 'zero point' of infinite novelty, was set at 21 December 2012, matching the end of the Maya long count.

The problems

The derivation is arbitrary. The King Wen sequence of hexagrams is a historical ordering with no known mathematical necessity, and the transformation from that sequence to a curve involves choices that are not constrained by anything. When the curve failed to match history, the parameters were adjusted.

The date was also adjustable: earlier versions of the theory put the zero point in 2011, and the choice of 2012 aligned it with a separate cultural bandwagon. The date passed without an event, which is the kind of test the claim could not survive.

What is established

Documented: the theory, its construction, and its 2012 endpoint.

Documented: the 2012 date passed without incident.

Not derived: the curve from any measurement. It is a construction with free parameters.

Not predictive: no successful prediction that was made in advance and survived.

Why the label is debunked: it made a dated prediction, the date passed, and the claim was not revised into a testable form.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's clearest example of a claim with a hard date attached — and hard dates are the best gift a claim can give a reader, because they can be checked.

  • Wikipedia, “2012 phenomenon” — the date and its failureen.wikipedia.org

Quantum Healing

The claim that consciousness can direct quantum processes to heal the body. It uses the vocabulary of quantum mechanics, and every one of its central assertions contradicts what quantum mechanics says about warm, wet tissue.

The claim

Deepak Chopra's Quantum Healing (1989) argued that the body is a quantum system and that consciousness can influence it at the quantum level — that intention, meditation or belief can act on 'quantum fields' to produce healing. The vocabulary spread widely: quantum touch, quantum energy, quantum coherence in the body.

What quantum mechanics actually says

Quantum effects in biology are real and are studied: photosynthesis uses coherence, and enzymes use tunnelling. But these are processes measured at ultrafast timescales, in structured molecular environments, at temperatures near absolute zero or in carefully shielded systems.

The central obstacle is decoherence. A quantum superposition in warm, wet tissue collapses in around 10⁻²⁰ seconds — twelve orders of magnitude faster than the millisecond timescales of neural activity. A 'quantum field' of the kind the claim requires cannot survive in a brain long enough to do anything.

None of this rules out that meditation or belief can help people feel better. The placebo effect is real, and the mind does affect the body through ordinary physiology. The quantum story is not the mechanism.

What is established

Documented: quantum effects occur in some biological systems, at specific scales.

Documented: decoherence timescales exclude the kind of effect the claim needs.

Documented: placebo and mind–body effects are real and are not quantum.

Not established: any quantum mechanism of intention, energy or healing.

The pattern: borrowed vocabulary doing the work of evidence, which is the most common move in the whole fringe literature.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's clearest case of a claim that sounds more credible the less physics you know — and because the honest alternative, that the mind affects the body through measurable physiology, is more interesting than the metaphor.
