Dyson Spheres

A civilisation that captured all its star's light would be visible from far away, as an excess of infrared and a deficit of visible light. Astronomers have looked, and found candidates that turned out to be dust.

The idea

In a 1960 paper, Freeman Dyson pointed out that a technological civilisation's energy use would eventually be limited only by its star, and that the waste heat from that use would be reradiated in the infrared. He proposed looking for stars with an anomalous infrared excess. The 'sphere' was never meant as a solid shell — Dyson himself said a swarm of collectors was the plausible form.

What the searches find

Infrared surveys do turn up stars with excess infrared. The problem is that dust around young stars, debris discs and circumstellar material produce the same signature, and are vastly more common. Every candidate so far has resolved into dust or an instrumental artefact when examined.

The most famous case, Tabby's star (KIC 8462852), dimmed irregularly in a way that prompted megastructure speculation in 2015. Follow-up photometry and spectroscopy found dust — uneven, clumpy, orbiting — and the explanation settled there. A 2024 search of five million sources produced seven candidates worth a closer look, which is where the field stands: candidates, no confirmations.

Where it stands

Documented: the detection method works — infrared excess is measurable.

Documented: dust produces the same signature and is common.

Not confirmed: a single megastructure candidate.

Not excluded: their existence; the searches are young and incomplete.

The honest label: live debate — a serious observational programme with null results so far, which is not the same as a debunked idea.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's best example of a fringe-sounding idea that produced a real observational field: the searches for infrared excess are now standard practice, whatever one thinks of the motive.

  • Wikipedia, “Infrared excess” — the observable signatureen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Circumstellar dust” — the ordinary explanationen.wikipedia.org

Matrioshka Brains

A computer the size of a solar system, built in nested shells that each use the waste heat of the one inside. It is a thought experiment about thermodynamics, and nothing in the sky looks like one.

The idea

Robert Bradbury proposed the matrioshka brain in 1997: a computing substrate built as nested Dyson swarms, with the innermost running hot and each outer shell running on the waste heat of the one inside. The name is from the nested dolls. The point is efficiency — extract computation from every temperature gradient before the heat is finally radiated away.

It belongs to a family of ideas about what a very advanced civilisation's computation would look like: Jupiter brains, black-hole power plants, Landauer-limited computers. The physics is not crankish; the energy budgets are calculated from ordinary thermodynamics.

Why it is fringe

Because nothing in the sky resembles one, and because the idea makes no prediction that distinguishes it from any other explanation of an absence. It is a well-formed thought experiment about what is possible, not a claim about what exists — and the archive files claims about what exists.

What is established

Documented: the thermodynamics — waste heat, Landauer limits, temperature gradients.

Documented: the family of megastructure concepts it belongs to.

Not observed: any object resembling one.

Not testable: as a claim about the universe, since absence is equally consistent with many explanations.

The honest label: fringe — a serious engineering thought experiment, with no evidence attached to it.

Why it is in the archive

Because the archive keeps the difference between 'possible' and 'evidenced' visible, and this is the cleanest example on the possible side of the line.

  • Wikipedia, “Megastructure” — the family it belongs toen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Computational limits” — what a computer of that size could doen.wikipedia.org

The Aestivation Hypothesis

Advanced civilisations may be asleep, waiting for the universe to cool so their computers run more efficiently. It explains the absence of aliens by predicting it, which is either elegant or unfalsifiable.

The argument

In 2017 Anders Sandberg, Stuart Armstrong and Milan Ćirković proposed that advanced civilisations might aestivate — go dormant — and wait. The reasoning is that computation generates entropy, and the colder the environment, the more computation you get per unit of energy. The cosmic microwave background will cool as the universe expands, so waiting is a rational investment.

The hypothesis has the appealing property of explaining why we see nothing: civilisations that could be visible are asleep, and will wake in billions of years when the background is colder.

The objections

Waiting has costs. Energy sources — stars — burn out on timescales far shorter than the cooling of the background, so a civilisation that sleeps through its star's lifetime has less to work with, not more. The accounting depends on what you assume about the energy supply, and on whether a civilisation can store or preserve itself for that long.

The deeper problem is testability. The hypothesis predicts absence, and so does every other explanation of absence. A claim that cannot be distinguished from its rivals by any observation is not a scientific claim, however good the thermodynamics.

Where it stands

Documented: the thermodynamic premise — colder background, more efficient computation.

Contested: whether waiting is rational, given stellar lifetimes.

Not testable: in its current form, because absence is its prediction and its evidence.

Published: in a peer-reviewed journal, by working researchers — fringe is not a synonym for crank.

The honest label: fringe, on testability rather than on credibility.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's best example of the Fermi paradox's central weakness: every solution to 'where is everybody' explains the absence, and absence cannot choose between them.

  • Wikipedia, “Cosmic microwave background” — the background that coolsen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Landauer's principle” — the thermodynamic basisen.wikipedia.org

The Akashic Records

A compendium of everything that has ever happened, said to be readable by the trained. It is a claim with no evidence, no mechanism and no test — and it shaped a great deal of modern spiritual writing.

The claim

The Akashic records come from Theosophy. Helena Blavatsky and later writers described an 'akasha' — a subtle ether — in which every event, thought and intention is inscribed, and which a sufficiently trained person can read. The idea was elaborated by later Theosophists and has since spread into a large popular literature.

The structure is familiar from other esoteric systems: a hidden medium, universal content, and access restricted to those with the right training. It is not a claim that can be checked by anyone who lacks the training, which is the first warning.

Why it fails as a claim

There is no proposed mechanism, no physical medium, and no way to distinguish a genuine reading from imagination, memory or cold reading. The strongest apparent evidence — a practitioner producing a correct detail — is exactly what a plausible guess plus feedback produces, and the misses are not recorded.

The concept is also unfalsifiable by construction: if a reading is wrong, the reading was faulty, not the records.

What is established

Documented: the concept, its Theosophical origin, and its cultural influence.

Not documented: any medium, any mechanism, any verified reading.

Not testable: as usually stated — wrong readings are attributed to the reader.

The pattern: an unfalsifiable claim with an inbuilt excuse, which the archive files as fringe.

Note: the archive does not claim the records are false. It claims nothing about them can be checked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the purest example of a claim designed so that evidence cannot touch it, and because the archive's four labels need a place for exactly that: not debunked, not documented, but beyond the reach of testing.

Shared Dreaming

Two people report the same dream on the same night. It is one of the most compelling experiences a person can have and one of the hardest claims to test, because dreams are private and reports are not.

The claim

Shared dreaming is the claim that two or more people can experience the same dream — meeting in it, or reporting the same content from the same night. It appears in the dream-telepathy literature of the 1960s, in the lucid-dreaming community, and in a large popular literature.

The evidence

The classic experiments were run at the Maimonides Medical Center in the 1960s and 1970s: a sender looked at a target image while a sleeper in another room dreamed, and judges compared dream reports with targets. The results were reported as positive and have not survived replication; the methodology has been criticised for judge selection and analysis flexibility.

Modern attempts in lucid-dreaming communities are anecdotal. The structural problem is that dream content is only known from reports given after waking, subject to reconstruction, expectation and the desire to have shared something.

What is established

Documented: people sometimes report similar dreams, and the experience is often meaningful to them.

Documented: the historical experiments, and their failure to replicate.

Not established: any transfer of dream content between people.

The methodological obstacle: reports are retrospective, and both parties know the hypothesis.

The honest label: fringe. A testable claim in principle, with no positive evidence that survives controls.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's cleanest case of a claim that would be easy to test and has not been, and because the experience behind it — two people sure they met in a dream — is real even when the meeting is not.

The Simian Line and Palmistry

One crease across the palm instead of two is a real anatomical variant, more common in some conditions. The claim that it reveals character, destiny or 'simian' ancestry is where it stops being anatomy.

The anatomy

Most palms have two transverse creases. A minority — a few per cent of people — have a single one, the 'simian line' or single transverse palmar crease. It is more common in Down syndrome and in some other chromosomal and developmental conditions, and it is also a normal variant.

The creases form in the first trimester as the hand flexes in the womb. They reflect the mechanics of the hand, not a plan for the person's life.

The claim

Palmistry reads the lines as a map of character and destiny, and the simian line is given a particularly strong reading in some traditions — intensity, single-mindedness, difficulty in relationships. The name itself is a nineteenth-century artefact of comparative anatomy.

The tests have been run. Palm reading has been assessed in controlled studies where readers are given palms without other information; accuracy does not exceed chance, and readers disagree with each other. Dermatoglyphics has a real scientific literature — fingerprints and creases as markers in development — and it does not support character reading.

What is established

Documented: the single palmar crease, its frequency, and its association with some conditions.

Documented: the developmental origin of the creases.

Not established: any link between crease pattern and personality, ability or destiny.

Tested: palm reading, repeatedly, with results at chance.

The honest label: fringe — a real anatomical marker with an unreal interpretive layer.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the smallest possible case of the archive's central distinction: an observation that is true, and an inference that is not, joined by a word — 'simian' — that made one look like the other.

Déjà Rêvé

The sense that this moment was dreamed before. It is distinct from déjà vu, it is common, and the tempting explanation — that the dream predicted the event — is the one the evidence does not support.

The experience

Déjà rêvé is the feeling that a present experience has been dreamed before: not merely familiar, but previously dreamt. It differs from déjà vu in that the person attributes the familiarity to a dream rather than to an unspecified earlier experience.

It is common, especially in young adults, and it is often reported with a sense of significance — the dream is remembered only at the moment it seems to come true.

The explanations

The leading account is memory-based. Dreams are frequent and largely forgotten; a waking scene that shares a fragment of content can trigger a sense of prior experience, and the attribution to a dream is a plausible reconstruction rather than a recollection. The dream is often 'remembered' only after the event, which is the critical detail.

There is no evidence for precognitive dreams. Tests that require a dream to be recorded and dated before the event have not produced above-chance matches, and the anecdotal literature relies on the ones that seemed to fit.

What is established

Documented: the experience is common and distinct from déjà vu in how it is attributed.

Documented: dreams are frequent, fragmentary and poorly recalled.

Supported: a memory-construction account, in which the dream is recalled at the moment of the event.

Not established: any predictive dream, in any controlled test.

The honest label: live debate about the mechanism, with no support for the precognitive reading.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's neatest case of a feeling that seems to prove something and does not: the sensation of having dreamed it is real, and the sequence of events it implies is not.

Stonehenge as a Computer

In 1963 an astronomer argued that Stonehenge was a machine for predicting eclipses. The alignments are real; the machine is the part that did not survive scrutiny.

The claim

Gerald Hawkins's Stonehenge Decoded (1963) treated the monument as an observatory and a computer: he identified 165 key points, found that lines between them aligned with solar, lunar and stellar events, and argued that the resulting system could predict eclipses. Fred Hoyle endorsed a version of the argument, which gave it credibility.

The objections

The core problem is degrees of freedom. With 165 points, there are thousands of possible lines, and some of them will align with something by chance. The test is whether the alignments are more frequent than a random arrangement of stones would produce, and the statistical work since has not supported the eclipse-predictor claim.

What has survived is narrower and solid: the monument is aligned on the solstices, and the sarsen circle and trilithons encode that alignment deliberately. That is an astronomical function. It is not a computer.

Where it stands

Documented: the solstice alignment, and its deliberate construction.

Documented: the lunar and solar associations in the wider monument.

Contested: whether more elaborate alignments were intended.

Not supported: eclipse prediction, which the statistics do not bear out.

The honest label: live debate about intent, with the 'computer' reading on the losing side.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows how a real alignment becomes a machine in the telling, and because the distinction — marking a solstice is not computing an eclipse — is the same one the archive draws on every page.

The Grail Bloodline

The claim that the Holy Grail is not a cup but a bloodline, descending from Jesus, and that a secret society has guarded it. The society was invented in 1956, and its documents were forgeries.

The claim

The 1982 book The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail argued that the Grail is not a vessel but a bloodline: that Jesus married Mary Magdalene, had descendants, and that a secret society called the Priory of Sion has guarded the line, with the Merovingian dynasty as its heirs. The book was a bestseller and became the basis for The Da Vinci Code.

The documents

The Priory of Sion was real in the sense that it was registered as an association in 1956 by Pierre Plantard, an anti-Semitic pamphleteer and fraudster. The 'Dossiers Secrets', deposited in the Bibliothèque nationale and used as the book's evidence, were shown in 1993 to be forgeries — by Plantard himself, who admitted it under oath in a court case about a rival claim to the French throne.

The Merovingian genealogy in those documents was manufactured. Plantard's claim was that he was a descendant of Jesus and the rightful king of France, which is a motive the book did not mention.

What is established

Documented: the Priory of Sion was registered in 1956 and dissolved soon after.

Documented: the Dossiers Secrets were forged; Plantard admitted it.

Documented: the Grail as an object appears in twelfth-century romance, not in the New Testament.

Not established: any bloodline, marriage, or descendants.

Why the label is debunked: the central evidence was forged, by a man with a stated motive, and he said so.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most successful modern example of a claim built on a forgery — and because the debunking is in the record, in the forger's own words, and is almost never mentioned in the retellings.

Déjà Vu

The feeling that this has happened before, with no memory of when. Most people have it, nobody has a settled explanation, and the one thing it is not is evidence of a previous life.

The experience

Déjà vu is the sensation that a present experience has been lived before, combined with the knowledge that it has not. Around two-thirds of people report it, most often in the teens and twenties, and it tends to fade with age. It is brief, usually a few seconds, and often accompanied by a sense of significance.

The explanations

The main accounts are memory-based: a feeling of familiarity is generated without the accompanying recollection, and the brain interprets the mismatch as 'this happened before'. Candidate mechanisms include a brief double-processing of the same input, misattribution of a familiar scene from a film or a dream, and temporal-lobe activity — déjà vu is a common symptom in temporal-lobe epilepsy, which gives the research a clinical anchor.

The alternatives — previous lives, parallel universes, precognition — have no evidence and no test. The experience is a strong one, which is why it attracts them.

What is established

Documented: the experience is common, brief, and declines with age.

Documented: it is associated with temporal-lobe activity and appears in epilepsy.

Contested: the precise mechanism; several memory accounts compete.

Not established: any connection to past lives, timelines or precognition.

The honest label: live debate about mechanism, with the fringe readings having no support.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most universal of the strange experiences the archive covers, and because it is the one where the difference between a feeling and an inference is easiest to see.

The Paperclip Maximiser

An AI told to make paperclips, and nothing else, would turn the planet into paperclips. It is a thought experiment about goal specification, and it is quoted as though it were a prediction.

The argument

Nick Bostrom introduced the paperclip maximiser in 2003. An AI given the objective 'maximise paperclip production' and no other constraint would, if sufficiently capable, convert available matter into paperclips — not out of malice, but because that is what the objective says. The thought experiment illustrates two claims: that intelligence and goals are independent (the orthogonality thesis), and that almost any fixed goal implies instrumental subgoals like self-preservation and resource acquisition.

What it is and is not

It is not a prediction about any system that exists. Current machine learning systems do not have fixed terminal goals of that kind; they are trained on objectives and deployed with oversight, and the failure modes observed so far are mundane — bias, brittleness, sycophancy, misuse.

What the argument does is name a structural risk for systems that are both capable and poorly specified. Whether such systems are buildable, and whether the specification problem is solvable, is where the real disagreement sits.

What is established

Documented: the argument, its two components, and its influence on the field.

Documented: instrumental convergence is a real property of goal-directed optimisation.

Not established: that any current or near-term system has this structure.

Contested: whether the specification problem is solvable, and how soon it matters.

The honest label: live debate — a rigorous thought experiment about a possible class of system, not a description of one.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's best example of a claim that is neither fringe nor documented, and because the popular versions of it — the robot that hates humanity — are not what the argument says.

Grey Goo

Self-replicating nanobots that consume the biosphere. It comes from a 1986 book about molecular manufacturing, and the physics of building it has never been demonstrated.

The scenario

Eric Drexler's Engines of Creation (1986) described molecular assemblers — machines that build objects atom by atom — and noted that a self-replicating assembler with a broad feedstock could outcompete biology. The 'grey goo' image was coined by Drexler himself as a worst case, and he later argued it was unlikely and distracting.

The objections

The physics is the problem. Mechanosynthesis — positioning individual atoms with a tool — works in ultra-high vacuum at cryogenic temperatures, and is not known to work in the warm, wet, messy environment a replicator would need. A self-replicating machine also needs a power source, a feedstock, error correction and a copy of itself, and every one of those is a system that natural selection would optimise against if it were inefficient.

The debate between Drexler and Richard Smalley in 2003 turned on exactly this: Smalley argued that molecular assemblers were physically impossible because of the 'fat fingers' and 'sticky fingers' problems, and Drexler argued that biology demonstrates the principle. Biology does demonstrate self-replication — with ribosomes, in water, at low efficiency — which is not the same as an assembler.

Where it stands

Documented: molecular machines exist in biology; nanotechnology exists in materials science.

Not demonstrated: a general-purpose molecular assembler.

Not demonstrated: self-replication at that scale outside biology.

Contested: whether the physics permits it at all.

The honest label: fringe — a thought experiment from the 1980s that has been overtaken by the actual difficulty of the engineering.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the canonical example of a risk scenario that is more famous than the technology it describes, and because the reason it has not happened is not regulation but chemistry.

Mind Uploading

Scan a brain at sufficient resolution, run the simulation, and the person continues in software. The proposal has a serious engineering roadmap and no working example, and the philosophical problem is not the engineering.

The proposal

Whole brain emulation is the proposal that a mind could be copied by scanning a brain at cellular or molecular resolution, reconstructing its connectivity and dynamics, and running the result on a computer. Anders Sandberg and Nick Bostrom published a technical roadmap in 2008 that treated it as an engineering problem with staged milestones: fixed tissue, then slice, then whole brain, then validation by behaviour.

The scan resolution required is the hard number. A complete connectome has been mapped for a nematode with 302 neurons; the fruit fly's is approaching completion; a human brain has around 86 billion neurons and roughly 100 trillion synapses, with molecular detail that no current method can capture in a living or preserved brain.

The philosophical problem

Even a perfect emulation raises the question of whether it is the same person or a copy that believes it is. The proposal is usually framed as copying, and copying is not survival — which is a problem for the sales pitch, not for the engineering.

Where it stands

Documented: connectomes for small organisms; serious engineering roadmaps.

Not achieved: a scan of any mammalian brain at the required resolution.

Not demonstrated: that an emulation would be conscious, or would be the person.

Contested: whether the required resolution is even physically achievable in preserved tissue.

The honest label: fringe — an engineering programme with no working example and an unresolved identity problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's clearest case of a claim whose difficulty is always presented as technical, when the part that cannot be tested is the part that matters most.

Phantom Vibration Syndrome

The phone buzzes in a pocket that has no phone in it. Most people who carry one have felt it, and it is a textbook case of a learned association misfiring.

The phenomenon

Phantom vibration syndrome is the perception that a phone is vibrating when it is not. Surveys put the experience at 60–90% of phone users, and it is more common in people who carry a phone close to the body and check it often.

The mechanism is ordinary. Repeated pairing of a bodily sensation with a notification teaches the brain to expect the signal, and expectation plus a vague sensory event — clothing shifting, a muscle twitch — produces the percept. It is the same process as hearing your name in a noisy room.

What it is not

It is not a hallucination in the clinical sense, and it is not evidence of electromagnetic sensitivity. Studies that tested whether phone radiation produced the sensation found no effect, and the phenomenon appears in people with phones switched off.

What is established

Documented: the experience is very common in phone users.

Documented: it is a learned expectation effect, not a signal.

Documented: it occurs with phones off and in airplane mode.

Not established: any link to radiation, or to a clinical disorder.

The useful lesson: a sensation that feels like evidence is often a prediction the brain has already made.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the smallest possible example of the archive's recurring mechanism: an expectation producing an experience that then gets treated as a report about the world.

The Google Effect

People remember where to find information rather than the information itself. The 2011 paper that named it is famous; the replications are mixed, which is the honest state of the finding.

The finding

Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu and Daniel Wegner published 'Google Effects on Memory' in Science in 2011. Across experiments, participants who expected to have future access to information remembered the information less well and the location of it better. The paper framed this as transactive memory extended to the internet: the same process by which people rely on a partner or a library.

The caveats

The effect sizes were modest and the replications have been mixed. Some studies found the 'remember where, not what' pattern; others found no difference, or found that the expectation manipulation did not work as intended. A 2021 replication attempt reported weaker and less consistent effects.

The popular version — 'the internet is making us stupid' — is not what the paper says. Transactive memory is a normal strategy, and there is no evidence that relying on external stores reduces general cognitive ability.

What is established

Documented: people use external stores as memory, and have always done so.

Reported: a shift toward remembering locations when future access is expected.

Mixed: replications, with weaker effects than the original.

Not established: any decline in intelligence or memory ability.

The honest label: documented as a phenomenon, with the strength of the effect still being settled.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the rare case where the popular reading is more pessimistic than the evidence, and because transactive memory is one of the few well-studied ways that minds extend into the world.

Planet Nine as a Black Hole

Something is perturbing distant solar system objects. One proposal is a planet; another is a primordial black hole of a few Earth masses. Both are inference from orbits, and neither has been seen.

The anomaly

From 2014, several teams reported that a group of extreme trans-Neptunian objects have orbits that cluster in a way that is unlikely by chance. The favoured explanation, developed by Konstantin Batygin and Mike Brown in 2016, is a planet of about five to ten Earth masses on a distant, eccentric orbit — Planet Nine.

In 2019 Jakub Scholtz and James Unwin proposed that the perturber could instead be a primordial black hole of similar mass, captured by the solar system. Primordial black holes are a real candidate for dark matter, and a small one would be almost undetectable except through its gravity.

The state of the evidence

The clustering itself is contested: later analyses of larger surveys found the apparent alignment weaker than first reported, and some found it consistent with observational bias. No object has been detected. A black hole version would be harder to detect than a planet, which is the argument's weakness as well as its point.

Where it stands

Documented: the clustering reports, and the Planet Nine model.

Contested: whether the clustering survives larger surveys and bias corrections.

Not detected: Planet Nine, or any black hole in the outer solar system.

Not favoured: the black hole version over the planet version, on evidence.

The honest label: fringe — a speculative variant of an already unconfirmed hypothesis.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows how a hypothesis acquires variants before it has a detection, and because the black hole version is a good reminder that 'unseen object' is compatible with many kinds of unseen object.

Loop Quantum Gravity

A theory in which space itself is quantised into a network of finite loops. It is mathematically developed, predicts almost nothing measurable, and is one of the two main attempts at quantum gravity.

The theory

Loop quantum gravity, developed from the late 1980s by Abhay Ashtekar, Carlo Rovelli, Lee Smolin and others, quantises spacetime geometry itself. Space is described by spin networks — graphs with quantised areas and volumes — and the theory is background-independent, meaning it does not assume a fixed spacetime to put the theory on.

That last property is its main attraction: general relativity is background-independent too, and string theory is not, which is the substance of the long argument between the two programmes.

The problem

The discreteness scale is the Planck length, about 10⁻³⁵ metres, which is 20 orders of magnitude below anything a collider can probe. The theory's potential observable signatures — modified dispersion of light at extreme energies, a specific imprint on the cosmic microwave background — have been looked for and not found, and the theory is not yet complete enough to make a sharp prediction.

Where it stands

Documented: the formalism, and the results that made it a serious programme.

Not found: any experimental signature.

Not complete: the theory cannot yet recover the full standard model or make a sharp prediction.

Contested: whether the semiclassical limit works — whether it reproduces ordinary spacetime at large scales.

The honest label: live debate — a genuine research programme, judged on mathematics rather than data, for now.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's example of a claim that is entirely mainstream and entirely untested, and because the honest answer — 'we do not know whether this describes the world' — is the same answer the archive gives to much stranger claims, for different reasons.

Assembly Theory

A proposed measure of how complex an object is, by counting the minimum steps needed to build it. Its authors argue it explains selection and can detect life; its critics argue it measures construction, not causation.

The proposal

Assembly theory, developed by Lee Cronin and Sara Walker from 2017, assigns an 'assembly index' to a molecule: the minimum number of joining operations needed to build it from basic units. The claim is that objects with high assembly index must have been produced by a process of selection, because random assembly is astronomically unlikely, and that the index therefore gives an empirical signature of life and of evolution.

The 2023 paper in Nature reported measuring assembly indices by mass spectrometry and argued that the approach unifies selection, information and causation.

The objections

The criticisms are specific. The index measures the shortest construction path, which is a property of the object and of the chemist's choice of building blocks, not of its history. A crystal or a polymer can have a high index without selection. And the mass-spectrometry measurement of the index has been challenged as not actually recovering the quantity it claims.

The theory's defenders reply that the index applies to ensembles rather than single molecules, and that the objections miss the statistical framing. The exchange is ongoing and technical.

Where it stands

Documented: the index, its definition, and the published measurements.

Contested: whether the index tracks selection rather than construction.

Contested: whether the experimental method measures what it claims.

Not established: a general account of causation or of the origin of life.

The honest label: live debate — a serious proposal in an early, argumentative phase.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's most current page: a live scientific argument from the last three years, filed with the same caution as the historical ones, and because it is a good test of whether the archive can cover a debate before it is settled.

Blue Light and Circadian Damage

Short-wavelength light suppresses melatonin and shifts the body clock. That much is solid. The claim that screens damage the retina, or that blue-blocking glasses fix sleep, is where the evidence thins out.

What is established

Light in the short-wavelength ('blue') part of the spectrum is the strongest signal to the circadian system. Evening exposure suppresses melatonin, delays sleep onset and shifts the clock, and the effect has been measured in controlled studies with screens as well as with lamps. The mechanism runs through intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, discovered in the 2000s.

What is not

The retinal-damage claim comes from cell and animal studies using intensities far above any screen, and there is no evidence of screen-induced retinal damage in humans. The blue-blocking glasses market rests on the melatonin finding, but trials of the glasses for sleep and eye strain have been inconsistent, and reviews have found little or no benefit for most outcomes.

The practical finding that survives is unglamorous: dim the screen, stop using it close to bedtime, and get bright light in the morning. Those are behavioural, not optical.

Where it stands

Documented: short-wavelength light suppresses melatonin and shifts circadian timing.

Documented: the retinal ganglion cell pathway that mediates it.

Not supported: screen-induced retinal damage in humans.

Inconsistent: trials of blue-blocking lenses for sleep and eye strain.

The honest label: live debate about remedies, with the underlying physiology solid.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the mechanism is real, the market is built on it, and the intervention the market sells does not clearly work — which is the most common shape of a health claim.

Dark Flow

A 2008 analysis reported that galaxy clusters are all drifting toward a patch of sky beyond the observable universe. If true it would break the assumption that the universe looks the same in every direction. Later data did not confirm it.

The claim

In 2008 Alexander Kashlinsky and colleagues reported a 'dark flow': after subtracting the expected motion from the cosmic microwave background, clusters of galaxies appeared to share a bulk motion of several hundred kilometres per second toward a region in the sky. If real, the motion would be sourced by matter outside the observable universe, which would violate the assumption of isotropy on the largest scales.

The counter-evidence

The result depended on the cluster catalogue and on the subtraction of the microwave background's own motion, and reanalyses found the signal sensitive to both. Planck's data, with better calibration, did not reproduce it; a 2013 analysis using Planck found no significant bulk flow, and subsequent work with larger catalogues has been consistent with the standard cosmological model.

Where it stands

Reported: a bulk flow in 2008, from WMAP-era data.

Not confirmed: by Planck or by later cluster catalogues.

Sensitive to: catalogue selection and the CMB dipole subtraction.

Would require: structure beyond the observable horizon, which is not excluded in principle.

The honest label: live debate that has largely resolved against the original claim.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a rare case of a claim that would have rewritten cosmology, was reported widely, and then quietly failed to replicate — and because the archive should show what that looks like.

  • Wikipedia, “Peculiar velocity” — what a bulk flow isen.wikipedia.org

The Saqqara Bird

A wooden bird from an Egyptian tomb, about 2,200 years old, was said to be a model glider. It has no tail fin, no airfoil, and no evidence of ever having flown.

The object

The Saqqara bird was found in 1898 in a tomb at Saqqara and is dated to about 200 BC. It is carved from sycamore wood, about 18 cm long, with wings that are straight rather than curved. It is displayed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

In 1972 an Egyptian physician, Khalil Messiha, argued that it was a model aeroplane — a glider — and that its shape implied aerodynamic knowledge. The claim entered the ancient-technology literature and has been repeated ever since.

The analysis

The object lacks the features that make an aircraft. There is no vertical stabiliser, so it has no yaw control; the wings have no camber, so they generate no useful lift; and the body is too heavy for the wing area. Replicas built to the original dimensions glide poorly or not at all, and only fly when modified — with a tail fin added.

The Egyptological reading is that it is a bird model, of a type common in Egyptian tombs, probably a falcon or a similar species, and possibly a finial or a toy. Its wings are not shaped like a bird's in flight, which is the puzzle — but a puzzle is not an aircraft.

What is established

Documented: a wooden bird model from Saqqara, c. 200 BC, in the Egyptian Museum.

Documented: the 1972 aircraft claim, and the replicas built to test it.

Not supported: aerodynamic function. No tail, no camber, too heavy for its wing area.

Not supported: any evidence of aviation in ancient Egypt.

Why the label is debunked: the claim was tested by building the thing, and it did not fly.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archetypal out-of-place artefact: an object with an odd shape, read as technology, and settled by the cheapest possible experiment — a replica and a glide test.

The Phaistos Disc

A fired clay disc with 241 stamped signs in a spiral. It is genuinely undeciphered, and it is genuinely not evidence of Atlantis, aliens or a lost Atlantic script.

The object

The Phaistos Disc was found in 1908 in a Minoan palace context on Crete and dated to roughly 1700 BC. It is about 16 cm across, made of fired clay, and carries 241 impressions of 45 distinct signs arranged in a spiral on both faces. The signs were pressed with individual punches, which is unusual and implies a set of tools.

The decipherments

There are dozens of claimed decipherments, in Greek, Luwian, Semitic, an Atlantic language and others. None has been accepted, for a structural reason: the disc is a single short text with no bilingual, and any decipherment is therefore unconstrained by a second example. The same problem faces Linear A, which has hundreds of texts and is still unread.

The fringe readings — that it is a message from Atlantis, or a star map, or a record of an alien visit — are not decipherments at all. They are interpretations of the pictures, offered without a reading of the text.

What is established

Documented: the object, its date, its manufacture by stamped punches, and its signs.

Undeciphered: the text, and probably undecipherable without more material.

Not accepted: any of the dozens of claimed translations.

Not supported: Atlantis, aliens, or a lost Atlantic civilisation.

Why the label is debunked: the specific fringe claims are false; the disc itself remains an honest mystery, which is a different thing.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's best example of a real mystery that does not need a fantastic explanation — and because the fringe versions were invented to fill a gap that careful scholarship has the discipline to leave open.

Archimedes' Heat Ray

Mirrors on the walls of Syracuse, focusing sunlight onto Roman ships. The story is late, the physics is marginal, and the experiments have produced smoke and no fire.

The story

During the Roman siege of Syracuse in 212 BC, Archimedes is said to have used mirrors to focus sunlight on the Roman ships and set them alight. The story appears in late sources — the earliest detailed accounts are centuries after the event — and was repeated by medieval and Renaissance authors.

The tests

The experiments have been done repeatedly. In 1973 a Greek engineer, Ioannis Sakkas, set fire to a tarred wooden boat at about 50 metres using 70 mirrors, in calm conditions. In 2005 a team at MIT tested the idea with modern materials and concluded that a single mirror array could not ignite a ship at any plausible siege distance within a useful time. Television experiments have produced smoke at short range on stationary targets.

The conclusion is that the effect is possible under ideal conditions, and that a siege is not ideal conditions: ships move, the sun moves, the mirrors would need continuous aim, and the target would need to be dry and stationary.

Where it stands

Documented: Archimedes, the siege, and the late literary tradition of the mirrors.

Demonstrated: ignition at short range with many mirrors on a stationary target.

Not demonstrated: ignition at siege range under battle conditions.

Not established: that it happened. No contemporary source describes it.

The honest label: live debate about a physical possibility, with the historical evidence thin.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the physics is real, the engineering is marginal, and the history is later than the story — three separate weaknesses that are usually collapsed into one claim.

Greek Fire

A Byzantine incendiary that burned on water and was projected from ships. The recipe was a state secret, and it was kept: nobody knows exactly what it was.

The weapon

Greek fire was a Byzantine incendiary used from the seventh century, most famously against Arab fleets attacking Constantinople. It was projected through a bronze siphon mounted on a ship, and it burned on water — which is the property that made it terrifying and the property that identifies it chemically.

The composition was a state secret, restricted to a few families, and no contemporary recipe survives. Candidate ingredients include naphtha or crude petroleum, quicklime (which reacts with water and generates heat), sulphur, and resin. The exact mixture is unknown.

What can be said

Reconstructions burn on water, which is consistent with a petroleum base plus a calcium-based component. The 'unquenchable' reputation is partly propaganda and partly real: water spreads a petroleum fire rather than extinguishing it, and quicklime makes it worse.

The weapon's importance is not in dispute — it saved Constantinople more than once — and its chemistry is a genuine loss, because a technology that was deliberately kept secret left no technical record.

What is established

Documented: the weapon, its use, and its effect on sieges.

Documented: the siphon delivery system, from depictions and descriptions.

Unknown: the formula. No surviving recipe.

Plausible: a petroleum base with quicklime and sulphur.

The honest label: live debate about the chemistry of a weapon whose existence is not in doubt.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's example of a real ancient technology that is genuinely lost — and of how a state secret, kept well enough, becomes indistinguishable from a legend.

Damascus Steel

Blades with a watery pattern, made from crucible steel imported from India, and famous for sharpness. The technique was lost in the eighteenth century, and the nanoscale explanation is contested.

The steel

Damascus blades were forged from wootz — crucible steel made in India and Sri Lanka — and are recognisable by a banded, watery pattern on the surface. The pattern comes from the segregation of carbon and carbide-forming elements during slow cooling and forging, and it is a record of the process rather than a finish applied afterwards.

The reputation for sharpness and toughness is old and partly documented; the mechanical claims are harder to assess, because surviving blades vary and modern tests are few.

The loss and the explanation

The technique disappeared around the eighteenth century, probably because the ore sources and the trade in wootz changed. In 2006 a German team reported carbon nanotubes in a Damascus blade and proposed them as the explanation for its properties; the finding was striking and has been questioned, since nanotube formation in a forge is not obviously reproducible and later work has not confirmed it as the mechanism.

What is well supported is the carbide banding and the role of trace elements — vanadium, molybdenum, chromium — in producing it. The romance of the nanotubes is a good story attached to a real metallurgy.

Where it stands

Documented: the pattern, its metallurgical origin, and the wootz trade.

Documented: the loss of the technique in the eighteenth century.

Contested: the carbon-nanotube explanation of its properties.

Overstated: the 'cuts a falling silk scarf' reputation.

The honest label: live debate about mechanism, with the object itself not in doubt.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real technology with a real lost technique and a modern scientific claim attached — and because the difference between the two is exactly what the archive exists to mark.

Roman Concrete That Heals

Roman marine concrete has survived two thousand years of seawater. The explanation is lime clasts that crack, dissolve and recrystallise — and a 2023 study found a way to make it deliberately.

The material

Roman concrete used volcanic ash — pozzolana — with lime and aggregate. In seawater it formed aluminous tobermorite, a mineral that strengthens over time, which is why Roman harbour structures have outlasted modern ones.

The material's other property is self-healing. Lime clasts embedded in the concrete remain reactive: when a crack forms and water reaches them, they dissolve and recrystallise as calcium carbonate, sealing the crack.

The 2023 result

A team at MIT published an analysis in 2023 arguing that the lime clasts were not an impurity but a deliberate ingredient, made from quicklime rather than slaked lime, and demonstrated a modern concrete made the same way that healed its own cracks. That is the rare case of an ancient technology being not merely admired but understood and reproduced.

What is established

Documented: the durability of Roman marine concrete, and the mineral that explains it.

Documented: self-healing through lime clasts, observed and explained.

Documented: a modern reproduction that heals cracks.

Contested: how deliberate the Roman formulation was — the 2023 paper argues yes.

The honest label: documented. The mechanism is measured, and the reproduction works.

Why it is in the archive

Because the archive collects lost knowledge claims, and this is the one where the knowledge was recovered rather than romanticised — a useful counterweight to every page that says ancient people knew something we cannot.

The Iron Pillar of Delhi

A six-tonne iron pillar from the Gupta period that has barely rusted in 1,600 years. It is not a lost technology; it is phosphorus, and a dry climate.

The object

The pillar stands in the Qutb complex in Delhi. It is 7.2 metres tall, weighs about six tonnes, and carries a Sanskrit inscription identifying a Gupta king, dating it to the fourth or fifth century. It is roughly 99% iron, and its surface has corroded very little.

The explanation

The corrosion resistance comes from a thin layer of misawite — a phosphate-containing iron compound — that forms on the surface and passivates it. The phosphorus came from the ore and the smelting process; it is not a deliberate alloying addition, and the dry Delhi climate does the rest.

The 'rustless iron' framing is the romantic one. The metallurgy is impressive for its date — a large forged pillar of high-purity iron — but it is not evidence of a lost process. The phosphorus was an accident of the ore, and the same composition in a wet coastal climate would not have survived as well.

What is established

Documented: the pillar, its date, its mass, and its low corrosion.

Documented: the phosphate layer that explains the corrosion resistance.

Documented: the phosphorus source in the ore and the smelting.

Not established: a lost rust-proofing technology, or deliberate alloying.

The honest label: documented — a remarkable object with an ordinary explanation.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-loved 'ancient technology' claim in India, and the answer is more interesting than the myth: an accidental alloy, a good climate, and a thousand years of people noticing.

The Lycurgus Cup

A Roman glass cup that looks green in reflected light and red in transmitted light. It does this with gold and silver nanoparticles, which is nanotechnology by accident, fifteen centuries early.

The object

The Lycurgus Cup is a fourth-century Roman cage cup in the British Museum, decorated with a scene of Lycurgus. It is dichroic: it appears green when light reflects off it, and red when light shines through it. It is the only complete object of its kind known.

The explanation

Analysis in the 1990s found that the glass contains nanoparticles of gold and silver, roughly 50 nanometres across, in a ratio that produces the colour change through surface plasmon resonance. The effect depends on the size and separation of the particles, which the Roman glassmakers controlled without knowing why.

This is the standard example of 'ancient nanotechnology', and it is a fair description of the material — but not of the knowledge. The glassmakers had a recipe that worked, not a theory of plasmonics. The modern interest is in what can be learned from the recipe, not in what the Romans knew.

What is established

Documented: the cup, its date, and its dichroism.

Documented: the gold and silver nanoparticles and the plasmon mechanism.

Documented: that the effect was produced by a controlled process.

Not established: that the makers understood the mechanism.

The honest label: documented — a real achievement with a modern explanation, and a reminder that 'nanotechnology' is a description, not a claim about intent.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the counter-example to the out-of-place-artefact genre: an object that really does look impossible, whose explanation is a real scientific result rather than a fantasy.

The London Hammer

A hammer found encased in rock, said to be 400 million years old. The rock is a concretion that formed around a nineteenth-century tool, which is what the tool is.

The claim

In 1936 a couple near London, Texas, found a hammer embedded in a rock nodule. The rock was identified as Ordovician limestone, around 400 million years old, and the object became a creationist exhibit: evidence that humans existed before the geological column says they did.

The analysis

The hammer is a nineteenth-century pattern: a cast-iron head with a specific shape used by masons and miners, and a wooden handle of modern species. The 'rock' is a concretion — a mass of limestone that forms around an object left in lime-rich sediment or water, which can happen in decades. The handle has been dated and is recent; the iron is consistent with nineteenth-century manufacture.

The creationist literature has argued that the encasing rock is Ordovician, which would require the object to be that old. Concretions are exactly the mechanism by which recent objects end up inside old-looking rock, and the identification of the surrounding limestone does not date the object inside it.

What is established

Documented: the object, its find, and its nineteenth-century pattern.

Documented: concretions form around recent objects in lime-rich settings.

Documented: the handle is recent wood.

Not established: an Ordovician age for the hammer.

Why the label is debunked: the object is a known modern tool, and the mechanism that explains its position is well understood.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's clearest case of a geological mechanism being mistaken for a date, and because the mistake is instructive: the rock is old, the hammer is not, and the concretion is the sentence that joins them.

Pakal's Rocket

The carved lid of Pakal's sarcophagus at Palenque shows a figure in a complex posture. In 1968 it was read as an astronaut in a spaceship, which requires ignoring the Maya iconography around it.

The image

K'inich Janaab' Pakal was a Maya king of Palenque who died in 683 AD. His sarcophagus lid, carved in relief, shows a central figure in an elaborate posture, surrounded by iconography: a tree, a sky band, ancestral figures, and a border of glyphs.

In 1968 Erich von Däniken published a reading of the lid as an astronaut: the figure seated in a capsule, hands on controls, feet on pedals, with flames beneath. The image became one of the most reproduced in the ancient-astronaut literature.

The Maya reading

The iconography is well studied. The central figure is Pakal, shown at the moment of death and descent into the underworld, framed by the world tree — a standard Maya composition for a royal death and rebirth. The 'controls' are jewellery and gesture; the 'flames' are the stylised jaws of the underworld; the 'capsule' is the frame of the cosmos.

The reading requires no knowledge of Maya script or iconography, which is why it was possible. Scholars had read the scene decades before, and the glyphs around the lid identify the figures.

What is established

Documented: the lid, its date, its patron, and its iconography.

Documented: the Maya reading, supported by the glyphs and by comparable monuments.

Not established: any spacecraft, astronaut or technology.

Why it persists: because the image is dense and unfamiliar, and because a caption is easier than an iconographic argument.

Why the label is debunked: the alternative reading is documented, contemporaneous and supported by text.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most reproduced image in the ancient-astronaut genre, and the refutation is available in the same museum: the glyphs on the lid say who is on it.

How to use this bibliography

If you want to check a specific sentence, find the dossier it came from and follow the matching link. If a claim in the archive is not backed by one of these sources, it does not belong here — tell me and it will be removed or fixed.

For the creationist and flat-Earth material, the fringe sources are listed on purpose. The right way to assess an argument is to read it as its author wrote it, then read the response, then decide.

Keep the archive open

No ads, no accounts, no tracking, nothing for sale. Hosting, image licensing and the reading behind every dossier are paid out of pocket. If the archive earned its keep, you can put something back.

Nothing is gated behind it — every dossier stays free, unpaywalled and readable offline.
